Abstract: url: /article/10.1007/s00248-015-0724-2/metrics
          - text: Explore all metrics
    - region "Abstract":
      - heading "Abstract" [level=2]
      - paragraph:
        - text: Speculation surrounds the importance of ecologically cryptic Symbiodinium spp. (dinoflagellates) that occur at low abundances in reef-building corals and in the surrounding environment. Evidence acquired from extensive sampling, long-term monitoring, and experimental manipulation can allow us to deduce the ecology and functional significance of these populations and whether they might contribute to the response of coral-dinoflagellate mutualisms to climate change. Quantitative PCR was used here to diagnose the prevalence, seasonal variation, and abundances of Symbiodinium spp. within and between colonies of the coral, Alveopora japonica. Consistent with broader geographic sampling, only one species comprised 99.9 %, or greater, the population of symbionts in every sample. However, other Symbiodinium including the non-mutualistic species, Symbiodinium voratum, were often detected, but at estimated cell densities thousands-fold less than the dominant symbiont. The temporal variation in prevalence and abundances of these “background” Symbiodinium could not be definitively related to any particular environmental factor including seasonality and water chemistry. The prevalence (proportion detected among host samples), but not abundance, of S. voratum may weakly correspond to increases in environmental inorganic silica (SiO
        - subscript: "2"
        - text: ) and possibly nitrogen (NO
        - subscript: "3"
        - text: ). When multiple background Symbiodinium occurred within an individual polyp, the average cell densities were positively correlated, suggesting non-specific processes of cell sorting and retention by the animal.       - text: Every month from July 2012 to September 2013, we collected 30 colonies of A. japonica (4–7 cm in diameter, Fig.

      - link "1d":
        - /url: /article/10.1007/s00248-015-0724-2#Fig1

      - superscript: "2"
      - text: . Water samples were collected at the surface (~300 mL) for chemical analysis and the detection of Symbiodinium in the water column. Bottom water from around colonies of A. japonica was also collected in March 2013. Nutrient and chlorophyll a concentration analyses were conducted on these samples as described by [
      - link "Reference 40":

        - text: "40"
      - text: "]."

      - text: Colonies were transported to the laboratory at Seoul National University and then individually acclimated in 1-L glass beakers with filtered seawater (FSW) at a temperature range of 18–25 °C under a photon flux density of 50 μmol quanta m
      - superscript: −2
      - text: s
      - superscript: −1
      - text: (14 L/10D), simulating the corresponding temperature, salinity, and irradiance at the sampling site. These colonies were maintained for one to several days before further processing (see below).
    - paragraph:
      - text: Environmental water temperatures and salinities were measured at the site of sampling using a YSI Professional Plus instrument (YSI Inc., Yellow Springs, OH, USA). Sea surface temperature and chlorophyll a (as a proxy for phytoplankton abundance) data were acquired from the Giovanni online data system (
      - link "http://gdata1.sci.gsfc.nasa.gov/daac-bin/G3/gui.cgi?instance_id=mairs_monthly_hres":

      - text: ), mai
season: flagellate mutualisms to climate change. Quantitative PCR was used here to diagnose the prevalence, seasonal variation, and abundances of Symbiodinium spp. within and between colonies of the coral, Alveopora japonica. Consistent with broader geographic sampling, only one species comprised 99.9 %, or greater, the population of symbionts in every sample. However, other Symbiodinium including the non-mutualistic species, Symbiodinium voratum, were often detected, but at estimated cell densities thousands-fold less than the dominant symbiont. The temporal variation in prevalence and abundances of these “background” Symbiodinium could not be definitively related to any particular environmental factor including seasonality and water chemistry. The prevalence (proportion detected among host samples), but not abundance, of S. voratum may weakly correspond to increases in environmental inorganic silica (SiO
        - subscript: "2"
        - text: ) and possibly nitrogen (NO
        - subscript: "3"
        - text: ). When multiple background Symbiodinium occurred within an individual polyp, the average cell densities were positively correlated, suggesting non-specific processes of cell sorting and retention by the animal. While these findings substantiate the existence of a broader, yet uncharacterized, diversity of Symbiodinium, we conclude that only those species which can occur in high abundance and are temporally stable are ultimately important to coral-dinoflagellate mutualisms. Many transient Symbiodinium spp., which occur only at trace abundances in the coral’s microbiome, belong to different functional guilds and likely have little, if any, importance to a coral’s physiology. The successful integration between host and symbiont into a stable functional unit should therefore be considered when defining host-symbiont specificity.

Eligible design, but likely overlaps an included study

Lewis et al. (2024) clearly satisfies the biological criteria, but its Palau colonies and 2013–2022 sampling period appear likely to overlap the already-included Turnham et al. (2025) dataset. I would not add it as independent data without matching colony and sample identifiers:

Lewis, A. M., Butler, C. C., Turnham, K. E., Wham, D. F., Hoadley, K. D., Smith, R. T., Kemp, D. W., Warner, M. E., & LaJeunesse, T. C. (2024). The diversity, distribution, and temporal stability of coral ‘zooxanthellae’ on a Pacific reef: from the scale of individual colonies to across the host community. Coral Reefs, 43(4), 841–856. DOI.

Important exclusions included population-level resampling without colony identity (LaJeunesse et al. 2009; Boulotte et al. 2016; Lee et al. 2016) and aquarium, transplant or induced-bleaching experiments. “None stated” means no repository was reported in the article, not that unpublished data cannot exist.

Can you explain why these weren’t included? A reviewer specifically recommended that they should be. Rerun the search after evaluating these papers. You can modify search criteria slightly, but do not return studies that did not track colonies longitudinally, experimentally manipulated coral, or did not track colonies under field conditions.

Three of the reviewer’s four papers—Chen (2005), Kemp (2014), and LaJeunesse (2010)—were included in my previous results. The genuine omission was Cunning et al. (2016). I’ll verify its colony tracking and field protocol in full text, then rerun a broader search using the reviewer’s papers as citation seeds while retaining your three non-negotiable exclusions. I’m using the PDF/full-text workflow because abstracts alone often hide whether colonies were individually tracked or experimentally handled.

                                  89 heading Abstract, Value: 2
                                      90 text Abstract
                                  91 container
                                      92 text Both bacteria and algal symbionts (genus  Symbiodinium ), the two major microbial partners in the coral holobiont, respond to fluctuations in the environment, according to current reports; however, little evidence yet indicates that both populations have any direct interaction with each other in seasonal fluctuation. In this study, we present field observations of a compositional change in bacteria and  Symbiodinium  in the coral  Isopora palifera  in three separate coral colonies following monthly sampling from February to November in 2008. Using massively parallel pyrosequencing, over 200 000 bacterial V6 sequences were classified to build the bacterial community profile; in addition, the relative composition and quantity of  Symbiodinium  clades C and D were determined by real-time PCR. The results showed that coral-associated bacterial and  Symbiodinium  communities were highly dynamic and dissimilar among the tagged coral colonies, suggesting that the effect of host specificity was insignificant. The coral-associated bacterial community was more diverse (Shannon index up to 6.71) than previous estimates in other corals and showed rapid seasonal changes. The population ratios between clade C and D groups of  Symbiodinium  varied in the tagged coral colonies through the different seasons; clade D dominated in most of the samples. Although significant association between bacteria and symbiont was not detected, this study presents a more detailed picture of changes in these two major microbial associates of the coral at the same time, using the latest molecular approaches.
                                  93 container
                                      94 text Keywords:  coral, bacterial community,  Symbiodinium , metagenomics, tag pyrosequencing
                              95 container sec1
                                  96 heading Introduction, Value: 2
                                      97 text Introduction
                                  98 container
                                      99 text Corals generally associate with a variety of microorganisms, including algae, bacteria, archaea and viruses (
                                      100 link (collapsed) Description: Knowlton and Rohwer, 2003, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      101 text ; 
                                      102 link (collapsed) Description: Wegley et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      103 text ; 
                                      104 link (collapsed) Description: Marhaver et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      105 text ). Among these associated partners, the most well known are the algal symbionts (genus  Symbiodinium ) and various bacteria.  Symbiodinium  are photosynthetic algal symbionts providing energy for corals (
                                      106 link (collapsed) Description: Baker, 2003, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      107 text ). Based on their ribosomal DNA sequences,  Symbiodinium  can be categorized into eight distinct phylogenetic clades (A–H), five of which (A–D, F) are associated with corals (
                                      108 link (collapsed) Description: Baker, 2003, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      109 text ).  Symbiodinium  are geographically specific; the clades C and D are dominant in the corals dwelling in western Pacific Ocean, whereas other types are detected in other oceans, for example, the Caribbean Sea (
                                      110 link (collapsed) Description: Baker, 2003, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      111 text ).  Symbiodinium  are functionally diverse and, typically, display variations in tolerance against high temperature and irradiance (
                                      112 link (collapsed) Description: Baker, 2003, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      113 text ; 
                                      114 link (collapsed) Description: Stat et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      115 text ; 
                                      116 link (collapsed) Description: Mieog et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      117 text ; 
                                      118 link (collapsed) Description: Takahashi et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      119 text ). For instance,  Symbiodinium  clade D is more heat tolerant and is thus found more often in corals subject to conditions of higher temperature or irradiance (
                                      120 link (collapsed) Description: Baker, 2001, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      121 text ; 
                                      122 link (collapsed) Description: Rowen, 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      123 text ). Because of differences in the physiological characteristics of each type, the population composition of  Symbiodinium  in a coral may change under different environmental conditions, such as season (
                                      124 link (collapsed) Description: Chen et al., 2005, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      125 text ), latitude (
                                      126 link (collapsed) Description: LaJeunesse et al., 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      127 text ) and depth (
                                      128 link (collapsed) Description: Toller et al., 2001, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      129 text ; 
                                      130 link (collapsed) Description: Frade et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      131 text ).
                                  132 container
                                      133 text Coral-associated bacteria are highly diverse (
                                      134 link (collapsed) Description: Rohwer et al., 2002, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      135 text ) and their population compositions are affected by environmental factors such as geographic differences (
                                      136 link (collapsed) Description: Hong et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      137 text ; 
                                      138 link (collapsed) Description: Littman et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      139 text ), seasonal changes (
                                      140 link (collapsed) Description: Koren and Rosenberg, 2006, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      141 text ; 
                                      142 link (collapsed) Description: Hong et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      143 text ), coastal pollution (
                                      144 link (collapsed) Description: Klaus et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      145 text ) and nutrient status (
                                      146 link (collapsed) Description: Garren et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      147 text ). They potentially have functions relating to coral health, nutrition and disease (
                                      148 link (collapsed) Description: Reshef et al., 2006, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      149 text ; 
                                      150 link (collapsed) Description: Rosenberg et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      151 text ; 
                                      152 link (collapsed) Description: Wegley et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      153 text ), but their definitive role remains unclear. Many questions also remain about the dynamics of coral-associated bacteria. What factors affect their composition? What are the ecological implications of their compositions and dynamics?
                                  154 container
                                      155 text To determine the composition of a coral bacterial population, one of the most common methods has been construction of a 16S rRNA gene clone library (
                                      156 link (collapsed) Description: Amann et al., 1995, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      157 text ; 
                                      158 link (collapsed) Description: Rohwer et al., 2002, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      159 text ; 
                                      160 link (collapsed) Description: Lampert et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      161 text ; 
                                      162 link (collapsed) Description: Hong et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      163 text ; 
                                      164 link (collapsed) Description: Reis et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      165 text ). Surveying the range of bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences from such a library provides more detailed taxonomic information of bacterial community than other older methods. This culture-independent method has circumvented the difficulty of unculturable bacteria detection and offers considerable understanding of bacterial biodiversity and ecology (
                                      166 link (collapsed) Description: Amann et al., 1995, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      167 text ; 
                                      168 link (collapsed) Description: Rohwer et al., 2002, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      169 text ). However, the clone library method has long been limited in the number of colonies picked, mainly because of cost considerations (
                                      170 link (collapsed) Description: Rohwer et al., 2002, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      171 text ; 
                                      172 link (collapsed) Description: Lampert et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      173 text ; 
                                      174 link (collapsed) Description: Hong et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      175 text ; 
                                      176 link (collapsed) Description: Reis et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      177 text ). As a result, practical application of this method is unfeasible to present the profile of the very diverse bacterial communities found in most environmental samples. To define such a community more precisely, large survey size is crucial. For example, picking 1000 16S rRNA sequences from a clone library would be minimally sufficient to define a coastal bacterial community (
                                      178 link (collapsed) Description: Acinas et al., 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      179 text ). Similarly, with the current limitations on sampling number, studies of coral-associated bacterial communities with extensive temporal or spatial scales would be impossible.
                                  180 container
                                      181 text Massively parallel pyrosequencing (MPP) offers a high-throughput and cost-effective system for survey of bacterial communities by revealing the sequence of a hypervariable region of the 16S rRNA gene (
                                      182 link (collapsed) Description: Sogin et al., 2006, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      183 text ). Compared with the full-length rRNA gene sequence, the information from the hypervariable region sequence provides nearly equivalent taxonomic data (
                                      184 link (collapsed) Description: Huse et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      185 text ). This robust method has recently been employed to analyze the biodiversity of complex bacterial communities in different habitats such as the human gut (
                                      186 link (collapsed) Description: Huse et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      187 text ), hydrothermal vents (
                                      188 link (collapsed) Description: Huber et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      189 text ) and soil (
                                      190 link (collapsed) Description: Roesch et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      191 text ). Moreover, modifying the PCR primers with unique sequences in the sequencing reaction makes the method more economical and practical. DNA amplification with different unique-sequence-designed primers for each sample from different sources allows sequencing of all the amplicons from multiple sources in a single reaction run and still offers a sufficient number of sequences for the unbiased analysis of a bacterial community. The sequences in each sample can be simply sorted according to unique sequences of the primers (
                                      192 link (collapsed) Description: Binladen et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      193 text ; 
                                      194 link (collapsed) Description: Andersson et al., 2010, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      195 text ; 
                                      196 link (collapsed) Description: Barriuso et al., 2010, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      197 text ).
                                  198 container
                                      199 text In this study, we adopted the MPP technique and a newly improved quantitative PCR method to study the dynamics of bacterial and symbiotic algal communities in  Isopora palifera  with a monthly sampling survey from February to November in 2008. These rich data sets have provided much detail about the dynamics of these two microbial communities, bacteria and  Symbiodinium .
                              200 container sec2
                                  201 heading Materials and methods, Value: 2
                                      202 text Materials and methods
                                  203 container
                                      204 text The experimental methods used to analyze the composition of microorganisms in coral  I. palifera  are illustrated in Supplementary Figure S1, which presents a flowchart of the procedure from bench work to bioinformatics analysis.
                                  205 container sec3
                                      206 heading Study site and sampling, Value: 3
                                          207 text Study site and sampling
                                      208 container
                                          209 text Coral samples and seawater samples were collected from Tan-Tzei Bay (21°57′N, 120°46′E), Ken-Ting National Park, located in Heng-Chun Township at the southern tip of Taiwan. Three colonies of the coral  I. palifera , at 2 to 3 m depth, were tagged as 351, 352 and 353.  I. palifera  is a plate form in this area (Supplementary Figure S6). Near the tagged coral colonies, we deposited a thermograph to record water temperature.
                                      210 text All tagged colonies were sampled near-monthly for the 7 months of February (winter), April (spring), May (spring), June (summer), July (summer), August (summer) and November (winter) in 2008. Coral fragments (∼2 × 2 cm) were collected with hammer and chisel. In addition, 1000 ml sea water was collected from the area near the tagged colonies.
                                      211 text Coral samples were washed twice with sterile synthetic sea water and then sprayed with TE buffer (10 m Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 1 m EDTA, pH 8.0) to collect the tissue, using an airbrush. Coral tissue was stored in liquid nitrogen until DNA extraction. Seawater samples were filtered through membrane paper (pore size 0.2 μm; Adventec, Tokyo, Japan) to collect the microbial particles. After filtering, the paper was kept at −20 °C until DNA extraction.
                                  212 container sec4
                                      213 heading DNA extraction, Value: 3
                                          214 text DNA extraction
                                      215 text The coral tissues were recovered from the TE buffer by centrifugation; after discarding the supernatant, tissue pellets were then resuspended with 1 ml TE buffer, and homogenized in a mortar and pestle with liquid nitrogen. The homogenized solution was transferred to a clean tube, and total DNAs were extracted with a PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit (MoBio, Solana Beach, CA, USA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. To isolate the total DNAs of seawater samples, the filter membrane paper with adsorbed microbial sample was cut into smaller pieces and placed into a clean tube, and the total DNA again extracted using a PowerSoil DNA Isolation Kit (MoBio). Finally, the DNA was resuspended in 150 μl sterile Milli-Q water, aliquoted into PCR microtubes (each tube 10 μl) and stored at −80 °C.
                                  216 container sec5
                                      217 heading PCR of bacterial V6 hypervariable region of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene and DNA tagging PCR, Value: 3
                                          218 text PCR of bacterial V6 hypervariable region of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene and DNA tagging PCR
                                      219 container
                                          220 text For amplification of the bacterial V6 hypervariable region of the 16S ribosomal RNA gene, two bacterial universal primers were used: 967F, 5′-CAACGCGAAGAACCTTACC-3′ and 1046R, 5′-CGACAGCCATGCANCACCT-3′ (
                                          221 link (collapsed) Description: Sogin et al., 2006, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          222 text ) with the following PCR conditions: an initial step of 94 °C for 3 min, 30 cycles of 94 °C for 30 s, 57 °C for 10 s and 72 °C for 30 s, followed by a final step of 72 °C for 2 min. The amplification mixture contained 0.5 μl of 5 U  TaKaRa Ex Taq  HS (Takara Bio, Otsu, Japan), 5 μl of 10 ×  Ex Taq  buffer, 4 μl of 2.5 m deoxynucleotide triphosphate mixture, 1 μl of each primer (10 μ) and 5 μl (10–20 ng) template DNA in a volume of 50 μl. The PCR amplicons of the V6 region were checked by 15% native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis with TAE buffer. The expected DNA band (∼100 bp) was cut and DNA extracted by electroelution (
                                          223 link (collapsed) Description: Sambrook and Russell, 2001, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          224 text ). The quality of the purified product was assayed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific, Vantaa, Finland).
                                      225 text DNA tagging PCR (DT-PCR) was used to add unique tags to each of the PCR products isolated from different samples (Supplementary Figure S2a). Each tag primer was designed with four overhanging nucleotides at the 5′ end of the 967F and 1046R primers. The arrangements of the four nucleotides ensured 256 different kinds of unique tags. In this study, 28 unique tags were used for DT-PCR.
                                      226 container
                                          227 text In DT-PCR, the PCR products from individual sample were extended with different unique-tagged primer sets by low-cycle PCR under the following conditions: an initial 94 °C for 3 min, then 5 cycles of 94 °C for 30 s, 57 °C for 10 s and 72 °C for 30 s, followed by 72 °C for 2 min. The DT-PCR mixture contained 0.5 μl of 5 U  TaKaRa Ex Taq  HS, 5 μl of 10 ×  Ex Taq  Buffer, 4 μl of 2.5 m deoxynucleotide triphosphates, 1 μl of each primer (10 μ) and 20 μl (50–100 ng) V6 amplicon in a volume of 50 μl. To confirm the success of the tagging reaction, we checked the PCR products after DT-PCR using non-denatured polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis on 15% gels run at 100 V for 6 h and stained with SYBR-Gold (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). In comparison with the V6 PCR products, the tagged V6 DNA would shift to a higher position in the gel because of their larger molecular mass (Supplementary Figure S2b). Once the tagging reaction was successful, we then purified the tagged amplicon DNAs using PCR Purification Kits (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA). The qualities and concentrations of the purified tagged DNA samples were determined using NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo Scientific).
                                  228 container sec6
                                      229 heading Parallel pyrosequencing, Value: 3
                                          230 text Parallel pyrosequencing
                                      231 container
                                          232 text Pooled 200 ng lots of each tagged V6 DNA samples (28 samples in total) were used for parallel pyrosequencing on a Roche 454 Genome Sequencer FLX System at Mission Biotech (Taipei, Taiwan). Ambiguous reads were trimmed off if the sequences had mismatched sequences to the forward and reverse primers or the sequences were shorter than 75 bases. A total of 205 082 sequences were generated and sorted according to unique tags using an in-house sorting tool (
                                          233 link Description: External, opens in a new tab. http://tanglab.csie.org/~tanglab/proj1/, Value: tanglab.csie.org/~t…
                                          234 text ).
                                  235 container sec7
                                      236 heading Value: 3, Determination of Symbiodinium population by PCR length heteroplasmy (PCR-LH) analysis and quantitative PCR
                                          237 text Determination of 
                                          238 text Symbiodinium
                                          239 text  population by PCR length heteroplasmy (PCR-LH) analysis and quantitative PCR
                                      240 container
                                          241 text For PCR heteroplasmy analysis, we designed new primers specific for clades C and D of algal symbionts: SymITS2-F (5′-TATGTYTGCTTCAGTGCTTA-3′), Clade-C-ITS2-R (5′-AATTAACAAGCCATTGGC-3′), and Clade-D-ITS2-R (5′-ACTCAGCAAGCCATGGGC-3′) according to the internal transcribed spacer 2 (ITS2) region sequences of  Symbiodinium  from the NCBI (National Center for Biotechnology Information) database (Supplementary Figure S3). The PCR mixture contained 0.5 μl of 5 U  TaKaRa Ex Taq  HS, 5 μl of 10 ×  Ex Taq  Buffer, 4 μl of 2.5 m deoxynucleotide triphosphate mixture, 1 μl of 10 μ SymITS2-F, 0.5 μl of 10 μ Clade-C-ITS2-R, 0.5 μl of 10 μ Clade-D-ITS2-R and 2–5 ng template DNA in a total volume of 50 μl. The amplified condition had the following steps: an initial 94 °C for 3 min, then 35 cycles of 94 °C for 30 s, 50 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 20 s, and finally 72 °C for 2 min.
                                      242 text After the DNA of ITS2 partial region was amplified, 4 μl of the PCR products of each sample was mixed with 4 μl of 2 × DNA loading dye (0.05% bromophenol blue, 0.05% xylene cyanol, 20 m EDTA and 10% glycerol), and analyzed by electrophoresis on 15% polyacrylamide gels with 7  urea. Gels were run at 85 V for 16 h in 0.5 × Tris-borate–EDTA (TBE) buffer (45 m Tris-borate and 1 m EDTA) at a constant temperature of 55 °C and stained with SYBR-Gold. The relative intensities of each expected band (clades C and D) were quantified using ImageQuant TL (Amersham Bioscience, GE Healthcare, Waukesha, WI, USA).
                                      243 container
                                          244 text For the quantitative PCR analysis (Q-PCR), we designed two pairs of specific primers for the ITS1 partial region (∼100 bp) of  Symbiodinium  clades C and D according to the ITS1 region sequences of  Symbiodinium  from the NCBI database. Three primers were designed: QPCR ITS1-F (5′-TGCGGAAGGATCATTCGCAC-3′) for both algal symbiont populations, and QPCR-SymITSC-R (5′-CCTCGAGTTCTGCCAGCAGAT-3′) specific for clade C and QPCR-SymITSD-R (5′-TGAACGCGCATCTCACCACTG-3′) specific for clade D. To avoid pipette error, the total DNA of the coral sample was diluted ninefold before Q-PCR: 10 μl DNA was mixed with 80 μl ddH 2 O. The Q-PCR reaction solution contained 9 μl of diluted coral tissue total DNA, 0.2 μ of QPCR ITS1-F (universal primer), 0.2 μ of QPCR-SymITSC-R (for clade C) or QPCR-SymITSD-R (for clade D) and 1 × SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA) in a total volume of 20 μl. Q-PCR analysis was performed in an ABI 7300 Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) under the following conditions: 50 °C for 2 min, 95 °C for 10 min; 40 cycles of 95 °C for 10 s and 62 °C for 27 s, followed by 95 °C for 15 s, 60 °C for 1 min, 95 °C for 15 s, and 60 °C for 15 s for the dissociation step. A standard curve was constructed with a series dilution of template DNA from ITS PCR products of known concentration. The data were analyzed using ABI 7300 System SDS Software (Applied Biosystems).
                                  245 container sec8
                                      246 heading Diversity indices and OTU definition, Value: 3
                                          247 text Diversity indices and OTU definition
                                      248 container
                                          249 text We aligned sequences from individual samples using MUSCLE software (
                                          250 link Description: External, opens in a new tab. http://www.drive5.com/muscle/, Value: drive5.com/muscle/
                                          251 text ) and calculated distances matrices based on the Juke–Cantor model. The distance matrices were then used as input to the DOTUR software (
                                          252 link (collapsed) Description: Schloss and Handelsman, 2005, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          253 text ) to define the operational taxonomic units (OTUs) with a 3% cutoff value and to estimate the Shannon-Weaver diversity index, Chao1 estimator and Simpson index, and to construct rarefaction curves. Calculations of evenness and richness were also based on the number of OTUs.
                                  254 container sec9
                                      255 heading Taxonomic identification of bacterial V6 sequences, Value: 3
                                          256 text Taxonomic identification of bacterial V6 sequences
                                      257 container
                                          258 text We identified the taxonomic information of the V6 sequences (205 082 reads) using Ribosomal Data Project (RDP) SeqMatch software (
                                          259 link Description: External, opens in a new tab. http://rdp.cme.msu.edu/seqmatch/seqmatch_intro.jsp, Value: rdp.cme.msu.edu/seq…
                                          260 text ) with 5 KNN match. Those sequences identified as ‘unclassified bacteria' by SeqMatch were reconfirmed using an in-house program, Greedy Fetching (GF; C-H Tseng  et al. , unpublished), based on the BLASTn results to assign taxonomy of V6 reads with a similarity threshold of 0.7 and the approved hits were all at lease with 0.91 alignment identity, which is enough to define taxonomy at class level. GF provided a more extensive calculation in sequence similarity searching and enabled us to detect missing information that could not be determined using SeqMatch. The outcome of GF was merged with the results of the RDP SeqMatch analysis.
                                      261 text To analyze the dynamics of the coral-associated bacteria community in the different months, we examined 45 314 unique groups from 205 082 V6 sequences according to sequence similarity; any mismatch or inserted or deleted base between two V6 sequences was regarded as a different unique V6 sequence group. Through plotting and comparing these unique groups in the monthly samples, we were able to survey more detailed information of the compositional changes of the bacterial community. The unique sequence groups were classified taxonomically into different groups at the class level by SeqMatch and GF.
                                  262 container sec10
                                      263 heading Non-metric multidimensional scaling (nMDS) ordination, Value: 3
                                          264 text Non-metric multidimensional scaling (nMDS) ordination
                                      265 container
                                          266 text The relationships among samples were determined by the statistical method, nMDS ordination (
                                          267 link (collapsed) Description: Kenkel and Orlóci, 1986, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          268 text ), using each different V6 sequence group as an OTU. To refine OTUs, we aligned these 45 314 unique group sequences from all samples using the program MUSCLE (
                                          269 link Description: External, opens in a new tab. http://www.drive5.com/muscle/, Value: drive5.com/muscle/
                                          270 text ) and calculated distance matrices based on the Juke–Cantor model. These distance matrices were input to DOTUR software (
                                          271 link (collapsed) Description: Schloss and Handelsman, 2005, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          272 text ) to define the OTUs with a 3% cutoff value. This calculation estimated 11 236 OTUs. Then, the relative percentages of each OTU in each sample were incorporated into a matrix to estimate a distance matrix (via City-Block distance) to present the nMDS profile using Primer 6 software (PRIMER-E, Lutton, Ivybridge, UK).
                                  273 container sec11
                                      274 heading Hierarchical cluster analysis, Value: 3
                                          275 text Hierarchical cluster analysis
                                      276 container
                                          277 text Hierarchical cluster analysis was used to analyze the relationship between environmental factors (seawater temperature, sunlight intensity and rainfall), bacterial community and symbiotic algal population. We used the software Gene Cluster 3.0 (
                                          278 link (collapsed) Description: de Hoon et al., 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          279 text ) from 
                                          280 link Description: External, opens in a new tab. http://www.falw.vu/~huik/cluster.htm, Value: falw.vu/~huik/clust…
                                          281 text  to construct the clusters. The population ratio of each bacterial group was derived from the sequence data sets (classified by SeqMatch and GF at the class level), and the population proportion of the two symbiotic algal groups was determined according to the Q-PCR data sets. Data on sunlight intensity and rainfall were collected from the Central Weather Bureau of Taiwan in Heng-Chun Township, at the southern tip of Taiwan. In the hierarchical cluster analysis, the distance matrix was constructed with normalized data. To normalize the data, we deducted the raw value of each data point from the relevant mean value and then divided by the standard deviation. The cluster constructed was based on the distance matrix with the uncentered correlation distance and complete linkage, two options in Gene Cluster 3.0 (
                                          282 link (collapsed) Description: de Hoon et al., 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          283 text ). We then visualized the clustering map using Java Treeview software, downloaded from 
                                          284 link Description: External, opens in a new tab. http://jtreeview.sourceforge.net/, Value: jtreeview.sourcefor…
                                          285 text , with a contrast value of 1.5 to enhance readability.
                              286 container sec12
                                  287 heading Results, Value: 2
                                      288 text Results
                                  289 container sec13
                                      290 heading I. palifera-associated bacterial community and its diversity, Value: 3
                                          291 text I. palifera
                                          292 text -associated bacterial community and its diversity
                                      293 container
                                          294 text Coral samples of three tagged  I. palifera  colonies were collected near-monthly in 2008 (from February to November) at Tan-Zi Bay in Ken-Ting National Park, Taiwan. The V6 hypervariable regions of bacterial 16S ribosomal RNA genes were surveyed to determine bacterial community composition of the monthly samples. After V6 DNA amplification by PCR with universal primers and DNA tagging (Supplementary Figure S2), we performed MPP to acquire sequence data.
                                      295 container
                                          296 text The number of V6 sequences in each sample varied from 657 to 21 091 (
                                          297 link Description: Table 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          298 text ); however, the rarefaction curves (with a 3% cutoff value) of the samples showed that the sampling size (read number) was generally sufficient (Supplementary Figure S4).
