                                      896 container
                                          897 text I. palifera -associated bacterial communities were highly diverse (
                                          898 link Description: Table 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          899 text ). Shannon's index ranged from 3.64 to 6.71 in the coral samples and from 3.85 to 6.32 in the sea water. Simpson's index in coral samples ranged from 0.009 to 0.069 and in sea water ranged from 0.006 to 0.037. Student's  t -test was used to describe the difference between coral and seawater samples. The  P -value was 0.96 in Shannon's index and 0.94 in Simpson's index. There was no significant difference in Shannon's and Simpson's indices between the coral and seawater samples. In addition, the seasonal tendency of the diversity indices was irregular. Overall, the bacterial communities in both coral and seawater samples were highly diverse.
                                  900 container sec14
                                      901 heading Composition of I. palifera-associated bacterial community, Value: 3
                                          902 text Composition of 
                                          903 text I. palifera
                                          904 text -associated bacterial community
                                      905 container
                                          906 text The most abundant bacterial groups in the coral or seawater samples were  Alphaproteobacteria  (10–50%) and  Gammaproteobacteria  (12–50%); however, the specific composition of each bacterial community in the coral tissues clearly differed from the sea water (
                                          907 link Description: Figure 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          908 text ). There were more bacteria of  Betaproteobacteria ,  Actinobacteria ,  Acidobacteria  and  Nitrospira  groups in the coral tissues, whereas seawater samples had more bacteria in the  Flavobacteria  and  Cyanobacteria  groups (
                                          909 link Description: Figure 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          910 text ).
                                      911 container fig1
                                          912 heading Figure 1., Value: 4
                                              913 text Figure 1.
                                          914 link Description: Figure 1 🔍, Value: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/co…
                                          915 link Description: Open in a new tab, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          916 container
                                              917 text Bacterial composition profile. The bacterial compositions were analyzed using two methods, SeqMatch alone online at RDP ( a ) and a combination method, SeqMatch-Greedy Fetching (GF) ( b ). ( a ) With SeqMatch, high proportions (5–50%) of unclassified bacteria were detected in the samples. ( b ) With SeqMatch-GF method, the unclassified bacteria were reduced to <5%. In these figures, bacteria composition in  I. palifera  was different from sea water, and the bacterial composition in  I. palifera  varied in different coral colonies and at different months.
                                      918 container
                                          919 text In our study, high proportions (5–50%) of unclassified bacteria were detected in the coral samples using the program SeqMatch from the RDP; in contrast, the seawater samples contained only approximately 5% unclassified bacteria (
                                          920 link Description: Figure 1a, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          921 text ). To confirm this observation, we assessed the same data sets using a self-developed method, the GF technique (see Materials and methods). In the coral samples, GF reassigned 32 655 unclassified sequences in the RDP SeqMatch analysis to different taxonomic classes; in all, 28 508 (87%) unclassified sequences were reassigned to known taxa (
                                          922 link Description: Figure 1b, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          923 text ). In seawater samples, 4790 sequences were assigned to unclassified bacteria by RDP SeqMatch. After GF analysis, these were reduced to 1174 sequences of unclassified bacteria (75% unclassified sequences reassigned to known taxa; 
                                          924 link Description: Figure 1b, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          925 text ).
                                      926 container
                                          927 text In addition, by GF refinement, we discovered a group of novel bacteria, which was closely related to  Chlamydia  (
                                          928 link Description: Figures 1a and b, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          929 text ). The  Chlamydia -like bacteria (CLB; 88% similarity to  Chlamydia  based on NCBI database) were specifically found only in the coral samples. This bacterial group was the major population (up to 33%) of bacterial communities in the coral samples.
                                  930 container sec15
                                      931 heading The distribution profile of unique bacterial V6 sequence group, Value: 3
                                          932 text The distribution profile of unique bacterial V6 sequence group
                                      933 container
                                          934 text We used the unique V6 sequence group profiles to analyze the bacterial composition below the class level to detect dominant bacteria and their population changes. Overall, most of the bacterial groups in the coral or seawater samples remained minor components of the population most of the time. It was evident, however, that a few particular bacterial groups in the coral samples, such as CLB,  Rhodobacteraceae ,  Sphingomonadales ,  Escherichia ,  Pseudomonas  and  Chroococcidiopsis , largely appear at particular times; however, they became dominant for only brief periods of time (
                                          935 link Description: Figure 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          936 text ). In the seawater samples, SAR11 was the constant predominant group (comprising 3–4% of total bacteria in most months).
                                      937 container fig2
                                          938 heading Figure 2., Value: 4
                                              939 text Figure 2.
                                          940 link Description: Figure 2 🔍, Value: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/co…
                                          941 link Description: Open in a new tab, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          942 container
                                              943 text The V6 unique sequence groups in each sample. This profile illustrates dominant bacteria groups and how bacterial communities changed. Variations in the composition of bacterial community within each of the coral samples was rapid and mainly resulted in temporary predominance of bacteria such as  Rhodobacteraceae ,  Sphingomonadales ,  Escherichia  and CLB. The  y  axis shows the percentage of each unique group in each sample from three colonies and sea water. The color bars on  x  axis indicate the taxonomy of the bacteria. Each vertical black bar signifies the proportion (%) of a unique bacterial group (labeled). Some dominant groups could not be defined to Family; therefore, these groups were labeled with class name (such as CLB and  Deltaproteobacteria ) or cluster name (such as SAR11).
                                      944 container
                                          945 text The variation of the composition of bacterial community within each of the coral samples was mainly because of the temporary predominance of a particular bacteria with a considerable population. For instance, the increase of  Gammaproteobacteria  in April and May (
                                          946 link Description: Figure1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          947 text  and Supplementary Figure S5) was caused by an increase in  Escherichia  (
                                          948 link Description: Figure 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          949 text ). In colonies 352 and 353, the increase of  Alphaproteobacteria  in June (Supplementary Figure S5) was caused by an increase in  Rhodobacteraceae  (
                                          950 link Description: Figure 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          951 text ). In colony 352, the spike of  Deltaproteobacteria  (20%) in June resulted from increasing presence of an unclassified  Deltaproteobacterial  group. Similarly, the enrichment of  Cyanobacteria  in February (
                                          952 link Description: Figure1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          953 text  and Supplementary Figure S5) resulted from  Chroococcidiopsis  (
                                          954 link Description: Figure 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          955 text ).
                                      956 container
                                          957 text In addition, the distribution profile of unique bacterial V6 sequence groups provided a more detailed resolution of changes in the bacterial community when compared with an analysis of bacterial groups based on higher taxonomic levels (for example, Class; 
                                          958 link Description: Figure 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          959 text ). In the seawater samples,  Gammaproteobacteria  was the major group in February and August; however, the compositions of  Gammaproteobacteria  in these two months were distinct.  Acinetobacter  was the most abundant  Gammaproteobacterial  group in February, but  Alteromonas  was most abundant in August (
                                          960 link Description: Figure 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          961 text ). Similarly, in colony 352,  Gammaproteobacteria  was the major group in June and July; however, the compositions of  Gammaproteobacteria  in these two months were distinct.  Rhodobacter  was predominant in June, whereas  Sphingomonadale  predominated in July. CLB was abundant in May and November in colony 352; however, the predominant group of CLB in May was different to that in November. On the contrary, in colony 351, the predominant groups of CLB remained the same in all months.
                                  962 container sec16
                                      963 heading Comparison of I. palifera-associated bacterial communities, Value: 3
                                          964 text Comparison of 
                                          965 text I. palifera
                                          966 text -associated bacterial communities
                                      967 container
                                          968 text Based on sequence similarity, a total of 11 236 OTUs were classified by DOTUR using the Juke–Cantor model with a cutoff value of 3%. The OTU percentages in each sample were incorporated into the nMDS matrix and analyzed by city-block distance. The coral-associated bacterial communities were relatively closer to each other and significantly different from the bacterial community of the sea water in the two-dimensional nMDS map, which also supports the result of the analysis of the bacterial taxonomy (
                                          969 link Description: Figure 3, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          970 text ).
                                      971 container fig3
                                          972 heading Figure 3., Value: 4
                                              973 text Figure 3.
                                          974 link Description: Figure 3 🔍, Value: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/co…
                                          975 link Description: Open in a new tab, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          976 text Non-metric multidimensional scaling ordination (nMDS) analysis. We used the relative percentages of each OTU (at 3% cutoff value) in each sample to perform nMDS mapping (see Materials and methods). In this map, each dot signifies the bacterial population of an individual sample. The square boxes show coral samples, and blue circles show seawater samples. In the coral samples, different colors represent different months. The coral-associated bacterial communities were relatively close to each other and significantly different from the bacterial community of the sea water. Moreover, the bacterial compositions of the coral samples collected in the same month tended to cluster together. The color reproduction of this figure is available on the html full text version of the manuscript.
                                      977 container
                                          978 text In addition, the bacterial communities of the coral samples collected in the same month clustered together closely (
                                          979 link Description: Figure 3, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          980 text ). The bacterial compositions of the samples of spring and summer were more similar to each other, whereas the winter samples also congregated together.
                                  981 container sec17
                                      982 heading Symbiodinium communities, Value: 3
                                          983 text Symbiodinium
                                          984 text  communities
                                      985 container
                                          986 text Two methods, PCR-LH and Q-PCR, were adopted to quantify the population of  Symbiodinium  clades C and D (symbiotic algae). Initially, we adopted the PCR-LH technique to detect the population proportions of two  Symbiodinium  clades. Two distinguishable specific PCR products (102 and 96 bp) of ITS2 region of clades C or D were analyzed using urea-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (Supplementary Figure S7a). The relative proportions of these two populations in the coral samples were determined by band intensity. The histogram shows the profile of the C/D ratio in the different coral samples and months (Supplementary Figure S7b). In colony 351, clade D was the constant predominant group in all the samples, and the symbiotic algal communities were more stable than those in colonies 352 and 353.
                                      987 container
                                          988 text Using specific primers based on the indel mutation region in ITS1 of clades C and D, we performed three independent Q-PCRs to confirm the result of PCR-LH. The Q-PCR results (
                                          989 link Description: Figure 4, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          990 text ) were similar to those from PCR-LH (Supplementary Figure S7). However, inaccuracy of the relative ratio of clades C and D occurred when using PCR-LH because that technique failed to represent the correct measured value if the band's color intensity exceeded the saturation threshold, and the proportion of an abundant group was therefore underestimated. For instance, in 351-Feb, the clade D proportion was estimated at ∼80% and 99% in PCR-LH and Q-PCR analysis, respectively. On the other hand, in 352-Apr, the clade C proportion was estimated to be 60% in PCR-LH but 80% in Q-PCR.
                                      991 container fig4
                                          992 heading Figure 4., Value: 4
                                              993 text Figure 4.
                                          994 link Description: Figure 4 🔍, Value: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/co…
                                          995 link Description: Open in a new tab, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          996 container
                                              997 text Symbiodinium  population analysis by real-time quantitative-PCR. Two populations of  Symbiodinium  clades C and D were determined by real-time quantitative PCR of the ITS. All the coral colonies contained both clades C and D but the relative proportion of the  Symbiodinium  members varied at different times and between coral colonies. In April, the temperature shifting point, there was a sharp increase in the clade C population (>60% proportion) in colonies 352 and 353. However, the  Symbiodinium  spp. population of colony 351 was dominated by clade D (>98% proportion) throughout our survey. The green bar is the proportion of clade C and the blue bar is the proportion of clade D. The right  y  axis is percentage and the left  y  axis is temperature (°C). The color reproduction of this figure is available on the html full text version of the manuscript.
                                      998 container
                                          999 text According to the results of Q-PCR and PCR-LH, all coral colonies contained both clades C and D (
                                          1000 link Description: Figure 4, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1001 text  and Supplementary Figure S7). In April, there was a sharp increase in the clade C population (>60% proportion) in colonies 352 and 353. However, the  Symbiodinium  spp. population of colony 351 was dominated by clade D (>98% proportion) throughout our survey (
                                          1002 link Description: Figure 4, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1003 text ). Take together, these results show that  Symbiodinium  composition in  I. palifera  varied at different times and that the extent of this effect varied in different colonies.
                                  1004 container sec18
                                      1005 heading Hierarchical clustering analysis, Value: 3
                                          1006 text Hierarchical clustering analysis
                                      1007 container
                                          1008 text We used hierarchical clustering analysis to examine the relationships between environmental factors (seawater temperature, sunlight intensity and rainfall), bacterial community and symbiotic algal population. The proportion of  Clostridia  reached a maximum in April, whereas proportions of  Chlorobia  and  Chloroflexi  were high in February and April. Rainfall and the population of  Bacilli  had a similar profile (
                                          1009 link Description: Figure 5, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1010 text ), which supported the association of a high  Bacilli  proportion with rainfall (Supplementary Figure S8). There were no associations between seawater temperature or sunlight intensity and the variation of various bacterial groups at the class level (
                                          1011 link Description: Figure 5, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1012 text ). The proportion of  Symbiodinium  clade C increased in April, whereas the clade D proportion decreased at the same time. The changes in  Symbiodinium  proportion were not similar to the variation of bacterial groups at the class level (
                                          1013 link Description: Figure 5, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1014 text ).
                                      1015 container fig5
                                          1016 heading Figure 5., Value: 4
                                              1017 text Figure 5.
                                          1018 link Description: Figure 5 🔍, Value: ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/co…
                                          1019 link Description: Open in a new tab, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1020 container
                                              1021 text Hierarchical cluster analysis. Single-way clustering method was used to dissect relationships between the abundance of 35 individual bacterial groups at class level, the abundance of  Symbiodinium  (containing both clades C and D) and environmental parameters (seawater temperature, sunlight intensity and rainfall) in the seven months of February, April, May, June, July, August and November. Lighter colors (yellow) mean more members of the bacterial and  Symbiodinium  group detected, or higher values of environmental conditions. Darker colors (dark blue) mean fewer bacteria or  Symbiodinium  or lower values of environmental conditions. In this map, rainfall and population of  Bacilli  were correlated. Potential nitrogen fixation bacteria ( Cyanobacteria ,  Clostridia ,  Chlorobia  and  Chloroflexi ) were enriched in February and April. The proportion of symbiont clade C was increased in April. Heat map intensities were calculated from normalized data (see Materials and methods) with the uncentered correlation distance and complete linkage, the two options in the Gene Cluster 3.0. Blue: potential nitrogen fixation bacteria, labeled by  * . Red: environmental factors, seawater temperature, sunlight intensity and rainfall. Orange: the  Symbiodinium  clades. The color reproduction of this figure is available on the html full text version of the manuscript.
                              1022 container sec19
                                  1023 heading Discussion, Value: 2
                                      1024 text Discussion
                                  1025 container
                                      1026 text In this study, we suggest that both bacterial and  Symbiodinium  populations in the coral  I. palifera  vary at different times and to different extents in different colonies; notably, the compositional changes of bacterial community are likely to be associated with seasonal changes. The extensive information provided by the recently developed technique of MPP clearly defines monthly changes of the coral-associated bacterial community that were unavailable in previous surveys using older methods or shorter sampling timescales (
                                      1027 link (collapsed) Description: Rohwer et al., 2002, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      1028 text ; 
                                      1029 link (collapsed) Description: Koren and Rosenberg, 2006, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      1030 text ; 
                                      1031 link (collapsed) Description: Hong et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      1032 text ).
                                  1033 container sec20
                                      1034 heading Factors affecting fluctuation of the I. palifera-associated bacterial community, Value: 3
                                          1035 text Factors affecting fluctuation of the 
                                          1036 text I. palifera
                                          1037 text -associated bacterial community
                                      1038 container
                                          1039 text Our results suggest that three factors affected the coral-associated bacterial community, including the environment (rainfall) (
                                          1040 link Description: Figure 5, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1041 text  and Supplementary Figure S8), seasonal changes (
                                          1042 link Description: Figure 3, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1043 text ) and colony variation (
                                          1044 link Description: Figures 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1045 text  and 
                                          1046 link Description: 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1047 text ).
                                      1048 container
                                          1049 text Environmental factors were considerable drivers of the structure of the coral-associated bacterial community, as also suggested by other studies (
                                          1050 link (collapsed) Description: Koren and Rosenberg, 2006, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1051 text ; 
                                          1052 link (collapsed) Description: Garren et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1053 text ; 
                                          1054 link (collapsed) Description: Hong et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1055 text ; 
                                          1056 link (collapsed) Description: Littman et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1057 text ). Three factors (seawater temperature, sunlight intensity and rainfall) were available and included in this study in the association analysis with the bacterial groups. Among these environmental factors, rainfall seems to be the factor with greatest effect on the bacterial community of  I. palifera  at Ken-Ting. Changes in the pattern of  Bacilli  bacteria were associated with rainfall (
                                          1058 link Description: Figure 5, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1059 text  and Supplementary Figure S8). This bacterial group comprised 1% of the total bacterial community in the coral, and many  Bacili  are soil-borne bacteria. We speculate that these bacteria might come from terrestrial soil because in the summer months (from June to August), abundant rainfall (∼500 mm per month; Supplementary Figure S9) flushed out a great amount of soil from the land to the coastal waters around Ken-Ting (
                                          1060 link (collapsed) Description: Meng et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1061 text ). Soil-borne bacteria, such as  Bacilli , were likely disseminated to the reef where they took up brief residence in coral. A similar phenomenon has also been detected and discussed in another report (
                                          1062 link (collapsed) Description: Hong et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1063 text ), but there has been no other direct evidence.
                                      1064 container
                                          1065 text Based on the cluster analysis, unlike the rainfall effect on coral-associated bacteria (
                                          1066 link Description: Figure 5, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1067 text ), there was no association between seawater temperatures and bacterial group variation (
                                          1068 link Description: Figure 5, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1069 text ). The water temperature in Ken-Ting changed over a small range (24–28 °C) during our study (Supplementary Figure S9). This result suggests that water temperature might not be a decisive factor triggering the compositional change of bacterial community in  I. palifera  at Ken-Ting. Perhaps, larger temperature changes might have more effect, or other unknown environmental factors that still require further investigation may be involved.
                                      1070 container
                                          1071 text Seasonal variation was another potential factor prompting compositional change of the bacterial communities. In the nMDS analysis, the bacterial composition profiles of the coral samples collected in the same month tended to cluster together (
                                          1072 link Description: Figure 3, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1073 text ). Moreover, the bacterial compositions of the samples of spring (April and May) and summer (June, July and August) were similar to each other, and the samples of winter (February and November) clustered separately (
                                          1074 link Description: Figure 3, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1075 text ), similar to our cluster analysis (data not shown). The composition of the  I. palifera -associated bacterial community had seasonal-dependent variation. Apart from water temperature, other environmental conditions accompanying seasonal changes may have caused the bacterial composition to alter significantly. To confirm seasonal changes or temporal dynamics on the coral-associated bacterial community, a longer survey and a larger sample size should be able to provide more information.
                                      1076 container
                                          1077 text Alphaproteobacteria  and  Gammaproteobacteria  were the two constant predominant groups in  I. palifera , as seen in previous observations on the coral  Acropora  (a coral genus closely related to  Isopora ) in the Great Barrier Reef (
                                          1078 link (collapsed) Description: Hong et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1079 text ; 
                                          1080 link (collapsed) Description: Littman et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1081 text ). Both of these bacterial groups comprised >10% proportions of the bacterial communities in  Acropora  and  I. palifera . Importantly, however, CLB were abundant (up to 33%) in  I. palifera , but were not detected in Great Barrier Reef  Acropora  (
                                          1082 link (collapsed) Description: Littman et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1083 text ). This difference might be caused by differences in geography and coral species, or they may have been present but were undetected by previous methods.
                                      1084 container
                                          1085 text Escherichia  and  Rhodobacteraceae  were the major groups, respectively, of the  Alphaproteobacteria  and  Gammaproteobacteria  detected in  I. palifera .  Escherichia , the dominant group in April and May (
                                          1086 link Description: Figure 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1087 text ), appeared consistently in all colonies. In addition,  Escherichia  was assumed to be an animal-associated bacteria (
                                          1088 link (collapsed) Description: Feng et al., 2002, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1089 text ).  Escherichia  presence may be indicative of human and animal waste, because the coast of Ken-Ting is a popular tourist spot. However, the exact reason for the appearance of  Escherichia  still needs more evidence to prove conclusively.  Rhodobacteraceae,  a group of photosynthetic bacteria (
                                          1090 link (collapsed) Description: Paoli and Tabita, 1998, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1091 text ; 
                                          1092 link (collapsed) Description: Xiong et al., 2000, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1093 text ), appeared abundantly in colonies 352 and 353 in June (
                                          1094 link Description: Figure 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1095 text ). Potential functions of this particular group in corals have not been described. Notably, June brought together relatively high levels of rainfall, temperature and sunlight, as indicated in the clustering analysis. Is this appearance of  Rhodobacteraceae  associated with these environmental factors? The answer is still uncertain.
                                      1096 container
                                          1097 text The cyanobacteria  Chroococcidiopsis  was abundant in colony 353 in February (
                                          1098 link Description: Figure 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1099 text ).  Chroococcidiopsis  has been found on the rock in marine environments (
                                          1100 link (collapsed) Description: Díez et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1101 text ; 
                                          1102 link (collapsed) Description: Goh et al., 2009, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1103 text ). However, the reason for its appearance in coral is still unknown.
                                  1104 container sec21
                                      1105 heading Diversity of the coral-associated bacteria is very high, Value: 3
                                          1106 text Diversity of the coral-associated bacteria is very high
                                      1107 container
                                          1108 text In this study with a large survey (>200 000 reads using pyrosequencing), we have shown that the bacterial communities in sea water and coral are highly diverse, with Shannon's index as high as 6.71, much higher than the 4.95 found using the clone library method (reviewed in 
                                          1109 link (collapsed) Description: Reshef et al., 2006, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1110 text ). This is the highest index value of diversity ever detected in a coral-associated bacterial community. Despite the difference between the two methods of measuring the index value, our result suggests that the diversity of the coral-associated bacteria is much higher than previously thought. Moreover, our study also highlights that the survey number of a representative gene, such as the 16S ribosomal RNA gene, is critical in revealing the composition of a bacterial community. The rarefaction curves (at a 3% cutoff value) of the samples show that the sampling size (read number) in our survey, with over 1500 sequences for each coral sample (
                                          1111 link Description: Table 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1112 text ), was sufficient to reveal the bacterial community in  I. palifera  (Supplementary Figure S4).
                                  1113 container sec22
                                      1114 heading Potential nitrogen fixer groups, Value: 3
                                          1115 text Potential nitrogen fixer groups
                                      1116 container
                                          1117 text Corals can take up ammonium and nitrate compounds from surrounding water as a nitrogen source (
                                          1118 link (collapsed) Description: Grover, 2002, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1119 text , 
                                          1120 link (collapsed) Description: 2003, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1121 text ). However, as the reef ecosystem is a nutrient-limited environment (
                                          1122 link (collapsed) Description: Muscatine and Porter, 1977, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1123 text ), bacteria-driven nitrogen fixation can compensate for any deficiency of nitrogen source for coral holobiont (
                                          1124 link (collapsed) Description: Shashar et al., 1994, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1125 text ; 
                                          1126 link (collapsed) Description: Lesser et al., 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1127 text ). Nitrogen-fixing bacteria have been detected elsewhere in coral (
                                          1128 link (collapsed) Description: Shashar et al., 1994, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1129 text ; 
                                          1130 link (collapsed) Description: Lesser et al., 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1131 text ). In this study, we also detected several potential nitrogen fixers, including  Cyanobacteria  (
                                          1132 link (collapsed) Description: Meeks, 1998, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1133 text ; 
                                          1134 link (collapsed) Description: Berman-Frank et al., 2003, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1135 text ),  Clostridia  (
                                          1136 link (collapsed) Description: Chen et al., 2001, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1137 text ) , Chlorobia  (
                                          1138 link (collapsed) Description: Wahlund and Madigan, 1993, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1139 text ) and  Chloroflexi  (
                                          1140 link (collapsed) Description: Seshadri et al., 2005, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1141 text ; 
                                          1142 link (collapsed) Description: Kneip et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1143 text ). These potential nitrogen fixer groups in  I. palifera  greatly were enriched in February and April (
                                          1144 link Description: Figure 5, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                          1145 text ). Although better evidence is still lacking, we speculate that this phenomenon might be caused by a relative nitrogen limitation from February to April (
                                          1146 link (collapsed) Description: Meng et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1147 text ). During this period, the coral might be able to acquire some nitrogen from these potential nitrogen fixers. However, in the summer (June, July and August), the nitrogen-limited condition was released by abundant rainfall flushing a large amount of nutrients, including nitrogen sources, into coastal waters from river outflow as previously observed (
                                          1148 link (collapsed) Description: Meng et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1149 text ), and the potential bacterial nitrogen fixer population proportion also decreased.
                                  1150 container sec23
                                      1151 heading The fluctuation of the symbiotic algal composition, Value: 3
                                          1152 text The fluctuation of the symbiotic algal composition
                                      1153 container
                                          1154 text The composition of  Symbiodinium  in corals is known to be changeable (
                                          1155 link (collapsed) Description: Toller et al., 2001, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1156 text ; 
                                          1157 link (collapsed) Description: LaJeunesse et al., 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1158 text ; 
                                          1159 link (collapsed) Description: Chen et al., 2005, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1160 text ; 
                                          1161 link (collapsed) Description: Reimer et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1162 text ), varying with environmental conditions such as season (
                                          1163 link (collapsed) Description: Chen et al., 2005, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1164 text ), latitude (
                                          1165 link (collapsed) Description: LaJeunesse et al., 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1166 text ) and depth (
                                          1167 link (collapsed) Description: Toller et al., 2001, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1168 text ; 
                                          1169 link (collapsed) Description: Frade et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1170 text ). We also observed changes in the algal symbiont population in terms of number and composition. According to our PCR heteroplasmy and Q-PCR analyses, the algal symbiont composition in the coral samples continuously fluctuated but both clades C and D were always detectable in all three tagged colonies throughout our survey.
                                      1171 container
                                          1172 text What drives the change of dominance of the algal population? The relevant factors are probably highly complex. One factor may be the difference in physiological properties between the two clades (
                                          1173 link (collapsed) Description: Rowen, 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1174 text ). Most of  Symbiodinium  clade D is heat tolerant and they are commonly found in corals living in shallow and inshore reefs with more radiation and higher temperature fluctuation (
                                          1175 link (collapsed) Description: Baker, 2003, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1176 text ; 
                                          1177 link (collapsed) Description: Rowen, 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1178 text ; 
                                          1179 link (collapsed) Description: LaJeunesse et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1180 text ). Thus, harboring symbionts of clade D may increase the survival rate of the coral during bleaching events in hot seasons as suggested by 
                                          1181 link (collapsed) Description: Jones et al. (2008), Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1182 text . However, clade D may not be the perfect symbiotic partner all the time. In juvenile coral stages, corals infected with clade D grew slower than those with clade C (
                                          1183 link (collapsed) Description: Little et al., 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1184 text ), suggesting that members of clade C may provide other growth benefits than clade D algae despite their greater temperature sensitivity (
                                          1185 link (collapsed) Description: Rowen, 2004, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1186 text ). It should also be noted that not all subgroups of clade D confer temperature tolerance in corals (
                                          1187 link (collapsed) Description: Abrego et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1188 text ). Considering the complexity of physiological features in clades C and D, we suggest that a better analysis of each major subgroup of clades C and D may shed more light on their population dynamics during season changes. Although the reasons for the seasonal alterations in clade proportion are still unclear, these changes occurred internally in the coral because we did not detect any of the algal genes in the seawater samples (data not shown).
                                  1189 container sec24
                                      1190 heading Issues for use of nucleotide-tag primers in MPP, Value: 3
                                          1191 text Issues for use of nucleotide-tag primers in MPP
                                      1192 container
                                          1193 text MPP offers several advantages to surveys of microbial communities, including sufficient data, low cost, low labor requirements and avoidance of bias (
                                          1194 link (collapsed) Description: Sogin et al., 2006, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1195 text ; 
                                          1196 link (collapsed) Description: Binladen et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1197 text ; 
                                          1198 link (collapsed) Description: Huse et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1199 text ). However, when amplifying the 16S rRNA gene using universal bacterial primers with specific tag sequences, it has been argued that appending different tag sequences to the universal primers would bring extra bias during the amplification by PCR because of the differential hybridization efficiency of different primers. Similarly, we have also observed a similar problem in that universal primers with different code sequences may be a cause of differential amplification efficiency. To avoid such bias from different code sequences, we first amplified the bacterial V6 region with universal bacterial primers without tag sequences, and only then carried out DNA tagging PCR with a very low number of amplification cycles, a process that can specifically add individual code sequences to different PCR amplicons with universal bacterial primers containing different code sequences. Compared with the previous method, this newly modified technique for DNA coding generates less artificial bias.
                                      1200 container
                                          1201 text We strongly recommend the MPP approach for the study of the population dynamics of microbial patterns in coral because of the highly dynamic nature of such populations in response to temporal or seasonal factors and the evident variation among individual colonies in corals, such as  I. palifera . The robustness of the technique can provide the capacity to handle a large number of samples with affordable costs and low labor requirements (
                                          1202 link (collapsed) Description: Sogin et al., 2006, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1203 text ; 
                                          1204 link (collapsed) Description: Binladen et al., 2007, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1205 text ; 
                                          1206 link (collapsed) Description: Huse et al., 2008, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                          1207 text ).
                              1208 container ack1

                                      1210 text Acknowledgments
                                  1211 text We thank Garmin Hsu and the colleagues of Allen CL Chen for assistance with providing samples and seawater temperature data. This study was supported by thematic project funding of Academia Sinica, Taiwan, and by the Biodiversity Research Center, Academia Sinica, Taiwan.

  - heading "Patterns of bleaching and recovery of Montipora capitata in Kāne‘ohe Bay, Hawai‘i, USA" [level=1]
  - list:
    - link "Ross Cunning":
      - /url: "#Author"
    - link:
      - /url: "#"
    - link "Raphael Ritson-Williams":
      - /url: "#Author"
    - link "Ruth D. Gates":
      - /url: "#Author"
  - generic: "ABSTRACT:"
  - paragraph: As ocean warming causes more frequent and severe coral bleaching worldwide, it is critical to identify biotic and abiotic factors that promote bleaching resistance and recovery. In October 2014, many colonies of the key reef-building coral Montipora capitata in Kāne‘ohe Bay, O‘ahu, Hawai‘i, USA, were severely bleached, while others appeared unaffected. To elucidate the role of symbiotic algae in these contrasting responses and study subsequent patterns of recovery, we tracked abundances (symbiont to host cell ratios) of clade C and D Symbiodinium for 6 mo in 10 bleached and 10 non-bleached colonies at 3 reefs in the northern, central, and southern regions of Ka¯ne‘ohe Bay (n = 60 colonies) using quantitative PCR. Bleaching resistance was significantly associated with the dominant symbiont clade. All bleached colonies (n = 30) were dominated by clade C symbionts, while many non-bleached colonies (n = 16) were dominated by thermotolerant clade D. However, clade C Symbiodinium dominated 14 other colonies that did not bleach, indicating that an alternate mechanism such as host genetic adaptation may play a role in thermal tolerance of these colonies. Bleached corals recovered their symbionts within 1-3 mo (excepting 1 mortality) and remained C-dominated. However, colonies recovered 3 times faster at the northern reef, which experiences similar temperature but lower irradiance and higher water flow and turnover compared to the southern reef. This work indicates that both biotic (e.g. symbiont and host genotypic) and abiotic (e.g. hydrodynamic) factors influence the natural resistance and recovery of M. capitata, which can inform ecological predictions and conservation strategies for coral reefs under climate change.

Cunning et al. (2016) is unequivocally eligible: 60 tagged reef colonies were sampled at six field time points over six months, with no treatment, and clades C/D were quantified by qPCR. Its omission was a search miss, not a criterion-based exclusion; the title emphasizes bleaching recovery rather than longitudinal symbiont-community change. It also has a Zenodo dataset, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.53231.

- heading "Abstract" [level=2]: Abstract

- generic: Obligate endosymbioses between eukaryotes and their single-celled inhabitants form the basis of many ecosystems, yet little is known about the long-term impacts of climate change on them. On coral reefs, extensive studies have shown that climate change-driven heatwaves and other environmental stressors can disrupt the obligate symbiosis between reef-building corals and Symbiodiniaceae, with consequences for coral fitness and survival. However, despite coral symbioses playing a fundamental role in reef resilience to climate change, whether, and at what rate, they recover following heatwave disruption is largely unknown. We used ITS2 DNA metabarcoding to characterise symbiont assemblages in colonies (n = 237; 598 samples) of the brain coral Platygyra ryukyuensis over a decade (2014-2023), spanning from before to long after the 2015-2016 El Niño at its epicentre, Kiritimati, in the central equatorial Pacific. Although before the heatwave only P. ryukyuensis colonies exposed to high levels of chronic local disturbance were dominated by stress-tolerant Durusdinium symbionts, surviving colonies around the atoll transitioned during the heatwave from Cladocopium dominance to Durusdinium dominance. Here, we show that nearly eight years after this transition, these symbiotic partnerships had not recovered, but rather Durusdinium remained entrenched in virtually all (92%) Platygyra colonies. Recovery of symbionts in the genus Cladocopium was severely limited and restricted to taxa distinct from their 'C3' and 'C50a' pre-heatwave congenerics. Moreover, in th

- heading "Abstract" [level=2]: Abstract
- separator
- generic: Obligate endosymbioses between eukaryotes and their single-celled inhabitants form the basis of many ecosystems, yet little is known about the long-term impacts of climate change on them. On coral reefs, extensive studies have shown that climate change-driven heatwaves and other environmental stressors can disrupt the obligate symbiosis between reef-building corals and Symbiodiniaceae, with consequences for coral fitness and survival. However, despite coral symbioses playing a fundamental role in reef resilience to climate change, whether, and at what rate, they recover following heatwave disruption is largely unknown. We used ITS2 DNA metabarcoding to characterise symbiont assemblages in colonies (n = 237; 598 samples) of the brain coral Platygyra ryukyuensis over a decade (2014-2023), spanning from before to long after the 2015-2016 El Niño at its epicentre, Kiritimati, in the central equatorial Pacific. Although before the heatwave only P. ryukyuensis colonies exposed to high levels of chronic local disturbance were dominated by stress-tolerant Durusdinium symbionts, surviving colonies around the atoll transitioned during the heatwave from Cladocopium dominance to Durusdinium dominance. Here, we show that nearly eight years after this transition, these symbiotic partnerships had not recovered, but rather Durusdinium remained entrenched in virtually all (92%) Platygyra colonies. Recovery of symbionts in the genus Cladocopium was severely limited and restricted to taxa distinct from their 'C3' and 'C50a' pre-heatwave congenerics. Moreover, in the three immediate post-heatwave years, many tracked corals, and especially those at low local disturbance, high in-water visibility sites, hosted transient symbiont assemblages codominated by Durusdinium and the previously rare genus Symbiodinium. Our results demonstrate that heatwave-driven symbiont transitions can persist for longer than the average heatwave return time, potentially impairing coral resilience to future extreme weather events.

tagged:  P. ryukyuensis
  - text: colonies that were at least 20 cm in diameter and at least 5 m apart were tagged and sampled. Coral colony size can be used as a reasonably reliable proxy for age (Madin, Hoogenboom, et al.
  - link "2016":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-bib-0055"
  - text: ) and the congener
  - emphasis: Platygyra sinensis
  - text: has been found to increase slowly in diameter by 6–12 mm annually (Madin, Anderson, et al.
  - link "2016":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-bib-0054"
  - text: ). Hence the minimum size threshold of 20 cm diameter was used to select
  - emphasis: Platygyra ryukyuensis
  - text: colonies that were alive before peak heatwave exposure. Previously tagged colonies were re‐sampled whenever possible on subsequent expeditions and are referred to as tracked colonies (Figure
  - link "S3":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-supitem-0001"
  - text: ). However, substantial mortality of this species during the heatwave, especially at sites exposed to Very High disturbance (Claar et al.
  - link "2020":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-bib-0017"
  - text: ; Baum et al.
  - link "2023":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-bib-0005"
  - text: ), necessitated tagging new colonies on each post‐heatwave expedition. Tissue samples were taken from the central, uppermost surface of colonies using a woodworking chisel, and then stored in individual bags on ice until the end of each day, when ~1 cm
  - superscript: "3"
  - text: of tissue from each sample was transferred to microcentrifuge tubes containing a guanidinium isothiocyanate buffer. Samples were stored at 4°C until DNA extraction was performed. Samples were collected from colonies' uppermost surface for consistency and to avoid sampling shaded microhabitats in a colony's morphology, which can contain distinct Symbiodiniaceae (Kemp et al.
  - link "2015":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-bib-0039"
  - text: ; Lewis et al.
  - link "2022":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-bib-0053"
  - text: ).
- heading "2.4. Symbiodiniaceae DNA Extraction and Sequencing" [level=3]
- paragraph:
  - text: DNA was extracted from coral tissue samples preserved in guanidinium isothiocyanate buffer using a protocol designed for Symbiodiniaceae (Stat et al.
  - link "2009":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-bib-0086"
  - text: ). 200 μL subsamples of homogenised tissue/buffer slurry were incubated overnight at −20°C with an equal volume of isopropanol. Precipitated DNA was then collected into a pellet by centrifugation and washed three times with 70% ethanol before resuspension in 50 μL Tris buffer. The internal transcribed spacer 2 (ITS2) ribosomal DNA was amplified using a two‐step PCR for DNA metabarcoding. The first round of PCR used forward primer ITS‐DINO (Pochon et al.

- heading "2.1. Study Site" [level=3]
- paragraph:
  - text: This study was conducted at Kiritimati (Christmas Island), Republic of Kiribati, a remote atoll situated in the central equatorial Pacific Ocean (01°52′ N, 157°24′ W). Kiritimati is the largest atoll in the world by landmass (388 km
  - superscript: "2"
  - text: ), with a continuous fringing reef encircling the island. Kiritimati's population was estimated as 6500 in 2015, increasing by 14% to 7400 by 2020 (Kiribati National Statistics Office
  - link "2016":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-bib-0043"
  - text: ","
  - link "2021":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-bib-0044"
  - text: ), distributed mostly along the northeast lagoon face (Figure
  - link "1a":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-fig-0001"
  - text: ), exposing adjacent reefs to disturbance from wastewater runoff, subsistence fishing, coastal construction and dredging (Figure
  - link "1a":
    - /url: "#gcb70818-fig-0001"
  - text: ). A total of 12 sites were sampled for this study across this disturbance gradient, ranging from reefs adjacent to villages to minimally impacted reefs at the remote ends of the atoll. At each site, samples were collected along 60 m transects, laid along the 10–12 m isobath.
- link "FIGURE 1":
  - /url: /article/view/PMC13013739/figure/gcb70818-fig-0001/version/1
  - img "FIGURE 1"
- link "Open in a separate window":

- link "FIGURE 1":

- paragraph:
  - text: Spatiotemporal patterns of chronic and acute stressors on Kiritimati reefs (a) Labelled points indicate locations of the 12 reef sites sampled on a map of Kiritimati. Sites are categorised as very low, low, medium, high or very high human disturbance. Permanent settlements are depicted by red circles scaled according to population size. A dashed line bisects the island to indicate shores designated as windward or leeward. (b) Mean (+/− standard error) measurements of environmental metrics at each site from 2014 to 2023. Satellite‐derived sea‐surface chlorophyll
  - emphasis: a
  - text: concentration, surface water nitrate and nitrite concentration, and in‐water visibility are shown. Study sites are ordered along the x‐axis by location, moving clockwise windward to leeward. (c) Satellite‐derived sea‐surface temperature (°C) and accumulated heat stress (maximum degree‐heating‐weeks, DHW) are shown by blue and black line graphs, respectively. Colour fills under the DHW line represent periods over which thresholds of 4, 8,
Symbiodiniaceae: d other environmental stressors can disrupt the obligate symbiosis between reef-building corals and Symbiodiniaceae, with consequences for coral fitness and survival. However, despite coral symbioses playing a fundamental role in reef resilience to climate change, whether, and at what rate, they recover following heatwave disruption is largely unknown. We used ITS2 DNA metabarcoding to characterise symbiont assemblages in colonies (n = 237; 598 samples) of the brain coral Platygyra ryukyuensis over a decade (2014-2023), spanning from before to long after the 2015-2016 El Niño at its epicentre, Kiritimati, in the central equatorial Pacific. Although before the heatwave only P. ryukyuensis colonies exposed to high levels of chronic local disturbance were dominated by stress-tolerant Durusdinium symbionts, surviving colonies around the atoll transitioned during the heatwave from Cladocopium dominance to Durusdinium dominance. Here, we show that nearly eight years after this transition, these symbiotic partnerships had not recovered, but rather Durusdinium remained entrenched in virtually all (92%) Platygyra colonies. Recovery of symbionts in the genus Cladocopium was severely limited and restricted to taxa distinct from their 'C3' and 'C50a' pre-heatwave congenerics. Moreover, in the three immediate post-heatwave years, many tracked corals, and especially those at low local disturbance, high in-water visibility sites, hosted transient symbiont assemblages codominated by Durusdinium and the previously rare genus Symbiodinium. Our results demonstrate that heatwave-driven symbiont transitions can persist for longer than the average heatwave return time, potentially impairing coral resilience to future extreme weather events.

- heading "Abstract" [level=2]: Abstract
- separator
- generic: Obligate endosymbioses between eukaryotes and their single-celled inhabitants form the basis of many ecosystems, yet little is known about the long-term impacts of climate change on them. On coral reefs, extensive studies have shown that climate change-driven heatwaves and other environmental stressors can disrupt the obligate symbiosis between reef-building corals and Symbiodiniaceae, with consequences for coral fitness and survival. However, despite coral symbioses playing a fundamental role in reef resilience to climate change, whether, and at what rate, they recover following heatwave disruption is largely unknown. We used ITS2 DNA metabarcoding to characterise symbiont assemblages in colonies (n = 237; 598 samples) of the brain coral Platygyra ryukyuensis over a decade (2014-2023), spanning from before to long after the 2015-2016 El Niño at its epicentre, Kiritimati, in the central equatorial Pacific. Although before the heatwave only P. ryukyuensis colonies exposed to high levels of chronic local disturbance were dominated by stress-tolerant Durusdinium symbionts, surviving colonies around the atoll transitioned during the heatwave from Cladocopium dominance to Durusdinium dominance. Here, we show that nearly eight years after this transition, these symbiotic partnerships had not recovered, but rather Durusdinium remained entrenched in virtually all (92%) Platygyra colonies. Recovery of symbionts in the genus Cladocopium was severely limited and restricted to taxa distinct from their 'C3' and 'C50a' pre-heatwave congenerics. Moreover, in the three immediate post-heatwave years, many tracked corals, and especially those at low local disturbance, high in-water visibility sites, hosted transient symbiont assemblages codominated by Durusdinium and the previously rare genus Symbiodinium. Our results demonstrate that heatwave-driven symbiont transitions can persist for longer than the average heatwave return time, potentially impairing coral resilience to future extreme weather events.

  - button:
  - heading "Long-term monitoring of algal symbiont communities in corals reveals stability is taxon dependent and driven by site-specific thermal regime" [level=1]
  - list:
    - link "Andrew C. Baker":
      - /url: "#Author"
    - link "Tim R. McClanahan":
      - /url: "#Author"
    - link "Craig J. Starger":
      - /url: "#Author"
    - link "Roxane K. Boonstra":
      - /url: "#Author"
  - generic: "ABSTRACT:"
  - paragraph: Survival trajectories for coral reefs under climate change may depend in part on shifts in the composition of their algal symbiont communities (Symbiodinium spp.). Shifts favoring thermotolerant symbionts have been recorded in response to mass bleaching events but rarely tracked through time. A 10 yr monitoring study of Symbiodinium in a variety of Kenyan corals assessed their variability through time, across coral taxa and between sites, and their relationship to environmental conditions. Coral genera varied significantly in their propensity to host thermotolerant symbionts of Symbiodinium clade D, with some genera becoming dominated by clade D at annual maximum temperatures of 32°C but others showing clade D only rarely at 35°C. High annual maximum temperatures, high standard deviation, positive skewness and positive kurtosis characterized sites where clade D was common. In corals whose symbiont communities were thermally labile (e.g. Pocillopora) an increase in maximum annual temperature from 30 to 35°C resulted in 3- to 4-fold increases in dominance by clade D. There was no directional change in symbiont communities over the study period, but there was evidence for a ~6 yr decline in the incidence of mixed (C + D) communities following the 1998 bleaching event. These data illustrate how acute and chronic thermal stress caused by oceanographic and tidal oscillations interact to produce highly dynamic symbiotic communities. The clade D niche is a function of the environment and host taxon and, through a variety of mechanisms, is expected to expand with climate warming. Corals from warm and variable conditions represent conservation priorities because they establish a niche for these symbionts in contemporary reef environments.

Warning: i was declared with const; use let for reassignable variables.
Abstract" [level=2]: Abstract
- separator
- generic: Caribbean corals of the Montastraea annularis species complex associate with four taxa of symbiotic dinoflagellates (zooxanthellae; genus Symbiodinium) in ecologically predictable patterns. To investigate the resilience of these host-zooxanthella associations, we conducted field experiments in which we experimentally reduced the numbers of zooxanthellae (by transplanting to shallow water or by shading) and then allowed treated corals to recover. When depletion was not extreme, recovering corals generally contained the same types of zooxanthellae as they did prior to treatment. After severe depletion, however, recovering corals were always repopulated by zooxanthellae atypical for their habitat (and in some cases atypical for the coral species). These unusual zooxanthellar associations were often (but not always) established in experimentally bleached tissues even when adjacent tissues were untreated. Atypical zooxanthellae were also observed in bleached tissues of unmanipulated Montastraea with yellow-blotch disease. In colonies where unusual associations were established, the original taxa of zooxanthellae were not detected even 9 months after the end of treatment. These observations suggest that zooxanthellae in Montastraea range from fugitive opportunists and stress-tolerant generalists (Symbiodinium A and E) to narrowly adapted specialists (Symbiodinium B and C), and may undergo succession.

                              39 heading AI Overview, Value: 2
                                  40 text AI Overview
                              41 container
                                  42 text Longitudinal tracking of  tagged coral colonies provides critical insights into how 
                                  43 button Symbiodinium
                                  44 text  (and the broader 
                                  45 text Symbiodiniaceae
                                  46 text  family) assemblages shift and recover during and after 
                                  47 text natural bleaching events
                                  48 text .
                                  49 link Description: National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov), Value: google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVjxcmPpho6wG3z1xomPTJtCvkq_dgvqGDPLXIABWbzIGRWMp-TqqnFj7VzKPqUszFrjMMz9tyObO-okXevkQacPzF7uNqToDA55CfdvxE6btRvtRciCHdrGVSMuIGozkYentI9hXoNOM
                                  50 button National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov) (+1) - Related results
                                      51 text National Institutes of Health (NIH) | (.gov)
                                      52 text  +1
                              53 text Key takeaways from long-term research on tagged or tracked coral colonies during bleaching include:
                              54 heading 1. Decadal Shifts and Legacy Effects, Value: 3
                                  55 text 1. Decadal Shifts and Legacy Effects
                              56 container
                                  57 text Longitudinal studies reveal that marine heatwaves disrupt the highly specific, coevolved alliances between corals and their algal symbionts. A prominent  decade-long study (2014–2023)  in Kiritimati tracked 237 distinct colonies of 
                                  58 button Platygyra
                                  59 text  brain corals through the massive 2015–2016 El Niño-induced bleaching event. The research highlights that local chronic human disturbances compound the stress, dramatically reshaping symbiont competitive dynamics and leaving persistent physiological legacy effects long after temperatures return to normal.
                                  60 link Description: Science | AAAS, Value: google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVd-eLJdzzypwtHMzZjmxXCqnxlmY0-vwRRNY_xjg03GpgOxd8ZISetNYfCZzVMnsAvJUoAW1d1Raok9F1CaaDSHkLYZX8h4AkTtgyALCTl-N48BKKnnhRYr3irGHitPhwYjYIxkJPiPo
                                  61 button Science | AAAS (+1) - Related results
                                      62 text Science | AAAS
                                      63 text  +1
                              64 heading 2. Genetic Lineages and Symbiotic Turnover, Value: 3
                                  65 text 2. Genetic Lineages and Symbiotic Turnover
                              66 container
                                  67 text By keeping tabs on individual, mapped colonies, scientists can observe "cryptic" diversity and how specific coral genotypes react differently to bleaching:
                                  68 link Description: Science | AAAS, Value: google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVd-eLJdzzypwtHMzZjmxXCqnxlmY0-vwRRNY_xjg03GpgOxd8ZISetNYfCZzVMnsAvJUoAW1d1Raok9F1CaaDSHkLYZX8h4AkTtgyALCTl-N48BKKnnhRYr3irGHitPhwYjYIxkJPiPo
                                  69 button Science | AAAS - Related results
                                      70 text Science | AAAS
                              71 content list
                                  72 container
                                      73 AXListMarker • 
                                      74 text Differential Mortality:  In a 6-year study of 315 tracked 
                                      75 button Porites
                                      76 text  colonies, researchers discovered three genetically distinct coral lineages ( PKir-1 ,  PKir-2 ,  PKir-3 ) living side by side. During severe heat stress, one specific lineage ( PKir-3 ) suffered a staggering  85% mortality rate , while the other two only suffered 39–53%.
                                      77 link Description: Science | AAAS, Value: google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVd-eLJdzzypwtHMzZjmxXCqnxlmY0-vwRRNY_xjg03GpgOxd8ZISetNYfCZzVMnsAvJUoAW1d1Raok9F1CaaDSHkLYZX8h4AkTtgyALCTl-N48BKKnnhRYr3irGHitPhwYjYIxkJPiPo
                                      78 button Science | AAAS - Related results
                                          79 text Science | AAAS
                                  80 container
                                      81 AXListMarker • 
                                      82 text Shifting Communities:  The heat stress causes  symbiotic turnover —where surviving colonies switch or tilt their background algal communities toward more heat-tolerant clades. However, this often comes at the expense of erasing their original, highly tuned coevolutionary associations.
                                      83 link Description: Science | AAAS, Value: google.com/goto?url=CAESbQHrOzAVd-eLJdzzypwtHMzZjmxXCqnxlmY0-vwRRNY_xjg03GpgOxd8ZISetNYfCZzVMnsAvJUoAW1d1Raok9F1CaaDSHkLYZX8h4AkTtgyALCTl-N48BKKnnhRYr3irGHitPhwYjYIxkJPiPo
                                      84 button Science | AAAS (+1) - Related results
                                          85 text Science | AAAS
                                          86 text  +1
                              87 heading 3. Molecular Lag in Recovery, Value: 3
                                  88 text 3. Molecular Lag in Recovery
                              89 container
                                  90 text Tracking individual colonies longitudinally allows scientists to capture the timeline of physiological recovery at a molecular level:
                                  91 link Description: Pacific Environment Data Portal, Value: …
                                  92 button Pacific Environment Data Portal - Related results
                                      93 text Pacific Environment Data Portal
                              94 content list
                                  95 container
                                      96 AXListMarker • 
                                      97 text Studies tracking 
                                      98 button Acropora hyacinthus
                                      99 text  colonies following natural bleaching show that severe heat triggers a massive environmental stress response, altering about  20% of the host's transcriptome .
                                      100 link Description: Pacific Environment Data Portal, Value: …
                                      101 button Pacific Environment Data Portal - Related results
                                          102 text Pacific Environment Data Portal
                                  103 container
                                      104 AXListMarker • 
                                      105 text Notably, there is a major lag in health recovery: even after the visible coral color returns and  Symbiodiniaceae  populations bounce back to normal levels, the coral’s genes remain severely perturbed for  at least six months , with some genes failing to recover even 12 months post-bleaching.

The focused UI element is 1 AXWebArea "Patterns of bleaching and recovery" Zenodo 53231 - Google Search, URL: google.com/search?q=%22Patterns+of+bleaching+and+recovery%22+Zenodo+53231

The reviewer is correct on the substantive point: all four satisfy the ecological design. The earlier run did surface three of them; the real omission was Cunning et al. (2016), which was missed because its title foregrounds bleaching/recovery rather than symbiont-community time series. I’m now checking citation chains for similarly titled studies and screening overlap with datasets already in your meta-analysis.

                  55 heading Abstract, Value: 2, ID: Abs1
                      56 text Abstract
                  57 container
                      58 text Coral reefs are in rapid decline on a global scale due to human activities and a changing climate. Shallow water reefs depend on the obligatory symbiosis between the habitat forming coral host and its algal symbiont from the genus  Symbiodinium  (zooxanthellae). This association is highly sensitive to thermal perturbations and temperatures as little as 1°C above the average summer maxima can cause the breakdown of this symbiosis, termed coral bleaching. Predicting the capacity of corals to survive the expected increase in seawater temperatures depends strongly on our understanding of the thermal tolerance of the symbiotic algae. Here we use molecular phylogenetic analysis of four genetic markers to describe  Symbiodinium thermophilum , sp. nov. from the Persian/Arabian Gulf, a thermally tolerant coral symbiont. Phylogenetic inference using the non-coding region of the chloroplast  psbA  gene resolves  S. thermophilum  as a monophyletic lineage with large genetic distances from any other ITS2 C3 type found outside the Gulf. Through the characterisation of  Symbiodinium  associations of 6 species (5 genera) of Gulf corals, we demonstrate that  S. thermophilum  is the prevalent symbiont all year round in the world's hottest sea, the southern Persian/Arabian Gulf.

                      107 text Corals living in symbiosis with unicellular dinoflagellate algae (zooxanthellae) belonging to the genus  Symbiodinium  are primarily responsible for the formation of tropical shallow water reefs
                      108 link Description: Reference 9, Value: nature.com/articles…, ID: ref-link-section-d25339418e649, Help: Trench, R. K. The cell biology of plant-animal symbiosis. Annu. Rev. Plant Physiol. 30, 485–531 (1979).

                      111 text . Several environmental factors, including elevated or reduced seawater temperatures can trigger the loss of zooxanthellae from the host, a phenomenon known as “coral bleaching”

                      115 text . Over the past decades, mass bleaching events, caused primarily by elevated seawater temperatures (as little as 1°C above the average annual maximum), have become more frequent and contribute to the observed degradation of coral reefs
