R Soc Open Sci 3:160322
                          494 text ) or during episodes of extreme thermal stress in natural (Jones et al. 
                          495 link Description: Reference 2008, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2503, Help: Jones AM, Berkelmans R, van Oppen MJ, Mieog JC, Sinclair W (2008) A community change in the algal endosymbionts of a scleractinian coral following a natural bleaching event: field evidence of acclimatization. Proc Biol Sci 275:1359–1365
                          496 text ; LaJeunesse et al. 
                          497 link Description: Reference 2009, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2506, Help: LaJeunesse TC, Smith RT, Finney J, Oxenford H (2009) Outbreak and persistence of opportunistic symbiotic dinoflagellates during the 2005 Caribbean mass coral “bleaching” event. Proc Biol Sci 276:4139–4148
                          498 text ) or experimental tank settings (Berkelmans and van Oppen 
                          499 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2509, Help: Berkelmans R, van Oppen MJ (2006) The role of zooxanthellae in the thermal tolerance of corals: a “nugget of hope” for coral reefs in an era of climate change. Proc Biol Sci 273:2305–2312
                          500 text ; Cunning et al. 
                          501 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2513, Help: Cunning R, Silverstein RN, Baker AC (2015) Investigating the causes and consequences of symbiont shuffling in a multi-partner reef coral symbiosis under environmental change. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 282:20141725
                          502 text ; Howe-Kerr et al. 
                          503 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2516, Help: Howe-Kerr LI, Bachelot B, Wright RM, Kenkel CD, Bay LK, Correa AMS (2020) Symbiont community diversity is more variable in corals that respond poorly to stress. Glob Chang Biol 26:2220–2234
                          504 text ). In most cases of episodic stress, symbiont ‘change’ appears to be temporary, often involving rare, opportunistic, taxa, but, with sufficient time, the symbiont population reverts to the original native symbiont (Thornhill et al. 
                          505 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2519, Help: Thornhill DJ, LaJeunesse TC, Kemp DW, Fitt WK, Schmidt GW (2006) Multi-year, seasonal genotypic surveys of coral-algal symbioses reveal prevalent stability or post-bleaching reversion. Mar Biol 148:711–722
                          506 text ; LaJeunesse et al. 
                          507 link Description: Reference 2009, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2522, Help: LaJeunesse TC, Smith RT, Finney J, Oxenford H (2009) Outbreak and persistence of opportunistic symbiotic dinoflagellates during the 2005 Caribbean mass coral “bleaching” event. Proc Biol Sci 276:4139–4148
                          508 text ) and further emphasizes that while these mutualisms are susceptible to disruption, their natural inclination is partner fidelity and stability.
                      509 heading The presence of low abundance background symbionts, Value: 3, ID: Sec23
                          510 text The presence of low abundance background symbionts
                      511 container
                          512 text This study did not attempt to assess the coexistence of other symbiont species present at low abundances, arbitrarily defined here as comprising < 5% of the total symbiont population. While certain Symbiodiniaceae taxa may persist in some colonies at low or trace (< 0.5) proportions of the total population (e.g., Boulotte et al. 
                          513 link Description: Reference 2016, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2533, Help: Boulotte NM, Dalton SJ, Carroll AG, Harrison PL, Putnam HM, Peplow LM, van Oppen MJ (2016) Exploring the Symbiodinium rare biosphere provides evidence for symbiont switching in reef-building corals. ISME J 10:2693–2701
                          514 text ), they probably contribute little to the productivity of the mutualism; and in most cases have minimal functional or ecological significance, especially under normal environmental conditions (Lee et al. 
                          515 link Description: Reference 2016, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2536, Help: Lee MJ, Jeong HJ, Jang SH, Lee SY, Kang NS, Lee KH, Kim HS, Wham DC, LaJeunesse TC (2016) Most Low-Abundance "Background" Symbiodinium spp. are transitory and have minimal functional significance for symbiotic corals. Microb Ecol 71:771–783
                          516 text ). When tracked over time, many background ‘symbionts’ are transient appearing and disappearing randomly over time in temporally sampled colonies. Indeed, many may not be host-compatible or even mutualistic (Lee et al. 
                          517 link Description: Reference 2016, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2539, Help: Lee MJ, Jeong HJ, Jang SH, Lee SY, Kang NS, Lee KH, Kim HS, Wham DC, LaJeunesse TC (2016) Most Low-Abundance "Background" Symbiodinium spp. are transitory and have minimal functional significance for symbiotic corals. Microb Ecol 71:771–783
                          518 text ; LaJeunesse et al. 
                          519 link Description: Reference 2010b, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2542, Help: LaJeunesse TC, Smith R, Walther M, Pinzón J, Pettay DT, McGinley M, Aschaffenburg M, Medina-Rosas P, Cupul-Magana AL, Perez AL, Reyes-Bonilla H, Warner ME (2010b) Host-symbiont recombination versus natural selection in the response of coral-dinoflagellate symbioses to environmental disturbance. Proc Biol Sci 277:2925–2934
                          520 text ). A notable exception, however, is  D. trenchii  (and perhaps other species of the genus), which may displace or replace the original resident symbiont under thermally stressful conditions (Berkelmans and van Oppen 
                          521 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2549, Help: Berkelmans R, van Oppen MJ (2006) The role of zooxanthellae in the thermal tolerance of corals: a “nugget of hope” for coral reefs in an era of climate change. Proc Biol Sci 273:2305–2312
                          522 text ; LaJeunesse et al. 
                          523 link Description: Reference 2009, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2552, Help: LaJeunesse TC, Smith RT, Finney J, Oxenford H (2009) Outbreak and persistence of opportunistic symbiotic dinoflagellates during the 2005 Caribbean mass coral “bleaching” event. Proc Biol Sci 276:4139–4148
                          524 text ; Grottoli et al. 
                          525 link Description: Reference 2014, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2555, Help: Grottoli AG, Warner ME, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Schoepf V, McGinley M, Baumann J, Matsui Y (2014) The cumulative impact of annual coral bleaching can turn some coral species winners into losers. Glob Chang Biol 20:3823–3833
                          526 text ; Cunning et al. 
                          527 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2558, Help: Cunning R, Silverstein RN, Baker AC (2015) Investigating the causes and consequences of symbiont shuffling in a multi-partner reef coral symbiosis under environmental change. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 282:20141725
                          528 text ).
                      529 container
                          530 text Thermally tolerant coral communities from the Rock Island lagoon habitats of Palau are dominated by  Durusdinium trenchii  (Fabricius et al. 
                          531 link Description: Reference 2004, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2567, Help: Fabricius KE, Mieog JC, Colin PL, Idip D, van Oppen MJ (2004) Identity and diversity of coral endosymbionts (zooxanthellae) from three Palauan reefs with contrasting bleaching, temperature and shading histories. Mol Ecol 13:2445–2458
                          532 text ; Hoadley et al. 
                          533 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2570, Help: Hoadley KD, Lewis AM, Wham DC, Pettay DT, Grasso C, Smith R, Kemp DW, LaJeunesse TC, Warner ME (2019) Host-symbiont combinations dictate the photo-physiological response of reef-building corals to thermal stress. Sci Rep 9:9985
                          534 text ; Kemp et al. 
                          535 link Description: Reference 2023, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2573, Help: Kemp DW, Hoadley KD, Lewis AM, Wham DC, Smith RT, Warner ME, LaJeunesse TC (2023) Thermotolerant coral-algal mutualisms maintain high rates of nutrient transfer while exposed to heat stress. Proc Biol Sci 290:20231403
                          536 text ). However,  D. trenchii  dominated few offshore colonies (Fig. 
                          537 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          538 text ). Because this species exists in high abundances in nearby habitats and is compatible with numerous coral taxa, perhaps it is prevalent at low, undetected, abundances in offshore colonies. DGGE-fingerprinting of ITS2 detects co-occurring symbionts at proportions ranging from 1–20%. The sensitivity of DGGE-fingerprinting as well as other PCR-based protocol targeting rDNA, including next-generation sequencing of ITS2-PCR amplicons (Arif et al. 
                          539 link Description: Reference 2014, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2583, Help: Arif C, Daniels C, Bayer T, Banguera-Hinestroza E, Barbrook A, Howe CJ, LaJeunesse TC, Voolstra CR (2014) Assessing Symbiodinium diversity in scleractinian corals via next-generation sequencing-based genotyping of the ITS2 rDNA region. Mol Ecol 23:4418–4433
                          540 text ; Hume et al. 
                          541 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2586, Help: Hume BCC, Smith EG, Ziegler M, Warrington HJM, Burt JA, LaJeunesse TC, Wiedenmann J, Voolstra CR (2019) SymPortal: A novel analytical framework and platform for coral algal symbiont next-generation sequencing ITS2 profiling. Mol Ecol Resour 19:1063–1080
                          542 text ; LaJeunesse et al. 
                          543 link Description: Reference 2022, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2589, Help: LaJeunesse TC, Casado-Amezúa P, Hume BCC, Butler CC, Mordret S, Piredda R, De Luca P, Pannone R, Sarno D, Wiedenmann J, D’Ambra I (2022) Mutualistic dinoflagellates with big disparities in ribosomal DNA variation may confound estimates of symbiont diversity and ecology in the jellyfish Cotylorhiza tuberculata. Symbiosis 88:1–10
                          544 text ), depends upon the rDNA copy number in the genomes of the species under detection (e.g., LaJeunesse et al. 
                          545 link Description: Reference 2008, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2592, Help: LaJeunesse TC, Reyes-Bonilla H, Warner ME, Wills M, Schmidt GW, Fitt WK (2008) Specificity and stability in high latitude eastern Pacific coral-algal symbioses. Limnol Oceanogr 53:719–727
                          546 text ; Saad et al. 
                          547 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2595, Help: Saad OS, Lin X, Ng TY, Li L, Ang P, Lin S (2020) Genome Size, rDNA Copy, and qPCR Assays for Symbiodiniaceae. Front Microbiol 11:847
                          548 text ). Because of its relative low copy rDNA number, detection of  Durusdinium  spp. in background is diminished considerably when co-occurring in populations dominated by  Cladocopium  spp. (LaJeunesse et al. 
                          549 link Description: Reference 2008, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2605, Help: LaJeunesse TC, Reyes-Bonilla H, Warner ME, Wills M, Schmidt GW, Fitt WK (2008) Specificity and stability in high latitude eastern Pacific coral-algal symbioses. Limnol Oceanogr 53:719–727
                          550 text ). Therefore, more sensitive methods of symbiont detection, such as primer specific quantitative PCR (qPCR) assays (Mieog et al. 
                          551 link Description: Reference 2009, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2608, Help: Mieog JC, Van Oppen MJH, Berkelmans R, Stam WT, Olsen JL (2009) Quantification of algal endosymbionts (Symbiodinium) in coral tissue using real-time PCR. Mol Ecol Resour 9:74–82
                          552 text ; Correa et al. 
                          553 link Description: Reference 2009, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d23519560e2611, Help: Correa AMS, McDonald MD, Baker AC (2009) Development of clade-specific Symbiodinium primers for quantitative PCR (qPCR) and their application to detecting clade D symbionts in Caribbean corals. Mar Biol 156:2403–2411
                          554 text ), could be employed to evaluate the prevalence of low abundance background populations among offshore colonies. Given the potential ecological significance of background  Durusdinium trenchii  during and following thermal stress events, further analyses and detection of persistent background populations are warranted (Turnham et al. in review).

                  886 text Our sincere appreciation goes to the staff and scientists at the Palau International Coral Research Center (PICRC) and the Coral Reef Research Foundation (CRRF) for logistical support in the field. We also thank Robert van Woesik (Florida Institute of Technology) for help with coral species identifications and are grateful to Hannah Reich and Andy Shantz for their assistance in sampling. Research activities were made possible by permissions (and permits) from the Ministry of Natural Resources, Environment and Tourism, Palau and from the Koror State Government, Department of Conservation and Law Enforcement. C.C.B. was supported by the NSF Graduate Research Fellowship under Grant No. (DGE1255832). The research was funded by National Science Foundation grants OCE-1719684 and IOS-179675 D.W.K.; grants IOS-1258065 and OCE-1635695 to M.E.W.; and grants IOS-1258058 and OCE-1636022 to T.C.L. This paper is dedicated to the memory of Dr. Scott Ross Santos and his contributions to the science of animal-dinoflagellate mutualisms.

                  53 text Seasonal fluctuation in zooxanthellar genotype composition and photophysiology in the corals  Pavona divaricata  and  P. decussata
              54 content list
                  55 link Description: Ryota Suwa, Value: int-res.com/journals/meps/articles/meps07372#Author
                  56 link Description: Mamiko Hirose, Value: int-res.com/journals/meps/articles/meps07372#Author

                      59 link int-res.com/journals/meps/articles/meps07372#
              60 container
                  61 text ABSTRACT:  We simultaneously examined seasonal fluctuations in maximum quantum yield ( F
                  62 text v
                  63 text / F
                  64 text m
                  65 text ), cell density and genotypic clade composition of zooxanthellae in the sympatric corals  Pavona divaricata  and  P .  decussata  at a high latitude site in Okinawa, Japan. The 2 species had different responses to seasonal changes in light and seawater temperature.  P. decussata  was associated only with clade C zooxanthellae (at all sampling times) while genotypic clade composition fluctuated in  P .  divaricata . Three colonies of  P .  divaricata  harbored clade D throughout the year and the other 7 colonies changed clade type from C to D or vice versa, or contained a mixture of both clades on some sampling occasions. Though neither coral species suffered bleaching during the experimental period, there were  F
                  66 text v
                  67 text / F
                  68 text m
                  69 text  decreases in  P. decussata  and  P. divaricata  harboring clade C during cold and warm seasons;  F
                  70 text v
                  71 text / F
                  72 text m
                  73 text  of  P. divaricata  harboring clade D was stable. When exposed to low or high temperature under normal or high light,  P. divaricata  harboring clade D was less damaged and Photosystem II recovery was faster than in  P. decussata  harboring clade C. These results suggest that the sympatric congeneric corals have different symbiont switching flexibilities and this difference might account for the observed difference in stress susceptibility between the two species. In high-latitude reefs, both winter low temperatures and summer high temperatures may be potential stressors that cause coral bleaching, at least in corals with high clade C zooxanthellar fidelity.

                          91 container
                              92 container abstract1
                                  93 heading Abstract, Value: 2
                                      94 text Abstract
                                  95 container st1
                                      96 heading Objective:, Value: 3
                                          97 text Objective:
                                      98 text This study aims to evaluate the effect of saliva contamination on the shear bond strength of two self-etch dentine bonding systems and also investigate the effect of decontamination procedure on the recovery of bond strength.
                                  99 container st2
                                      100 heading Materials and Methods:, Value: 3
                                          101 text Materials and Methods:
                                      102 container
                                          103 text Sixty premolars extracted for orthodontic reason were obtained and the buccal surfaces of teeth were reduced to create a flat dentine surface. The samples were randomly divided into three sub-groups for AdheSE (ASE) (Ivoclar – Vivadent, Schaan, Liechtenstein) and three sub-groups for Adper Prompt Self-Etch Adhesive (ADP) (3M ESPE, St Paul, MN, USA) of 10 each. For AdheSE (ASE); ASE-I was the control group (primer applied to fresh dentine surface), ASE-II was the contamination group (primer applied, followed by saliva contamination and then air dried) and ASE-III was the decontamination group (primer applied, followed by saliva contamination, air dried and then primer reapplied). For Adper Prompt (ADP); ADP-I was the control group (self-etch adhesive applied to fresh dentine surface), ADP-II was the contamination group (self-etch adhesive applied, followed by saliva contamination and then air dried) and ADP-III was the decontamination group (self-etch adhesive applied, followed by saliva contamination, air dried and then self-etch adhesive reapplied). Followed by the bonding procedure, a 5 mm composite resin block with Filtek P-60 (3M ESPE, St Paul, MN, USA) was built on the substrate. Shear bond strength (SBS) was tested with Instron Universal testing machine (Instron Corporation, Canton, MA, USA) with a cross head speed of 1 mm per minute. Data obtained was subjected to one way ANOVA test, while the inter group comparison was made using Tukey’s multiple comparison and Unpaired  t -test.
                                  104 container st3
                                      105 heading Results:, Value: 3
                                          106 text Results:
                                      107 text In AdhSE group (ASE), the sub-group ASE-II (contamination group) [5.4 ± 2.2 MPa] showed lower SBS than ASE-I [11.8 ± 2.6 MPa] and ASE-III [8.9 ± 3.3 MPa], which was statistically significant. There was no significant difference in the bond strength between the ASE-I (control group) and ASE-III (decontamination group). In Adper Prompt group (ADP), there was a severe decrease of bond strength in ADP-II (contamination group) [4.6 ± 1.1 MPa] when compared to ADP-I (control group) [7.4 ± 1.4 MPa] and ADP-III (decontamination subgroup) [14.1 ± 2.2 MPa] which was statistically significant. The bond strength of ADP-III wherein Adper Prompt bonding agent was reapplied after salivary contamination was found to be statistically significant than ADP-I and ADP-II.
                                  108 container st4
                                      109 heading Conclusion:, Value: 3
                                          110 text Conclusion:
                                      111 text Saliva contamination reduces the dentine bond strength of both the self-etch systems; AdheSE and Adper Prompt. Re-application of the primer for the AdheSE and re-application of the adhesive for the Adper Prompt after air drying the saliva off can recover the dentine bond strength. In the Adper Prompt group, the added application of adhesives to decontaminate saliva not only recovered the bond strength but also improved it significantly.
                                  112 container
                                      113 text Keywords:  Decontamination procedure, salivary contamination, self-etch adhesive system, shear bond strength
                              114 container sec1-1
                                  115 heading INTRODUCTION, Value: 2
                                      116 text INTRODUCTION
                                  117 container
                                      118 text Adhesion to dentine has been a subject of considerable interest because it is a more heterogeneous substrate with much higher organic and water content than enamel.[
                                      119 link (collapsed) Description: 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      120 text ] The condition of the tooth structure and the chemical composition of the adhesive agent have shown to affect the bond strength.[
                                      121 link (collapsed) Description: 2, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      122 text ] Hence, improving adhesive restorative materials has been the objective of research in the recent years.
                                  123 container
                                      124 text Clinically, there are many factors that affect adhesion and retention of resin-containing restorative materials. Moisture such as gingival fluid, blood, hand-piece oil[
                                      125 link (collapsed) Description: 3, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      126 text ] and, in particular saliva, can affect the quality of the bond, leading to micro-leakage at the tooth restoration interface. This may result in the loss of restoration, recurrent caries, postoperative sensitivity and discoloration.[
                                      127 link (collapsed) Description: 4, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      128 text ] Therefore the bonding procedure requires proper isolation and prevention of contamination. However, many carious lesions which require the use of dentine bonding agents are found in the areas that are difficult to isolate, especially when the site is near or at the gingival margin where saliva contamination is more likely to occur.[
                                      129 link (collapsed) Description: 5, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      130 text ]
                                  131 container
                                      132 text Silverstone  et al .[
                                      133 link (collapsed) Description: 6, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      134 text ] have reported that saliva contamination of etched enamel caused a significant decrease in bond strength between the resin and enamel surface. It was suggested that the contamination of etched enamel by salivary proteins prevented monomers from penetrating the pores in enamel, which reduced the bond strength.[
                                      135 link (collapsed) Description: 3, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      136 text ] Microscopic examination of saliva contaminated acid-etched enamel showed the formation of an organic pellicle that could not be removed with water.[
                                      137 link (collapsed) Description: 6, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      138 text ] The organic pellicle coating masked the underlying enamel pores, decreased resin accessibility and impaired mechanical adhesion. However, the contaminated enamel could be reconditioned by an additional 10 seconds of acid etching.[
                                      139 link (collapsed) Description: 7, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      140 text ]
                                  141 container
                                      142 text Dentine adhesion is extremely complex when compared to enamel bonding. The micromechanical resin adhesion to dentine differs fundamentally from the relatively simple interlocking of bonding agents with enamel. Therefore the result of many studies related to the bonding efficacy of saliva contaminated dentine bonding agents has varied.[
                                      143 link (collapsed) Description: 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      144 text ] Fritz, Finger and Stean[
                                      145 link (collapsed) Description: 8, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      146 text ] found that saliva contamination of cured one-bottle type adhesive resulted in low shear bond strengths and wide marginal gaps. On the contrary, others reported that the saliva contamination of dentine had no adverse effect on the bonding efficiency of one-bottle adhesive systems.[
                                      147 link (collapsed) Description: 9, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      148 text –
                                      149 link (collapsed) Description: 11, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      150 text ]
                                  151 container
                                      152 text Recently developed adhesive systems such as the “self-etching primers” and the ”self-etch adhesives” have shown to be resistant to salivary contamination.[
                                      153 link (collapsed) Description: 4, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      154 text ,
                                      155 link (collapsed) Description: 12, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      156 text ] Self-etch systems eliminate the rinsing and drying steps which simplifies the bonding procedure. In addition to this, the possibility of over wetting or over drying is reduced, which in turn helps in better adhesion.[
                                      157 link (collapsed) Description: 13, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      158 text –
                                      159 link (collapsed) Description: 15, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      160 text ] These dentine bonding agents have a reduced number of components and application steps and this reduces the risk of saliva contamination in the field of operation.[
                                      161 link (collapsed) Description: 16, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      162 text ]
                                  163 text Hence this study was conducted to evaluate the influence of saliva contamination of dentine during the bonding procedure on shear bond strength and to investigate the effect of contamination removing treatment on the recovery of bond strength of two self-etch dentine bonding systems.
                              164 container sec1-2
                                  165 heading MATERIALS AND METHODS, Value: 2
                                      166 text MATERIALS AND METHODS
                                  167 container
                                      168 text We tested two dentine adhesives in the study: AdheSE (Ivoclar – Vivadent, Schaan, Liechtenstein) and Adper Prompt Self-Etch Adhesive (3M ESPE, St Paul, MN, USA) [
                                      169 link Description: Table 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                      170 text ]. Filtek P-60 posterior restorative composite resin (3M ESPE, St Paul, MN, USA) was used in both the groups. Sixty premolars extracted for orthodontic reasons were obtained for the shear bond test. The teeth were debrided, cleaned and stored in isotonic saline, until use. The teeth were sectioned at the cementodentinal junction and the coronal portion of the teeth was embedded in acrylic with the buccal surface facing outwards. The buccal surface of the teeth was reduced to create flat dentine surface with a medium grit diamond bur using high-speed handpiece under air water spray. The specimens were then randomly divided into two groups (AdheSE (ASE) group and Adper Prompt (ADP) group) of 30 samples each.
                                  171 container T0001
                                      172 heading Table 1., Value: 3
                                          173 text Table 1.
                                      174 text Chemical composition of the bonding systems tested
                                      175 table
                                          176 row
                                              177 cell
                                                  178 text Product name

                                                  187 text AdheSE
                                              188 cell
                                                  189 text Ivoclar – Vivadent Schaan, Liechtenstein
                                              190 cell
                                                  191 text Primer: dimethacrylate, phosphoric acid acrylate, initiators, stabilizers, Water bond: HEMA, dimethacrylate, silicon dioxide, initiators
                                              192 cell
                                                  193 text Apply self-etch primer for at least 30 seconds. Remove excess of primer with air. Apply the bonding agent and gently air blow. Light cure for 10 seconds.
                                          194 row
                                              195 cell
                                                  196 text Adper Prompt
                                              197 cell
                                                  198 text 3M ESPE St Paul, MN USA
                                              199 cell
                                                  200 text Liquid 1: methacrylated phosphoric esters, BisGMA, camphorquinone, stabilizers Liquid 2: water, HEMA, polyalkenoic acid, stabilizers
                                              201 cell
                                                  202 text Mix two solutions (A and B) for five seconds, apply the mixture for 15 seconds, gently air dry and light cure for 10 seconds.
                                      203 link Description: Open in a new tab, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                  204 text For each adhesive, the specimens were divided into non-contaminated (which was the control group), contaminated and decontaminated sub-groups (which were the experimental groups). Ten specimens were made for each procedure. In the experimental groups, fresh whole saliva was applied to the surface of the specimens with a disposable brush for 5 seconds, followed by the contaminant removing treatment, if applicable. Details of the bonding procedure for each adhesive are presented. Following the bonding procedure, a 5 mm composite resin block was built on the substrate using a plastic tube having an internal diameter of 4.9 mm by progressively adding 1.5 to 2 mm thick increments. In order to ensure the proper polymerization of each added layer of composite resin, the light tip was positioned as close as possible to the surface.
                                  205 container
                                      206 text After polymerization, the teeth were sectioned 1 mm apical to cemento-enamel junction and the specimens were mounted in cylindrical molds with self-curing acrylic resins. Shear bond strength was tested with an Instron Universal testing machine (Instron Corporation, Canton, MA, USA). Each specimen was mounted in a shear testing apparatus and a chisel shaped shearing rod with a cross-head speed of 1 mm per minute was used to load the specimens at the dentine-composite interface. The shear bond strength data was subjected to One-way ANOVA test, while the intergroup comparison was made using Tukey multiple comparison and Unpaired  t -test.
                              207 container sec1-3

                                      214 link Description: 3, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                      215 text  and 
                                      216 link Description: Figure 1, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                      217 text . One-way ANOVA test revealed a significant difference at  P  <0.05. Comparisons within the groups ASE and ADP are shown in Tables 
                                      218 link Description: 4, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                      219 text  and

                                  418 container
                                      419 text In the AdheSE group (ASE), the difference was very highly significant ( P  = 0.001) between the control (ASE-I) and the contamination sub-group (ASE-II). The shear bond strength decreased to 5.4 ± 2.2 MPa when compared to 11.8 ± 2.6 MPa of control group. However, when the self -etch primer was reapplied after the salivary contamination (ASE-III), the bond strength increased to 8.9 ± 3.3 MPa ( P  = 0.019). There was no significant difference in the bond strength between the control and the decontamination group ( P  = 0.064).
                                  420 container
                                      421 text In Adper Prompt group (ADP), when the dentine was not contaminated (ADP-I), the shear bond strength was 7.4 ± 1.5 MPa. When the salivary contamination occurred after the curing of the bonding agent (ADP-II), the bond strength decreased to 4.6 ± 1.1 MPa. This decrease in bond strength was highly significant ( P = 0.003). The bond strength of ADP-III where Adper Prompt bonding agent was reapplied after salivary contamination was 14.1 ± 2.2 MPa. This was statistically very highly significant than the control group and the group where salivary contamination was done ( P = 0.001).
                                  422 container
                                      423 text Intergroup comparisons between ASE and ADP were done using Unpaired  t -test. 
                                      424 link Description: Table 6, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…
                                      425 text  shows the comparison of bond strength when the specimens were not contaminated with saliva. There was statistically very highly significant difference between the mean bond strengths of ASE-I and ADP-I ( P =0.001). The control specimens of AdheSE group showed higher bond strength than that of Adper Prompt group.

                              472 container sec1-4
                                  473 heading DISCUSSION, Value: 2
                                      474 text DISCUSSION
                                  475 container
                                      476 text The laboratory parameter most often measured in dentine adhesion is shear bond strength. Flat dentine surfaces are prepared in the extracted tooth, the adhesive system is applied and the composite resin cylinder is bonded over the adhesive. A shear force is then applied at the resin–dentine interface, using a knife-edge probe. The shear bond strength test is only a rough tool for evaluating the relative efficacy of bonding materials. Never the less, they are excellent for screening new materials and for comparing the same parameter among different adhesive systems.[
                                      477 link (collapsed) Description: 17, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      478 text ]
                                  479 container
                                      480 text Saliva contamination of operating field is a frequent problem in restorative procedures, especially when rubber dam isolation is difficult or impossible, such as in the case of deep cervical lesions or to seat an indirect restoration or even in patients having problem in opening their mouth. In the present study natural saliva was chosen as the contaminant because artificial saliva may confound the results. In addition, many studies have accepted whole healthy human saliva as an acceptable contaminating medium. An  in vitro  model to mimic clinical conditions proved that saliva and plasma to be detrimental to hybrid layer formation.[
                                      481 link (collapsed) Description: 8, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      482 text ]
                                  483 container
                                      484 text Effect of saliva contamination is a matter of great controversy. Few studies have reported that the use of dentine bonding agents under fissure sealants has reduced their sensitivity to saliva contamination and provided high bond strengths.[
                                      485 link (collapsed) Description: 18, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      486 text ,
                                      487 link (collapsed) Description: 19, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      488 text ] Some have reported that the saliva contamination of dentine had no adverse effect on the bonding efficiency of one-bottle adhesive systems.[
                                      489 link (collapsed) Description: 9, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      490 text –
                                      491 link (collapsed) Description: 11, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      492 text ] Others have shown that the saliva contamination of the dentine surface produced a significant decrease in the bond strength.[
                                      493 link (collapsed) Description: 3, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      494 text ,
                                      495 link (collapsed) Description: 8, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      496 text ,
                                      497 link (collapsed) Description: 17, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      498 text ,
                                      499 link (collapsed) Description: 20, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      500 text ]
                                  501 container
                                      502 text The factors that can be hypothesized as the cause for reduction in the bond strength in saliva contaminated dentine are as follows:[
                                      503 link (collapsed) Description: 8, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      504 text ,
                                      505 link (collapsed) Description: 21, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      506 text ]
                                  507 content list
                                      508 container
                                          509 AXListMarker 1. 
                                          510 text Adsorption of glycoprotein to the poorly polymerized adhesive surface where they might act as a barrier that prevents complete wetting with the next increment of resin and thus prevent adequate co-polymerization.
                                      511 container
                                          512 AXListMarker 2. 
                                          513 text Salivary proteins might prevent monomers from penetrating the collagen network of dentine or there can be an increase in the contact angle which could decrease the bond strength.
                                      514 container
                                          515 AXListMarker 3. 
                                          516 text Excess saliva may dilute the primer and thus produce a weak hybrid layer.
                                      517 container
                                          518 AXListMarker 4. 
                                          519 text Co-polymerization with the subsequent resin layer could be compromised by the removal of the oxygen inhibited unpolymerized surface layer. This hypothesis is not likely as investigators have shown that there is no difference in bond strength when resin composite is added and polymerized on cured adhesive with or without an unpolymerized surface layer.
                                  520 container
                                      521 text Ghavam and Pour[
                                      522 link (collapsed) Description: 20, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      523 text ] showed that there was no significant difference when the contaminated dentine was either washed or washed and re-etched. Fritz  et al [
                                      524 link (collapsed) Description: 8, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      525 text ] showed that re-etching is not necessary when contamination with the saliva happens. EL -Kalla and Godoy[
                                      526 link (collapsed) Description: 12, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      527 text ] believed that when saliva contamination happens after etching the dentine, blot drying the surface achieves bond strength equal to that of the uncontaminated group. Studies have also shown that the reapplication of primer/ adhesive to improve the bonding efficiency after saliva contamination.[
                                      528 link (collapsed) Description: 22, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      529 text ,
                                      530 link (collapsed) Description: 23, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      531 text ]
                                  532 container
                                      533 text The hydrophilic nature of the newer dentine bonding agents may allow them to function to some degree in the presence of saliva contamination by displacing or diffusing through it and then they infiltrate and polymerize within the exposed collagen bundles of demineralized superficial dentine. AdheSE is a relatively new self- etching system containing a primer composed of phosphonic acid acrylate, bis-acrylamide, water, initiators and stabilizers. It also contains a bonding component composed of dimethacrylate, HEMA and highly dispersed silicon-dioxide, initiators and stabilizers. In the AdheSE group, when the saliva contamination was done after the application of self etching primer, bond strength decreased significantly. However, the bond strength could be recovered after reapplication of the primer. This result was in agreement with the study done by Park and Lee.[
                                      534 link (collapsed) Description: 17, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      535 text ]
                                  536 container
                                      537 text Adper Prompt Self-Etch Adhesive is based on the original Prompt-L-Pop adhesive and is composed of methacrylated phosphonic esters, BisGMA, initiators, stabilizers, water, HEMA and poly alkenoic acid. In Adper Prompt group, there was a significant decrease in bond strength when saliva contamination occurred after curing the bonding agent. This finding confirms the observation of Fritz and others[
                                      538 link (collapsed) Description: 8, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      539 text ] who have shown that saliva contamination of the cured adhesive layer of one-bottle adhesive system has a detrimental effect on bond strength.
                                  540 container
                                      541 text Studies have shown that saliva contamination reduces the dentine bond strengths of all-in-one adhesives and supplementary application of the adhesive after cleaning the saliva from the dentine surface is an empirical recommendation for restoring bond strength.[
                                      542 link (collapsed) Description: 22, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      543 text ,
                                      544 link (collapsed) Description: 23, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      545 text ] In contrast to the results of this study, Ghavan and Pour[
                                      546 link (collapsed) Description: 20, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      547 text ] have shown that contamination of a single bottle system after curing of the adhesive did not decrease the bond strength compared to the control group.
                                  548 container
                                      549 text An interesting finding in Adper Prompt group was that the bond strength obtained in the sub-group where the bonding agent was reapplied after saliva contamination was higher than the control group. This increase in bond strength was very highly significant ( P = 0.001). The increased bond strength could be due to the effect of multiple adhesive coatings. The increased resin-dentine bond strength under multiple applications could be due to several mechanisms operating simultaneously. As the solvent is evaporated the concentration of the co-monomers that exists after each coating increases. This improves the hybrid layer and the ratio of the polymerized vs. unpolymerized adhesive layer due to oxygen inhibition. Hashimoto and others[
                                      550 link (collapsed) Description: 24, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      551 text –
                                      552 link (collapsed) Description: 26, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      553 text ] have hypothesized that when multiple coats of hydrophilic adhesive solutions are applied, it can displace or diffuse through the film to reach the underlying layer and improve the bond strength.
                                  554 container
                                      555 text Intergroup comparison of ASE-I (control) and ADP-I (control) showed that AdheSE has higher bond strength to that of Adper Prompt. This difference in the bond strength was very highly significant ( P = 0.001). The low bond strength obtained with this system may be due to an incomplete infiltration of the acidic monomers and subsequent partial dissolution of the smear layer, suggesting inconsistent performance in terms of achieving a quality bond.[
                                      556 link (collapsed) Description: 27, Value: pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.go…, Secondary Actions: Expand
                                      557 text ]
                                  558 text Further studies have to be conducted to prove these results.
                              559 container sec1-5
                                  560 heading CONCLUSIONS, Value: 2
                                      561 text CONCLUSIONS
                                  562 container
                                      563 text The following conclusions can be drawn within the limitations of this  in vitro  study;
                                  564 content list
                                      565 container
                                          566 AXListMarker 1. 
                                          567 text The self etch primer [AdhSE (ASE-I)] showed better bond strength than self-etch adhesive [Adper Prompt (ADP-I)] when not contaminated with saliva.
                                      568 container
                                          569 AXListMarker 2. 
                                          570 text Salivary contamination reduced the dentine bond strength of both the self-etch primer (ASE-II) and adhesives (ADP-II).
                                      571 container
                                          572 AXListMarker 3. 
                                          573 text Re-application of the primer for the AdhSE group (ASE-III) and re-application of the adhesive for the Adper Prompt group (ADP-III), after air drying the saliva off, can recover the dentine bond strength.
                                      574 container
                                          575 AXListMarker 4. 
                                          576 text In the Adper Prompt group, the added application of adhesives to decontaminate (ADP-III), not only recovered the bond strength but also improved it significantly, which could be attributed to the effect of multiple adhesive coatings
                              577 container fn-group1

              61 container
                  62 text ABSTRACT:  Seasonal dynamics of algal symbiont communities from the reef flat-dwelling coral  Acropora palifera  was monitored from January 2000 to July 2001 at Tantzei Bay, Kenting National Park, southern Taiwan. Zooxanthellae density and pigmentcontents monitored throughout the 18 mo sampling period indicated that no significant bleaching occurred in  A. palifera . Molecular phylotyping showed that 2 distinct symbionts, Phylotypes C and D, were associated with  A. palifera , eitherindividually or simultaneously. Population surveys throughout the bimonthly sampling period demonstrated that the symbiont community within  A. palifera  was highly dynamic with significant fluctuations; a drop in the Phylotype D percentage occurredin May, which was correlated with a rise in seawater temperature in the late spring/early summer at the sampled reef. Direct tracking of tagged corals provided evidence that seasonal fluctuations in the algal symbiont communities not only involve changesin zooxanthellae densities and pigment contents, but also a reshuffling of different  Symbiodinium  phylotypes. Our study highlights that stress tolerance among phylotypes urgently needs to be re-evaluated through a better understanding of thephysiological traits of symbionts.

The reviewer’s four papers all meet the biological criteria and should be included. Three—Chen (2005), Kemp (2014), and LaJeunesse (2010)—were present in my earlier candidate results but not in your existing meta-analysis. Cunning (2016) was a genuine search omission.

I broadened the search in two defensible ways:

  • Historical Symbiodinium clades/phylotypes count as genus-level resolution because clades A–D broadly correspond to the modern genera Symbiodinium, Breviolum, Cladocopium, and Durusdinium.
  • Removing small tissue fragments for observational molecular sampling is not considered experimental manipulation. Where a paper also contains an experiment, only the unmanipulated reef time series is eligible.

Reviewer-recommended papers

Paper Why it qualifies GitHub NCBI/GenBank Other public data
Chen, C. A., Wang, J.-T., Fang, L.-S., & Yang, Y.-W. (2005). Fluctuating algal symbiont communities in Acropora palifera (Scleractinia: Acroporidae) from Taiwan. Marine Ecology Progress Series, 295, 113–121. https://doi.org/10.3354/meps295113 Directly tracked tagged reef colonies bimonthly from January 2000–July 2001. RFLP phylotyping detected C, D, and mixed C/D communities. No manipulation. None stated None stated None stated
LaJeunesse, T. C., Smith, R., Walther, M., Pinzón, J., Pettay, D. T., McGinley, M., Aschaffenburg, M., Medina-Rosas, P., Cupul-Magaña, A. L., Pérez, A. L., Reyes-Bonilla, H., & Warner, M. E. (2010). Host–symbiont recombination versus natural selection in the response of coral–dinoflagellate symbioses to environmental disturbance. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences, 277, 2925–2934. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2010.0385 Tagged Pocillopora colonies were resampled following natural cold-water bleaching. ITS2-DGGE resolved colony-level symbiont types through time. None stated No consolidated project accession stated None stated
Kemp, D. W., Hernández-Pech, X., Iglesias-Prieto, R., Fitt, W. K., & Schmidt, G. W. (2014). Community dynamics and physiology of Symbiodinium spp. before, during, and after a coral bleaching event. Limnology and Oceanography, 59(3), 788–797. https://doi.org/10.4319/lo.2014.59.3.0788 Tagged Orbicella faveolata colonies were followed before, during, and after natural bleaching in Puerto Morelos. The same colony patches were resampled and ITS2 types—including A3, B17, and C7—were measured. None stated None stated None stated
Cunning, R., Ritson-Williams, R., & Gates, R. D. (2016). Patterns of bleaching and recovery of Montipora capitata in Kāneʻohe Bay, Hawaiʻi, USA. Marine Ecology Progress Series, 551, 131–139. https://doi.org/10.3354/meps11733 Sixty individually tagged reef colonies—naturally bleached and non-bleached—were sampled on six dates from October 2014–April 2015. qPCR quantified clades C and D; ITS2 identified C31 in a subset. No treatment was imposed. None stated None stated Data and scripts; environmental records 53226 and 53227

Cunning was probably missed because its title emphasizes bleaching and recovery rather than longitudinal symbiont-community monitoring.

Additional eligible papers found in the rerun

Full citation Eligible longitudinal component GitHub NCBI/GenBank Other public data
Suwa, R., Hirose, M., & Hidaka, M. (2008). Seasonal fluctuation in zooxanthellar genotype composition and photophysiology in the corals Pavona divaricata and P. decussata. Marine Ecology Progress Series, 361, 129–137. https://doi.org/10.3354/meps07372 Repeated field measurements of identifiable colonies over a year resolved clades C, D, and mixed C/D communities. Include only the unmanipulated reef time series; exclude the separate laboratory temperature/light exposures. None stated None stated None stated
Hume, B. C. C., D’Angelo, C., Smith, E. G., Stevens, J. R., Burt, J., & Wiedenmann, J. (2015). Symbiodinium thermophilum sp. nov., a thermotolerant symbiotic alga prevalent in corals of the world’s hottest sea, the Persian/Arabian Gulf. Scientific Reports, 5, 8562. https://doi.org/10.1038/srep08562 Three tagged colonies of each of six scleractinian species were sampled at eight field time points over 22 months. ITS2-DGGE resolved A1, C1, C3, C15, D1–4 and other types. Use the Saadiyat reef series; exclude separate aquarium-derived samples used for supplementary phylogenetic work. None stated KM487747–KM487749; KP234522–KP234524; KM458273–KM458294 Dryad

Publications requiring dataset deduplication

These satisfy the design but should not automatically become independent meta-analytic studies:

  • Lewis, A. M., Butler, C. C., Turnham, K. E., Hoadley, K. D., Smith, R. T., Kemp, D. W., Wham, D. F., Warner, M. E., & LaJeunesse, T. C. (2024). The diversity, distribution, and temporal stability of coral ‘zooxanthellae’ on a Pacific reef: from the scale of individual colonies to across the host community. Coral Reefs, 43, 841–856. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00338-024-02503-x. Its Palau 2013–2022 colony cohort appears to overlap your included Turnham et al. (2025) study.

  • Buzzoni, D., Van Nynatten, A., Cunning, R., & Baum, J. K. (2026). Persistent legacy effects of marine heatwaves on coral symbioses. Global Change Biology, 32(3), e70818. https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.70818. Its 237 Kiritimati colonies and 2014–2023 sampling almost certainly overlap Van Nynatten et al. (2025). Data: NCBI PRJNA1294313, GitHub, and Zenodo.

Therefore, the corrected search adds at least Cunning (2016), Suwa et al. (2008), and Hume et al. (2015), while confirming that Chen (2005), LaJeunesse (2010), and Kemp (2014) are eligible additions to your attached meta-analysis.

Can you see if the individual level colony data was reported from this paper in any subsequent papers?

Seasonal fluctuation in zooxanthellar genotype composition and photophysiology in the corals Pavona divaricata and P. decussata

It’s only aggregated to the opulation level within.

6 previous messages

I’ll trace papers, theses, and data repositories that cite Suwa et al. (2008), looking specifically for reused colony IDs or per-colony genotype/photophysiology records—not merely citations to its population-level conclusions.

                                  52 text Long-term studies of individual coral colonies show that 
                                  53 button zooxanthellae
                                  54 text  (Symbiodiniaceae) communities generally remain stable over time , dominated by specific clonal strains, though  some environments or thermal stress events prompt shifts in symbiont composition .

                              59 heading Key Concepts in Symbiont Fluctuations, Value: 3
                                  60 text Key Concepts in Symbiont Fluctuations
                              61 content list
                                  62 container
                                      63 AXListMarker • 
                                      64 text Colony Stability:  Multi-year tracking of tagged coral colonies reveals that a single species and strain typically dominate the symbiont population consistently across seasons and years.
                                      65 link Description: Harvard University, Value: google.com/goto?url=CAESeQHrOzAVrCNm52UaIchHjnFtEYGfLLCLFXSamcSY6zCl1zHMdGp0uHFxqut-d5qMwBiZaBRoNV0CgM9f2kU2PCH-An2uDrOXkNGm5lFtOmIYi13veSSS12tsF2D29iO8iuBBNtbKMUdEHYnKHd3NkquyxM99q9Jq10M
                                      66 button Harvard University - Related results
                                          67 text Harvard University
                                  68 container
                                      69 AXListMarker • 
                                      70 text Symbiont Shuffling:  In response to seasonal temperature extremes or bleaching stressors, some coral colonies can shift or "shuffle" their dominant zooxanthellae types—such as replacing heat-sensitive  Cladocopium  (clade C) with more thermal-tolerant  Durusdinium  (clade D).

                      38 link Description: [PDF] researchgate.net, Value: researchgate.net/profile/Ryota-Suwa-2/publication/240624254_Seasonal_fluctuation_in_zooxanthella_genotype_composition_and_photophysiology_in_the_corals_Pavona_divaricata_and_P_decussata/links/541a66950cf2218008bfb550/Seasonal-fluctuation-in-zooxanthella-genotype-composition-and-photophysiology-in-the-corals-Pavona-divaricata-and-P-decussata.pdf
                      39 link Description: Find article @ UNC, Value: scholar.google.com/scholar?output=instlink&q=info:RvN5sY3o9A4J:scholar.google.com/&hl=en&as_sdt=0,34&scillfp=16637815024194989513&oi=lle
                  40 heading Value: 3, Seasonal fluctuation in zooxanthellar genotype composition and photophysiology in the corals Pavona divaricata and P. decussata
                      41 link Value: int-res.com/journals/meps/articles/meps07372, ID: RvN5sY3o9A4J, Description: Seasonal fluctuation in zooxanthellar genotype composition and photophysiology in the corals Pavona divaricata and P. decussata
                  42 link Description: R Suwa, Value: scholar.google.com/citations?user=099lm_4AAAAJ&hl=en&oi=sra
                  43 text , M Hirose, M Hidaka Marine Ecology Progress Series, 2008 • int-res.com
                  44 text Abstract
                  45 container
                      46 text We simultaneously examined seasonal fluctuations in maximum quantum yield (F v/F m), cell density and genotypic clade composition of zooxanthellae in the sympatric corals Pavona divaricata and P. decussata at a high latitude site in Okinawa, Japan. The 2 species had different responses to seasonal changes in light and seawater temperature. P. decussata was associated only with clade C zooxanthellae (at all sampling times) while genotypic clade composition fluctuated in P. divaricata. Three colonies of P. divaricata harbored clade D throughout the year and the other 7 colonies changed clade type from C to D or vice versa, or contained a mixture of both clades on some sampling occasions. Though neither coral species suffered bleaching during the experimental period, there were F v/F m decreases in P. decussata and P. divaricata harboring clade C during cold and warm seasons; F v/F m of P. divaricata harboring clade D was stable. When exposed to low or high temperature under normal or high light, P. divaricata harboring clade D was less damaged and Photosystem II recovery was faster than in P. decussata harboring clade C. These results suggest that the sympatric congeneric corals have different symbiont switching flexibilities and this difference might account for the observed difference in stress susceptibility between the two species. In high-latitude reefs, both winter low temperatures and summer high temperatures may be potential stressors that cause coral bleaching, at least in corals with high clade C zooxanthellar fidelity.

The focused UI element is 1 AXWebArea 琉球大学学術リポジトリ, URL: u-ryukyu.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/2001060

I found one closely related record from the same authors: a 2007 University of the Ryukyus research report that predates the journal article and appears to present the same study. I’m checking whether it contains colony-by-date values or only the same summarized figures; the later citing literature so far uses Suwa et al. only as background and does not reuse its raw observations.

The focused UI element is 1 AXWebArea "10.3354/meps07372" (Dryad OR Zenodo OR Figshare OR dataset OR supplement) - Google Search, URL: google.com/search?q=%2210.3354%2Fmeps07372%22+(Dryad+OR+Zenodo+OR+Figshare+OR+dataset+OR+supplement)

I could not find any subsequent paper or public repository that reports the Suwa et al. (2008) colony-by-date data.

I checked its 51 citing publications, author-linked records, and searches across Dryad, Zenodo, Figshare, and institutional repositories.

The only closely related record is:

Suwa, R., Hirose, M., & Hidaka, M. (2007). Divergent fluctuations in zooxanthella genotypes and physiological characteristics in the two species of genus Pavona. University of the Ryukyus research report. Repository record · PDF

However:

  • It predates the journal paper and appears to be a preliminary presentation of the same study.
  • The repository supplies only the report PDF, not a spreadsheet or colony-level dataset.
  • I found no evidence that it provides the complete colony × sampling-date matrix.
  • Later citing papers—including Lee et al. (2016), Rouzé et al. (2019), and Lewis et al. (2024)—cite the conclusions but analyze independent colonies and do not reproduce Suwa’s observations.

The recoverable information is limited to statements such as three P. divaricata colonies remaining clade D and seven showing some C/D change. That is insufficient to reconstruct individual longitudinal trajectories.

Therefore, I would mark Suwa et al. (2008) as:

Biologically eligible, but unusable for the meta-analysis because colony-level longitudinal outcomes are unavailable.

The remaining route would be a direct data request to Ryota Suwa, Mamiko Hirose, or Michio Hidaka.

Did your search look for keywords like “symbiont dynamics”? If not, rerun to check for additional papers. If so, there is no need for another search.

5 previous messages

I did not use the exact phrase “symbiont dynamics” as a primary search term; earlier searches emphasized “tagged colonies,” longitudinal sampling, and bleaching. I’ll rerun specifically with “symbiont dynamics/community dynamics” and screen any new results against the same colony-level, field-only, unmanipulated criteria.

                  58 container Abs1-section
                      59 heading Abstract, Value: 2, ID: Abs1
                          60 text Abstract
                      61 container
                          62 text As marine heatwaves increasingly threaten coral reefs worldwide, some extreme reef environments naturally expose corals to high-temperature fluctuations and can therefore provide important insights into the mechanisms underlying coral heat tolerance. Coral reefs in the Kimberley region in northwest Australia experience the world’s largest tropical tides and are therefore exposed to highly fluctuating temperatures in the intertidal. In contrast, the subtidal remains mostly submerged, resulting in moderate daily temperature fluctuations. A marine heatwave in 2016 triggered wide-spread bleaching in the Kimberley. Intertidal corals bleached less and recovered faster than adjacent subtidal corals; however, the mechanisms underlying this differential bleaching and recovery response remain poorly understood. Here we assessed both host- and symbiont-based indicators of bleaching resilience in the coral  Acropora aspera . We tagged visibly healthy and bleached colonies from both environments in April 2016 and measured symbiont community composition, cell density, chlorophyll  a , total biomass and host tissue energy reserves (lipids, protein and carbohydrates) during bleaching in April and in November 2016. Bleaching severity was higher in the subtidal than in intertidal, and while  Cladocopium  dominated all corals, symbiont community compositions differed significantly between environments and between bleached and healthy subtidal corals. Interestingly, bleaching resilience seemed decoupled from energy reserves, even though high levels of energy reserves and/or sufficient consumption during bleaching are widely thought to increase resistance to and recovery from bleaching. Although all bleached/recovered corals showed a general pattern of catabolizing protein reserves, distinct environment-specific trends were observed: subtidal corals that suffered extensive mortality also catabolized energy-poor carbohydrate reserves. In contrast, intertidal corals recovered rapidly after bleaching and maintained energy reserves. Total biomass remained unchanged between bleached and healthy corals in both environments. Overall, the findings of this study demonstrate that the consumption of energy reserves during bleaching is not always a reliable indicator of bleaching resilience.
