                  91 heading Introduction, Value: 2, ID: Sec1
                      92 text Introduction
                  93 container Sec1-content
                      94 container
                          95 text Coral reefs provide a variety of ecosystem goods and services (Spalding et al. 
                          96 link Description: Reference 2017, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e655, Help: Spalding M, Burke L, Wood SA, Ashpole J, Hutchison J, Zu Ermgassen P (2017) Mapping the global value and distribution of coral reef tourism. Marine Policy 82:104–113
                          97 text ) and serve as a habitat for more than one-third of all marine species, despite only covering 0.2% of the world´s oceans (Fisher et al. 
                          98 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e658, Help: Fisher R, O’Leary RA, Low-Choy S, Mengersen K, Knowlton N, Brainard RE, Caley MJ (2015) Species richness on coral reefs and the pursuit of convergent global estimates. Curr Biol 25:500–505
                          99 text ). However, coral reefs are severely threatened by ocean warming and increasingly frequent and severe marine heatwaves (Hughes et al. 
                          100 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e661, Help: Hughes TP, Anderson KD, Connolly SR, Heron SF, Kerry JT, Lough JM, Baird AH, Baum JK, Berumen ML, Bridge TC (2018) Spatial and temporal patterns of mass bleaching of corals in the Anthropocene. Science 359:80–83
                          101 text ). This raises the question whether coral reefs will be able to persist into the future, and whether corals can recover from bleaching events fast enough to keep pace with climate change. In particular, we need to better understand which traits increase coral resistance to heat stress events and enable them to recover quickly from bleaching (i.e., the breakdown of the coral-algae symbiosis).
                      102 container
                          103 text The symbiosis between dinoflagellate algae (Family Symbiodiniaceae; LaJeunesse et al. 
                          104 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e667, Help: LaJeunesse TC, Parkinson JE, Gabrielson PW, Jeong HJ, Reimer JD, Voolstra CR, Santos SR (2018) Systematic revision of Symbiodiniaceae highlights the antiquity and diversity of coral endosymbionts. Curr Biol 28(2570–2580):e2576
                          105 text ) and the coral host is crucial for the establishment of coral reef structures because the symbionts provide healthy corals with up to 100% of their daily metabolic energy needs (Muscatine and Cernichiari 
                          106 link Description: Reference 1969, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e670, Help: Muscatine L, Cernichiari E (1969) Assimilation of photosynthetic products of zooxanthellae by a reef coral. Biol Bull 137:506–523
                          107 text ; Muscatine et al. 
                          108 link Description: Reference 1984, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e673, Help: Muscatine L, Falkowski PG, Porter JW, Dubinsky Z (1984) Fate of photosynthetic fixed carbon in light-and shade-adapted colonies of the symbiotic coral Stylophora pistillata. Proc R Soc Lond B 222:181–202
                          109 text ). Excess photosynthetically fixed carbon is stored as energy reserves in the form of lipids or proteins in the coral host (Muscatine and Cernichiari 
                          110 link Description: Reference 1969, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e676, Help: Muscatine L, Cernichiari E (1969) Assimilation of photosynthetic products of zooxanthellae by a reef coral. Biol Bull 137:506–523
                          111 text ). During bleaching, the breakdown of the symbiosis significantly limits both the transfer and the quality of essential photosynthetic products due to a loss of endosymbionts and/or photosynthetic pigments (Grottoli et al. 
                          112 link Description: Reference 2004, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e679, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Juarez C (2004) Lipids and stable carbon isotopes in two species of Hawaiian corals, Porites compressa and Montipora verrucosa, following a bleaching event. Mar Biol 145:621–631
                          113 text ; Hillyer et al. 
                          114 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e683, Help: Hillyer KE, Dias D, Lutz A, Roessner U, Davy SK (2018) 13 C metabolomics reveals widespread change in carbon fate during coral bleaching. Metabolomics 14:12
                          115 text ). This reduces both metabolic and growth rates, tissue biomass and energy reserves (Fitt et al. 
                          116 link Description: Reference 2000, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e686, Help: Fitt WK, McFarland FK, Warner ME, Chilcoat GC (2000) Seasonal patterns of tissue biomass and densities of symbiotic dinoflagellates in reef corals and relation to coral bleaching. Limnol Oceanogr 45:677–685
                          117 text ; Grottoli et al. 
                          118 link Description: Reference 2004, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e689, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Juarez C (2004) Lipids and stable carbon isotopes in two species of Hawaiian corals, Porites compressa and Montipora verrucosa, following a bleaching event. Mar Biol 145:621–631
                          119 text ; Rodrigues and Grottoli 
                          120 link Description: Reference 2007, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e692, Help: Rodrigues LJ, Grottoli AG (2007) Energy reserves and metabolism as indicators of coral recovery from bleaching. Limnol Oceanogr 52:1874–1882
                          121 text ) and ultimately threatens the survival of the coral (Rogers 
                          122 link Description: Reference 1979, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e695, Help: Rogers CS (1979) The effect of shading on coral reef structure and function. J Exp Mar Biol Ecol 41:269–288
                          123 text ).
                      124 container
                          125 text Naturally extreme reef environments expose resident coral populations to environmental conditions that often exceed those predicted to occur under future climate change (Camp et al. 
                          126 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e701, Help: Camp EF, Schoepf V, Mumby PJ, Hardtke LA, Rodolfo-Metalpa R, Smith DJ, Suggett DJ (2018) The future of coral reefs subject to rapid climate change: lessons from natural extreme environments. Front Mar Sci 5:4
                          127 text ). They can therefore provide new insights into the mechanisms that may enable coral resistance to various climate change stressors, including high temperatures. A recent review on extreme reef systems highlighted that frequent exposure to environmental extremes can indeed increase the resistance of corals to various abiotic stressors (Camp et al. 
                          128 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e704, Help: Camp EF, Schoepf V, Mumby PJ, Hardtke LA, Rodolfo-Metalpa R, Smith DJ, Suggett DJ (2018) The future of coral reefs subject to rapid climate change: lessons from natural extreme environments. Front Mar Sci 5:4
                          129 text ). For example, high-temperature fluctuations in thermally variable reefs have been shown to promote coral heat resistance (Oliver and Palumbi 
                          130 link Description: Reference 2011, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e707, Help: Oliver TA, Palumbi SR (2011) Do fluctuating temperature environments elevate coral thermal tolerance? Coral Reefs 30:429–440
                          131 text ; Palumbi et al. 
                          132 link Description: Reference 2014, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e710, Help: Palumbi SR, Barshis DJ, Traylor-Knowles N, Bay RA (2014) Mechanisms of reef coral resistance to future climate change. Science 344:895–898
                          133 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          134 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e713, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          135 text , 
                          136 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e717, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          137 text ) and reduce the risk of bleaching (Safaie et al. 
                          138 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e720, Help: Safaie A, Silbiger NJ, McClanahan TR, Pawlak G, Barshis DJ, Hench JL, Rogers JS, Williams GJ, Davis KA (2018) High frequency temperature variability reduces the risk of coral bleaching. Nat Commun 9:1–12
                          139 text ). However, significant knowledge gaps remain, particularly associated with how these extreme environments promote not only bleaching resistance, but enhanced recovery from heat stress events.
                      140 container
                          141 text Coral reefs along the macro-tidal Kimberley region in NW Australia are exposed to a naturally extreme environment where they experience the world’s largest tropical tides (up to 12 m during spring tides) (Rosser and Veron 
                          142 link Description: Reference 2011, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e726, Help: Rosser NL, Veron JEN (2011) Australian corals thriving out of water in an extreme environment. Coral Reefs 30:21–21
                          143 text ; Dandan et al. 
                          144 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e729, Help: Dandan SS, Falter JL, Lowe RJ, McCulloch MT (2015) Resilience of coral calcification to extreme temperature variations in the Kimberley region, northwest Australia. Coral Reefs 34:1151–1163
                          145 text ; Richards et al. 
                          146 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e732, Help: Richards ZT, Garcia RA, Wallace CC, Rosser NL, Muir PR (2015) A diverse assemblage of reef corals thriving in a dynamic intertidal reef setting (Bonaparte Archipelago, Kimberley, Australia). PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0117791
                          147 text ) and strong daily temperature fluctuations of up to 7 °C (Dandan et al. 
                          148 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e735, Help: Dandan SS, Falter JL, Lowe RJ, McCulloch MT (2015) Resilience of coral calcification to extreme temperature variations in the Kimberley region, northwest Australia. Coral Reefs 34:1151–1163
                          149 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          150 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e738, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          151 text ). Recent studies have shown that corals from a thermally variable intertidal environment were more heat tolerant (Schoepf et al. 
                          152 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e742, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          153 text , 
                          154 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e745, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          155 text ), bleached less (Le Nohaïc et al. 
                          156 link Description: Reference 2017, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e748, Help: Le Nohaïc M, Ross CL, Cornwall CE, Comeau S, Lowe R, McCulloch MT, Schoepf V (2017) Marine heatwave causes unprecedented regional mass bleaching of thermally resistant corals in northwestern Australia. Sci Rep 7:1–11
                          157 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          158 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e751, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          159 text ) and recovered remarkably better (Schoepf et al. 
                          160 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e754, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          161 text ) than corals from the adjacent but less thermally variable subtidal environment during the unprecedented mass bleaching event in 2016.
                      162 container
                          163 text One important factor associated with coral susceptibility to, and recovery from, bleaching is the presence of or shifts to more heat-tolerant algal symbiont types (Berkelmans and Van Oppen 
                          164 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e761, Help: Berkelmans R, Van Oppen MJH (2006) The role of zooxanthellae in the thermal tolerance of corals: a ‘nugget of hope’ for coral reefs in an era of climate change. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 273:2305–2312
                          165 text ; Stat and Gates 
                          166 link Description: Reference 2011, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e764, Help: Stat M, Gates RD (2011) Clade D Symbiodinium in scleractinian corals: a “nugget” of hope, a selfish opportunist, an ominous sign, or all of the above? J Mar Bio. https://doi.org/10.1155/2011/730715
                          167 text ; Grottoli et al. 
                          168 link Description: Reference 2014, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e767, Help: Grottoli AG, Warner ME, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Schoepf V, McGinley M, Baumann J, Matsui Y (2014) The cumulative impact of annual coral bleaching can turn some coral species winners into losers. Glob Change Biol 20:3823–3833
                          169 text ). However, little is known about the symbiont communities in these intertidal communities (Thomas et al. 
                          170 link Description: Reference 2014, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e770, Help: Thomas L, Kendrick GA, Kennington WJ, Richards ZT, Stat M (2014) Exploring Symbiodinium diversity and host specificity in Acropora corals from geographical extremes of Western Australia with 454 amplicon pyrosequencing. Mol Ecol 23:3113–3126
                          171 text ). Although corals from both intertidal and subtidal environments host symbionts of the genus  Cladocopium  (Schoepf et al. 
                          172 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e777, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          173 text , 
                          174 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e780, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          175 text ), it remains unclear how the presence of species within this genus, or other genera in low abundance, with inherent physiological differences (Baker 
                          176 link Description: Reference 2001, Help: Baker AC (2001) Reef corals bleach to survive change. Nature 411:765–776, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e783
                          177 text ) could influence the thermal tolerance of the coral (Howells et al. 
                          178 link Description: Reference 2012, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e786, Help: Howells EJ, Beltran VH, Larsen NW, Bay LK, Willis BL, Van Oppen MJH (2012) Coral thermal tolerance shaped by local adaptation of photosymbionts. Nat Clim Chang 2:116–120
                          179 text ). This highlights the need for investigating both symbiont dynamics and community composition at greater community resolution.
                      180 container
                          181 text In addition to symbiont community composition, both biomass quantity (total ash free dry weight (AFDW) cm −2 ) and quality (% lipid, protein and carbohydrate per g biomass), as well as nutritional flexibility of the coral host, can greatly influence the resistance to and recovery from bleaching (Grottoli et al. 
                          182 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e794, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Palardy JE (2006) Heterotrophic plasticity and resilience in bleached corals. Nature 440:1186–1189
                          183 text ). High levels of energy reserves typically promote bleaching resistance and recovery (e.g., Grottoli et al. 
                          184 link Description: Reference 2014, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e797, Help: Grottoli AG, Warner ME, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Schoepf V, McGinley M, Baumann J, Matsui Y (2014) The cumulative impact of annual coral bleaching can turn some coral species winners into losers. Glob Change Biol 20:3823–3833
                          185 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          186 link Description: Reference 2015b, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e800, Help: Schoepf V, Grottoli AG, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Baumann JH, Matsui Y, Warner ME (2015b) Annual coral bleaching and the long-term recovery capacity of coral. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 282:20151887
                          187 text ; Wall et al. 
                          188 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e803, Help: Wall CB, Ritson-Williams R, Popp BN, Gates RD (2019) Spatial variation in the biochemical and isotopic composition of corals during bleaching and recovery. Limnol Oceanogr 64:2011–2028
                          189 text ) because they can provide an alternative source of carbon to resource-limited bleached corals. Both energy reserve catabolism during bleaching and their overall concentration can differ strongly between species and have been linked to their differential bleaching resilience (Schoepf et al. 
                          190 link Description: Reference 2015b, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e807, Help: Schoepf V, Grottoli AG, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Baumann JH, Matsui Y, Warner ME (2015b) Annual coral bleaching and the long-term recovery capacity of coral. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 282:20151887
                          191 text ). Total biomass is generally a good indicator of coral health (Fitt et al. 
                          192 link Description: Reference 2000, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e810, Help: Fitt WK, McFarland FK, Warner ME, Chilcoat GC (2000) Seasonal patterns of tissue biomass and densities of symbiotic dinoflagellates in reef corals and relation to coral bleaching. Limnol Oceanogr 45:677–685
                          193 text ). Corals with high biomass levels and high tissue thickness typically have higher survival rates after bleaching (Thornhill et al. 
                          194 link Description: Reference 2011, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e813, Help: Thornhill DJ, Rotjan RD, Todd BD, Chilcoat GC, Iglesias-Prieto R, Kemp DW, LaJeunesse TC, Reynolds JM, Schmidt GW, Shannon T (2011) A connection between colony biomass and death in Caribbean reef-building corals. PLoS ONE 6:e29535
                          195 text ). The metabolic demand can also be met via heterotrophic feeding on zooplankton and dissolved and particulate organic particles (DOM and POM, respectively) (Grottoli et al. 
                          196 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e816, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Palardy JE (2006) Heterotrophic plasticity and resilience in bleached corals. Nature 440:1186–1189
                          197 text ; Houlbrèque and Ferrier-Pagès 
                          198 link Description: Reference 2009, Help: Houlbrèque F, Ferrier-Pagès C (2009) Heterotrophy in tropical scleractinian corals. Biol Rev 84:1–17, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e819
                          199 text ; Goldberg 
                          200 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e822, Help: Goldberg WM (2018) Coral food, feeding, nutrition, and secretion: a review marine organisms as model systems in biology and medicine. Springer, pp 377–421
                          201 text ). If the transfer of photosynthetic carbon is reduced (e.g., during bleaching), heterotrophic carbon can become a crucial, alternative energy source (Grottoli et al. 
                          202 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e826, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Palardy JE (2006) Heterotrophic plasticity and resilience in bleached corals. Nature 440:1186–1189
                          203 text ; Houlbrèque and Ferrier‐Pagès 
                          204 link Description: Reference 2009, Help: Houlbrèque F, Ferrier-Pagès C (2009) Heterotrophy in tropical scleractinian corals. Biol Rev 84:1–17, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e829
                          205 text ).
                      206 container
                          207 text The aim of this study was to explore potential mechanisms underlying the differential environment-specific trends in bleaching and recovery observed during unprecedented mass bleaching in 2016 (Le Nohaic et al. 
                          208 link Description: Reference 2017, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e835, Help: Le Nohaïc M, Ross CL, Cornwall CE, Comeau S, Lowe R, McCulloch MT, Schoepf V (2017) Marine heatwave causes unprecedented regional mass bleaching of thermally resistant corals in northwestern Australia. Sci Rep 7:1–11
                          209 text , Schoepf et al. 
                          210 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e838, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          211 text ). We investigated key indicators of bleaching resilience for the dominant coral holobiont at our study site,  Acropora aspera , by comparing healthy and bleached corals from both subtidal and intertidal environments during peak bleaching and after seven months of recovery. We hypothesized that higher bleaching resistance and rapid recovery, as indicated by greater retention of symbionts and chlorophyll  a  levels (Warner et al. 
                          212 link Description: Reference 1996, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e847, Help: Warner ME, Fitt WK, Schmidt GW (1996) The effects of elevated temperature on the photosynthetic efficiency of zooxanthellae in hospite from four different species of reef coral: a novel approach. Plant, Cell Environ 19:291–299
                          213 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          214 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e851, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          215 text ), is associated with the presence of a unique community of algal symbionts and/or high host energy reserve levels or sufficient energy reserve consumption during bleaching.
              216 container Sec2-section
                  217 heading Material and Methods, Value: 2, ID: Sec2
                      218 text Material and Methods
                  219 container Sec2-content
                      220 heading Study site and coral sampling, Value: 3, ID: Sec3
                          221 text Study site and coral sampling
                      222 container
                          223 text The study site was located at Shell Island, Cygnet Bay (16°28′46.8″S, 123°2′36.6″E), in the macro-tidal Kimberley region (up to 12 m tidal range) in northwestern Australia. A detailed site description can be found in Schoepf et al. (
                          224 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e866, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          225 text , 
                          226 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e869, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          227 text ). Briefly, the intertidal becomes a shallow tide pool during low tide with a slack water period for up to four hours, leading to high light levels (up to 2400 µmol m −2  s −1 ), daily temperature fluctuations of up to 7 °C (min. 22 °C, max. 38 °C short-term temperatures, Fig. S1) and frequent aerial exposure of the corals (Dandan et al. 
                          228 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e876, Help: Dandan SS, Falter JL, Lowe RJ, McCulloch MT (2015) Resilience of coral calcification to extreme temperature variations in the Kimberley region, northwest Australia. Coral Reefs 34:1151–1163
                          229 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          230 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e880, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          231 text ). In contrast, corals in the adjacent subtidal experience more moderate light (up to 1800 µmol m −2  s −1 ) and temperature levels, with daily fluctuations of up to 3 °C (min. 23 °C, max. 34 °C short-term temperatures, Fig. S1) and are only rarely exposed to air during the most extreme spring low tides (Dandan et al. 
                          232 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e887, Help: Dandan SS, Falter JL, Lowe RJ, McCulloch MT (2015) Resilience of coral calcification to extreme temperature variations in the Kimberley region, northwest Australia. Coral Reefs 34:1151–1163
                          233 text ; Schoepf et al., 
                          234 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e890, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          235 text ). Heat stress experiments and surveys conducted during the 2016 mass bleaching event in this region showed that intertidal corals have a higher heat tolerance and recovery capacity than subtidal corals (Schoepf et al. 
                          236 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e893, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          237 text , 
                          238 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e897, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          239 text ; Le Nohaïc et al. 
                          240 link Description: Reference 2017, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e900, Help: Le Nohaïc M, Ross CL, Cornwall CE, Comeau S, Lowe R, McCulloch MT, Schoepf V (2017) Marine heatwave causes unprecedented regional mass bleaching of thermally resistant corals in northwestern Australia. Sci Rep 7:1–11
                          241 text ).
                      242 container
                          243 text In April 2016, at the peak of a marine heatwave, both healthy and pale/bleached colonies from both environments were randomly tagged using cattle tags epoxied to the coral colony (Z-Spar) (intertidal: 11 healthy and eight bleached/pale colonies; subtidal: 12 healthy and ten bleached/pale colonies). The visual health status of all coral colonies was surveyed in April 2016 and again after 7 months of recovery in November 2016 using the Coral Health Chart (Siebeck et al. 
                          244 link Description: Reference 2008, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e906, Help: UE Siebeck, D Logan, NJ Marshall (2008) CoralWatch: a flexible coral bleaching monitoring tool for you and your group
                          245 text ). Each coral colony was labeled as either “bleached” (category 1–3.5) or “healthy” (category 3.6–6). Changes in brightness of at least two units symbolize a significant change in symbiont density and chlorophyll  a  content (i.e., the bleaching state of the coral) (Siebeck et al. 
                          246 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e912, Help: Siebeck UE, Marshall NJ, Klüter A, Hoegh-Guldberg O (2006) Monitoring coral bleaching using a colour reference card. Coral Reefs 25:453–460
                          247 text ).
                      248 container
                          249 text Four branch tips (~ 3 cm in length) were collected from all tagged colonies in April and November 2016, respectively, for physiological and symbiont sequence analyses (see below). Coral mortality in both environments during the heat stress period led to a reduction of surviving tagged colonies by November 2016 ( n  = 1–10 per health group and environment, Fig. S2, Table S3). The collected coral fragments were stored at − 80 °C until further processing.
                      250 heading Symbiont typing, Value: 3, ID: Sec4
                          251 text Symbiont typing
                      252 container
                          253 text DNA from coral branch tips was extracted using a DNeasy Blood and Tissue kit (Qiagen). Symbiodiniaceae internal transcribed spacer 2 (ITS2) marker genes in algal symbionts from a total of 53 coral colonies (April: intertidal: healthy: 8, bleached: 6; subtidal: healthy: 9, bleached: 9; November: intertidal: healthy: 6, bleached: 7; subtidal: healthy: 7, bleached: 1), PCR-negative controls (without DNA) and extraction blanks (without tissue) were then amplified via PCR using oligonucleotides that included the ITSD (5′-GTGAATTGCAGAACTCCGTG-′3) and ITS2-rev2 (5′-CCTCCGCTTACTTATATGCTT-′3) primers (Pochon et al. 
                          254 link Description: Reference 2001, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e929, Help: Pochon X, Pawlowski J, Zaninetti L, Rowan R (2001) High genetic diversity and relative specificity among Symbiodinium-like endosymbiotic dinoflagellates in soritid foraminiferans. Mar Biol 139:1069–1078
                          255 text ). PCR annealing temperatures differed for April (60 °C) and November (52 °C) samples as different library building methods were utilized (see Supplementary Material for details). Amplicon libraries were sequenced at the TrEnD Laboratory at Curtin University, Perth, Australia, and the Australian Genome Research Facility (AGRF). Raw sequence data are available at 
                          256 link Description: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/ZGUDR, Value: doi.org/10.17605/OS…
                          257 text . Raw FASTQ files for both time points were analyzed through Symportal (Hume et al. 
                          258 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e939, Help: Hughes TP, Kerry JT, Baird AH, Connolly SR, Chase TJ, Dietzel A, Hill T, Hoey AS, Hoogenboom MO, Jacobson M (2019) Global warming impairs stock–recruitment dynamics of corals. Nature 568:387–390
                          259 text ). This pipeline was designed specifically for the analysis of Symbiodiniaceae ITS2 metabarcoding data to overcome the issues associated with interpreting complex communities against a background of the intragenomic variation characteristic of the ITS2 marker. Symportal uses a minimum entropy decomposition (MED)-based approach which groups raw sequence data into distinct sequence nodes (Eren et al. 
                          260 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e942, Help: Eren AM, Morrison HG, Lescault PJ, Reveillaud J, Vineis JH, Sogin ML (2015) Minimum entropy decomposition: unsupervised oligotyping for sensitive partitioning of high-throughput marker gene sequences. ISME J 9:968–979
                          261 text ). In contrast to the operational taxonomic unit (OTU) approach, which uses a fixed 97% similarity threshold, these sequence nodes are based on the position of biologically informative sequences (Eren et al. 
                          262 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e945, Help: Eren AM, Morrison HG, Lescault PJ, Reveillaud J, Vineis JH, Sogin ML (2015) Minimum entropy decomposition: unsupervised oligotyping for sensitive partitioning of high-throughput marker gene sequences. ISME J 9:968–979
                          263 text ). Symportal analyzes all of the different ITS2 sequences within a sample to define complex ITS2 profiles (‘defining intragenomic variants’, DIVs) that comprise the most abundant ITS2 sequences based on the presence of multimodal distributions within an ITS2 set of sequences. DIVs are indicative of a genetically differentiated Symbiodiniaceae community and can distinguish between very low abundant ITS2 sequences that would have been below detection limit when using, for example, a 97% (OTU) approach (Hume et al. 
                          264 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e949, Help: Hume BC, Smith EG, Ziegler M, Warrington HJ, Burt JA, LaJeunesse TC, Wiedenmann J, Voolstra CR (2019) SymPortal: a novel analytical framework and platform for coral algal symbiont next-generation sequencing ITS2 profiling. Mol Ecol Resour 19:1063–1080
                          265 text ). We focused on these DIVs for the analysis of our data.
                      266 heading Physiological analyses, Value: 3, ID: Sec5
                          267 text Physiological analyses
                      268 text For total biomass analysis, coral tissue was separated from one branch tip using an airbrush. The tissue slurry was then homogenized and dried to constant weight at 50 °C for at least 24 h. The dried tissue was then burnt in a muffle furnace at 450 °C for at least four hours. The AFDW of the sample was standardized to surface area. See supplementary material for more information.
                      269 container
                          270 text To determine chlorophyll  a  concentration, a subsample of the airbrushed tissue slurry was centrifuged (2 × 10 min at 3000  g ) to separate host and symbiont cells. Chlorophyll  a  was extracted in 100% acetone in the dark at − 20 °C for 24 h, and the concentration determined spectrophotometrically (Jeffrey and Humphrey 
                          271 link Description: Reference 1975, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e972, Help: Jeffrey SWt, Humphrey GF, (1975) New spectrophotometric equations for determining chlorophylls a, b, c1 and c2 in higher plants, algae and natural phytoplankton. Biochem Physiol Pflanz 167:191–194
                          272 text ) and then standardized to both surface area (data reproduced from Schoepf et al. 
                          273 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e975, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          274 text ) and symbiont cell density (this study). Symbiont density was calculated using five replicate counts on a Neubauer hemocytometer. The surface area was calculated using the formula ( y  = 9.4871  \(\cdot\)  x 0.7729 ) derived from a previously determined relation between the skeletal mass ( x ) and the respective computer tomography-determined surface areas ( y ) of  A. aspera  skeletons from Shell Island, Cygnet Bay (Schoepf et al. 
                          275 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1011, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          276 text ).
                      277 container
                          278 text Soluble protein and carbohydrates were extracted from the host tissue (one whole ground branch tip; ~ 1 cm), and lipids from both host and symbiont tissue (another whole ground branch tip; ~ 2 cm), and determined after established methods (Dubois et al. 
                          279 link Description: Reference 1956, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1017, Help: Dubois M, Gilles KA, Hamilton JK, Rebers PAt, Smith F, (1956) Colorimetric method for determination of sugars and related substances. Anal Chem 28:350–356
                          280 text ; Folch et al. 
                          281 link Description: Reference 1957, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1020, Help: Folch J, Lees M, Stanley GHS (1957) A simple method for the isolation and purification of total lipides from animal tissues. J Biol Chem 226:497–509
                          282 text ; Smith et al. 
                          283 link Description: Reference 1985, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1023, Help: Smith PK, Krohn RI, Hermanson GT, Mallia AK, Gartner FH, Provenzano M, Fujimoto EK, Goeke NM, Olson BJ, Klenk DC (1985) Measurement of protein using bicinchoninic acid. Analytical biochem 150(1):76–85
                          284 text ; Grottoli et al. 
                          285 link Description: Reference 2004, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1026, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Juarez C (2004) Lipids and stable carbon isotopes in two species of Hawaiian corals, Porites compressa and Montipora verrucosa, following a bleaching event. Mar Biol 145:621–631
                          286 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          287 link Description: Reference 2013, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1029, Help: Schoepf V, Grottoli AG, Warner ME, Cai W-J, Melman TF, Hoadley KD, Pettay DT, Hu X, Li Q, Xu H (2013) Coral energy reserves and calcification in a high-CO2 world at two temperatures. PloS one. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0075049
                          288 text ), converted to kilojoules (kJ) (Gnaiger and Bitterlich 
                          289 link Description: Reference 1984, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1033, Help: Gnaiger E, Bitterlich G (1984) Proximate biochemical composition and caloric content calculated from elemental CHN analysis: a stoichiometric concept. Oecologia 62:289–298
                          290 text ) and then standardized to the AFDW of the fragment. In order to determine total energy reserves, the energetic value (kJ) of protein, carbohydrates and lipids was summed up. See supplementary material for more information.
                      291 heading Statistical analyses, Value: 3, ID: Sec6
                          292 text Statistical analyses
                      293 container
                          294 text Sequencing counts for ITS2 sequences and DIVs per sample were converted to square root-transformed percent abundance data. Differences in symbiont community composition (based on both all detected ITS2 sequences and ITS2 profiles represented as DIVs) between environment (intertidal and subtidal), health (healthy and bleached as determined in April 2016) and time (April and November) were tested using two-way Permutational Multivariate Analysis of Variance (PERMANOVA) and the Bray–Curtis similarity index with 9999 iterations in PAST, version 3.15. Principal component analyses were performed, and changes in diversity and evenness of the symbiont community composition were calculated using Shannon and Simpson diversity indices in PAST, version 3.15. For all physiological parameters, generalized linear mixed effect models were used to test for the above effects using SAS software version 9.4. The distribution of the physiological raw data was visually assessed using the quantile–quantile plot of the residuals. Raw data of both chlorophyll  a  normalized to symbiont cell and symbiont density were square root transformed. Biomass data were log transformed. No transformation was performed on the raw data of protein, carbohydrates and lipids. When main effects were significant, Tukey adjusted  p  values were used for post hoc tests. For each significant interaction, multiple post hoc pairwise comparisons were made by using Tukey adjusted  p  values. Differences between healthy and bleached corals in their respective environments at each time point were tested a priori.  p  values ≤ 0.05 were considered significant. Data for statistical analyses in PAST and SAS are available with code at 
                          295 link Description: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/ZGUDR, Value: doi.org/10.17605/OS…
                          296 text .
              297 container Sec7-section
                  298 heading Results, Value: 2, ID: Sec7
                      299 text Results
                  300 container Sec7-content
                      301 heading Sequencing results and clustering, Value: 3, ID: Sec8
                          302 text Sequencing results and clustering
                      303 container
                          304 text Amplicon sequencing returned 1,389,180 reads, resulting in 25,419 ± 10,042 (mean ± SD) reads per sample (Table S1), from the 53 colonies of intertidal (27 colonies) and subtidal (26 colonies)  A. aspera . After running the samples through the Symportal quality control pipeline and MED, we identified 80 unique ITS2 sequences and two DIVs. Five sequences from an extraction blank and two sequences from PCR-negative controls were identified as C3. However, the sequence found in high abundance in all samples was C3 (see below), and the number of reads in the controls was low compared to the number of reads in each coral sample. Therefore, the low level of cross-contamination detected was determined to have not influenced the results.
                      305 container
                          306 text The two identified DIVs consisted of the six and five, respectively, most abundant ITS2 sequences (Hume et al. 
                          307 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1082, Help: Hume BC, Smith EG, Ziegler M, Warrington HJ, Burt JA, LaJeunesse TC, Wiedenmann J, Voolstra CR (2019) SymPortal: a novel analytical framework and platform for coral algal symbiont next-generation sequencing ITS2 profiling. Mol Ecol Resour 19:1063–1080
                          308 text ): DIV1: C3-C1-1345_C-C1n-1329_C-1346_C; DIV2: C3-C1-C1n-C3v-C1q.  Cladocopium  C3 was the most abundant ITS2 sequence and dominant in all colonies (46% of reads from all samples; Fig. S3, Table S2). The second- and third-most abundant ITS2 sequences (C1 and C1n) accounted for 12% and 7%, respectively, of the total symbiont sequence data (Fig. S3, Table S2). The average Simpson index of 0.753 and an average Shannon index of 2.146 among all samples confirmed that the overall symbiont diversity was similar between colonies (Table S1).
                      309 heading Symbiont community composition, Value: 3, ID: Sec9
                          310 text Symbiont community composition
                      311 container
                          312 text The symbiont community composition based on DIVs was characterized by a significant effect of health and environment (Table 
                          313 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          314 text ). DIVs differed significantly between intertidal and subtidal environments in April and between healthy and bleached corals in both environments in April 2016 (Table 
                          315 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          316 text ). In the intertidal communities of April, DIV1 was identified in all healthy and in 67% of bleached corals (Fig. 
                          317 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          318 text , Fig. S3). One-third of the bleached intertidal corals were assigned DIV2 (Fig. 
                          319 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          320 text , Fig. S3). In contrast, in the subtidal communities in April, the majority of the bleached corals (78%) and 22% of the healthy corals were assigned DIV2, whereas DIV1 was identified in 78% of healthy corals (Fig. 
                          321 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          322 text , Fig. S3).
                      323 container
                          324 container Tab1
                              325 text Table 1 Multivariate Permutational Analyses of Variance (PERMANOVA) testing the effect of environment, health and time on Symbiodiniaceae ITS2 types of  Acropora aspera

                      327 container
                          328 text Fig. 1
                          329 image Fig. 1
