DIV1: C3-C1-1345_C-C1n-1329_C-1346_C; DIV2: C3-C1-C1n-C3v-C1q. IT: intertidal; ST: subtidal; NB: healthy; BL: bleached. Note that in November, BL stands for bleached/recovered. Note: DIVs only comprise the six and five, respectively; most abundant ITS2 types of all ITS2 types present in each sample. Therefore, the abundances do not add up to 100%
                      332 container
                          333 text The symbiont community composition of all corals based on ITS2 sequences was also characterized by significant effects of health and environment and by an interactive effect of environment and health (Table 
                          334 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          335 text ). In contrast to the DIVs composition, ITS2 sequences were significantly different between April and November (Table 
                          336 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          337 text , Fig. S4). However, the difference was driven by rare ITS2 sequences representing < 1% of the sequence data (Table 
                          338 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          339 text ). See supplementary material for more details.
                      340 heading Symbiont physiology, Value: 3, ID: Sec10
                          341 text Symbiont physiology
                      342 container
                          343 text We identified contrasting physiological responses between subtidal and intertidal corals during the bleaching event in 2016. Chlorophyll  a  data normalized to symbiont cell density (chl  a /cell) showed that both bleaching and recovery of both intertidal and subtidal  A. aspera  were driven by significant interactive effects of environment, health and time (Table S4). In April, bleached subtidal corals lost 56% of their chl  a /cell compared to the healthy corals, whereas bleached intertidal corals fully retained their chl  a /cell (Fig. 
                          344 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          345 text a). In November 2016, the one surviving bleached/recovered subtidal coral colony showed a trend of 36% higher chl  a /cell compared to corals that were visibly healthy during the bleaching event (Fig. 
                          346 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          347 text b). However, this difference was not statistically significant as only one bleached subtidal colony had survived/recovered from bleaching. In the intertidal, chl  a /cell did not differ between healthy and bleached/recovered corals at the same time point (Fig. 
                          348 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          349 text b).
                      350 container
                          351 text Fig. 2
                          352 image Fig. 2
                          353 link Description: Full size image figure 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          354 container
                              355 text reproduced from Schoepf et al. 
                              356 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1832, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                              357 text ) and symbiont density ( e ,  f ) ± standard error (SE) of  Acropora aspera . SE is missing for bleached/recovered subtidal corals in November 2016 as sample size was one (Table S3). Asterisks indicate significant differences between healthy and bleached/recovered corals within each environment. Significant environment (envo), health and time effects are indicated when present (Table S4). Note that the health status refers to the assessment in April 2016
                          358 container
                              359 text Symbiont physiology. Cell density-normalized chlorophyll  a  concentrations ( a ,  b ), area-normalized chlorophyll  a  concentrations ( c ,  d ;
                      360 container
                          361 text In April 2016, significantly more symbionts (88%) were lost in bleached vs. healthy corals in the subtidal, leading to significant interactive effects of environment and health (Table S4). Comparatively, bleached intertidal corals only showed a trend of 54% lower symbiont densities (Fig. 
                          362 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          363 text e). By November 2016, symbiont densities had fully recovered in the formerly bleached intertidal corals (Fig. 
                          364 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          365 text f). In contrast, in the subtidal, the one surviving bleached/recovered colony tended to have 36% lower symbiont densities compared to healthy corals in this environment. However, this difference was not statistically significant as only one bleached subtidal colony had survived/recovered from bleaching (Fig. 
                          366 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          367 text f). In addition, symbiont densities were overall 55% lower in April than November 2016 (Fig. 
                          368 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          369 text e, f, Table S4).
                      370 heading Host physiology, Value: 3, ID: Sec11
                          371 text Host physiology
                      372 container
                          373 text Tissue biomass of subtidal corals was 63% lower in April than in November 2016 which likely drove the observed significant interactive effect of time and environment (Fig. 
                          374 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          375 text i, k, Table S4). In contrast, intertidal corals maintained constant levels of tissue biomass between April and November 2016 (Fig. 
                          376 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          377 text i, k). In addition, tissue biomass did not differ between healthy and bleached/recovered corals within their respective environment at both time points (Fig. 
                          378 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          379 text i, k).
                      380 container
                          381 text Fig. 3
                          382 image Fig. 3
                          383 link Description: Full size image figure 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          384 container
                              385 text Energy reserves. Protein ( a ,  b ), carbohydrate ( c ,  d ), lipid ( e ,  f ), total energy reserve concentrations ( g ,  h ) and tissue biomass ( i ,  k ) ± standard error (SE) of  Acropora aspera . SE is missing for bleached/recovered subtidal corals in November 2016 as sample size was one (Table S3). Asterisks indicate significant differences between healthy and bleached/recovered corals within each environment. Significant environment (envo), health and time effects are indicated when present (Table S4). Note that the health status refers to the assessment in April 2016
                      386 container
                          387 text Protein concentrations were significantly higher (+ 15%) in healthy compared to bleached/recovered corals (Fig. 
                          388 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          389 text a, b, Table S4). In the intertidal, corals maintained similar levels of protein concentrations between April and November 2016. In contrast, protein levels in subtidal corals declined by 26% between April and November (Fig. 
                          390 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          391 text a, b) which drove the observed significant interactive effects of environment and time (Table S4). At both time points, protein concentrations did not differ between healthy and bleached/recovered corals within their respective environment (Fig. 
                          392 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          393 text a, b); the 30% decline in protein concentrations in bleached compared to healthy subtidal corals in November was not significant.
                      394 container
                          395 text A significant interactive effect of environment, health and time was observed for carbohydrate concentrations (Table S4). In the subtidal, bleached/recovered corals showed significantly lower carbohydrate concentrations compared to healthy corals in both April and November 2016 (33% and 46%, respectively) (Fig. 
                          396 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          397 text c, d). In contrast, both healthy and bleached/recovered intertidal corals maintained similar levels of carbohydrates irrespective of time (Fig. 
                          398 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          399 text c, d). Carbohydrate concentrations in bleached intertidal corals were 33% lower in April than in November 2016, whereas no difference was observed in bleached subtidal corals between the two time points (Fig. 
                          400 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          401 text c, d).
                      402 container
                          403 text Lipid stores significantly differed between time points (Table S4) as they were 41% lower in April than in November 2016, which was primarily because bleached corals had substantially less lipids than healthy corals during peak bleaching (Fig. 
                          404 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          405 text e, f). In April 2016, lipid concentrations in bleached versus healthy corals declined three times more in the intertidal than subtidal (30% vs. 11%, respectively); however, this trend was not significant (Fig. 
                          406 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          407 text e).
                      408 container
                          409 text Overall, total energy reserves of corals were significantly lower in April than in November 2016 (-20%). More specifically, total energy reserves of bleached corals showed a non-significant decline of 23% compared to healthy corals in the intertidal in April, but were fully recovered by November 2016 (Fig. 
                          410 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          411 text g, h). No difference in total energy reserves was observed between healthy and bleached subtidal corals at either time points (Fig. 
                          412 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          413 text g, h).
              414 container Sec12-section
                  415 heading Discussion, Value: 2, ID: Sec12
                      416 text Discussion
                  417 container Sec12-content
                      418 container
                          419 text In 2016, a marine heatwave caused unprecedented bleaching in the extreme macro-tidal Kimberley region in northwestern Australia (Le Nohaïc et al. 
                          420 link Description: Reference 2017, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1989, Help: Le Nohaïc M, Ross CL, Cornwall CE, Comeau S, Lowe R, McCulloch MT, Schoepf V (2017) Marine heatwave causes unprecedented regional mass bleaching of thermally resistant corals in northwestern Australia. Sci Rep 7:1–11
                          421 text ; Gilmour et al. 
                          422 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1992, Help: Gilmour JP, Cook KL, Ryan NM, Puotinen ML, Green RH, Shedrawi G, Hobbs J-PA, Thomson DP, Babcock RC, Buckee J (2019) The state of Western Australia’s coral reefs. Coral Reefs 38:651–667
                          423 text ; Schoepf et al., 
                          424 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1995, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          425 text ). Intertidal coral communities at our study site fully recovered, whereas the majority of adjacent subtidal coral communities did not survive this extreme climatic event (Schoepf et al. 
                          426 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e1998, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          427 text , this study). Here, we investigated potential drivers of bleaching resilience and recovery in this unique macro-tidal environment. Although all corals were dominated by the same ITS2 sequence (C3, Table S2), DIV profiles, which can be interpreted as putative species (Hume et al. 
                          428 link Description: Reference 2019a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2001, Help: Ward S, Harrison P, Hoegh-Guldberg O (2002) Coral bleaching reduces reproduction of scleractinian corals and increases susceptibility to future stress. In: Proceedings of the ninth international coral reef symposium, Bali, 23–27 October 2000, vol 2. pp 1123–1128
                          429 text , 
                          430 link Description: Reference b, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2005, Help: Hume BC, Smith EG, Ziegler M, Warrington HJ, Burt JA, LaJeunesse TC, Wiedenmann J, Voolstra CR (2019) SymPortal: a novel analytical framework and platform for coral algal symbiont next-generation sequencing ITS2 profiling. Mol Ecol Resour 19:1063–1080
                          431 text ), and ITS2 sequence composition differed significantly between environments and coral health status (Table 
                          432 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          433 text ). Surprisingly, however, survival and high bleaching resilience were decoupled from tissue energy reserves which typically promote recovery from bleaching (Grottoli et al. 
                          434 link Description: Reference 2014, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2011, Help: Grottoli AG, Warner ME, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Schoepf V, McGinley M, Baumann J, Matsui Y (2014) The cumulative impact of annual coral bleaching can turn some coral species winners into losers. Glob Change Biol 20:3823–3833
                          435 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          436 link Description: Reference 2015b, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2014, Help: Schoepf V, Grottoli AG, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Baumann JH, Matsui Y, Warner ME (2015b) Annual coral bleaching and the long-term recovery capacity of coral. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 282:20151887
                          437 text ).
                      438 heading Differential heat tolerance of intertidal and subtidal symbionts, Value: 3, ID: Sec13
                          439 text Differential heat tolerance of intertidal and subtidal symbionts
                      440 container
                          441 text The intertidal and subtidal differ strongly in terms of environmental conditions, especially daily temperature fluctuations (max. 7 °C vs. 3 °C, respectively; Fig. S1, Schoepf et al. 
                          442 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2024, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          443 text ), but also light intensities which were more moderate in the subtidal than intertidal (max. 1800 µmol m −2  s − 1 vs. 2400 µmol m −2  s − 1; Dandan et al. 
                          444 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2036, Help: Dandan SS, Falter JL, Lowe RJ, McCulloch MT (2015) Resilience of coral calcification to extreme temperature variations in the Kimberley region, northwest Australia. Coral Reefs 34:1151–1163
                          445 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          446 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2039, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          447 text ). Nevertheless, the symbiont communities of corals from both environments were dominated by the same ITS2 sequence (C3: 46% of reads from all samples, Fig. S3, Table S2). However, the bleaching response during the heat stress differed dramatically between intertidal and subtidal corals. Our results show a higher chlorophyll  a  per symbiont cell ratio, which is a better indicator of photodamage than chlorophyll  a  per area (Warner et al. 
                          448 link Description: Reference 1996, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2048, Help: Warner ME, Fitt WK, Schmidt GW (1996) The effects of elevated temperature on the photosynthetic efficiency of zooxanthellae in hospite from four different species of reef coral: a novel approach. Plant, Cell Environ 19:291–299
                          449 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          450 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2051, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          451 text ), in bleached corals in the highly variable (intertidal) than in the more moderate (subtidal) temperature environment (Fig. 
                          452 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          453 text ). Bleached intertidal  A. aspera  not only lost fewer symbionts (Fig. 
                          454 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          455 text e, this study) and chlorophyll  a  per area (Fig. 
                          456 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          457 text c, Schoepf et al. 
                          458 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2070, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          459 text ), but also fully maintained chlorophyll  a  on a per cell basis (Fig. 
                          460 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          461 text a), which was in stark contrast to bleached subtidal symbionts (Fig. 
                          462 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          463 text ). These findings are consistent with previous work from the Kimberley (Schoepf et al. 
                          464 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2083, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          465 text ) and other reefs with strong temperature gradients (Warner et al. 
                          466 link Description: Reference 1996, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2086, Help: Warner ME, Fitt WK, Schmidt GW (1996) The effects of elevated temperature on the photosynthetic efficiency of zooxanthellae in hospite from four different species of reef coral: a novel approach. Plant, Cell Environ 19:291–299
                          467 text ; Palumbi et al. 
                          468 link Description: Reference 2014, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2089, Help: Palumbi SR, Barshis DJ, Traylor-Knowles N, Bay RA (2014) Mechanisms of reef coral resistance to future climate change. Science 344:895–898
                          469 text ). Our findings therefore suggest that intertidal symbiont composition was more stable than subtidal symbionts, indicating that long-term acclimatization and/or local adaptation to the strong environmental gradient may have led to differential heat tolerance among symbionts. Furthermore, it is possible that observed differences in bleaching response were linked to intraspecific symbiont- (Howells et al. 
                          470 link Description: Reference 2012, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2093, Help: Howells EJ, Beltran VH, Larsen NW, Bay LK, Willis BL, Van Oppen MJH (2012) Coral thermal tolerance shaped by local adaptation of photosymbionts. Nat Clim Chang 2:116–120
                          471 text ) and/or holobiont-derived adaptation (Parkinson et al. 
                          472 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2096, Help: Parkinson JE, Banaszak AT, Altman NS, LaJeunesse TC, Baums IB (2015) Intraspecific diversity among partners drives functional variation in coral symbioses. Sci Rep 5:1–12
                          473 text ).
                      474 container
                          475 text Our results further suggest that bleached subtidal corals suffered from strong resource limitation at the time of peak heat stress. The loss of 88% of their symbionts and 56% of their cell-normalized chlorophyll  a  likely significantly reduced translocation of autotrophic carbon to the coral host (Grottoli et al. 
                          476 link Description: Reference 2004, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2105, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Juarez C (2004) Lipids and stable carbon isotopes in two species of Hawaiian corals, Porites compressa and Montipora verrucosa, following a bleaching event. Mar Biol 145:621–631
                          477 text ; Hillyer et al. 
                          478 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2108, Help: Hillyer KE, Dias D, Lutz A, Roessner U, Davy SK (2018) 13 C metabolomics reveals widespread change in carbon fate during coral bleaching. Metabolomics 14:12
                          479 text ). As a consequence, they may have been more reliant on alternative carbon sources, such as heterotrophic feeding on DOM, POM and zooplankton (e.g., Grottoli et al 
                          480 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2111, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Palardy JE (2006) Heterotrophic plasticity and resilience in bleached corals. Nature 440:1186–1189
                          481 text ; Goldberg et al. 
                          482 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2114, Help: Goldberg WM (2018) Coral food, feeding, nutrition, and secretion: a review marine organisms as model systems in biology and medicine. Springer, pp 377–421
                          483 text ) In contrast, bleached intertidal corals likely still received substantial photosynthetically derived nutrients from the symbionts given the high retention levels of both symbiont densities and chlorophyll  a  per cell during peak bleaching (Fig. 
                          484 link Description: 2, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          485 text a, e). This likely played an important role in the differential survival and recovery capacity of intertidal and subtidal corals.
                      486 heading The role of symbiont composition, Value: 3, ID: Sec14
                          487 text The role of symbiont composition
                      488 container
                          489 text Although all corals harbored  Cladocopium , DIV profiles nevertheless differed significantly between environments and between bleached and healthy corals within each environment at the peak of the heatwave in April 2016 (Fig. 
                          490 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          491 text ; Table 
                          492 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          493 text ). In April, DIV1 (C3-C1-1345_C-C1n-1329_C-1346_C) was present in most healthy subtidal corals and in all healthy and two-thirds of bleached intertidal corals (Figs. 
                          494 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          495 text , S3). Given the generally higher bleaching resilience and lower mortality of bleached intertidal corals (Schoepf et al. 
                          496 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2144, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          497 text ; this study), it is possible that the symbiont/s in these corals represented by DIV1 were linked to higher heat resistance. In contrast, 78% of all bleached subtidal corals were associated with DIV2 (C3-C1-C1n-C3v-C1q; Figs. 
                          498 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          499 text , S3). Since these corals bleached more severely and showed a much higher mortality compared to bleached intertidal corals (Schoepf et al. 
                          500 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2151, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          501 text ; this study), DIV2 potentially represented symbiont/s which that were either more heat-sensitive or at least unable to promote the bleaching resistance and recovery of these corals.
                      502 container
                          503 text Higher coral recovery capacity, as observed for bleached intertidal corals (Schoepf et al. 
                          504 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2157, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          505 text ; this study), is sometimes linked to a temporal shift in the dominant symbiont (e.g., Silverstein et al. 
                          506 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2160, Help: Silverstein RN, Cunning R, Baker AC (2015) Change in algal symbiont communities after bleaching, not prior heat exposure, increases heat tolerance of reef corals. Glob Change Biol 21:236–249
                          507 text ). However, not all coral species shuffle symbionts (Goulet 
                          508 link Description: Reference 2006, Help: Goulet TL (2006) Most corals may not change their symbionts. Mar Ecol Prog Ser 321:1–7, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2163
                          509 text ; Stat et al. 
                          510 link Description: Reference 2009, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2166, Help: Stat M, Loh WKW, LaJeunesse TC, Hoegh-Guldberg O, Carter DA (2009) Stability of coral-endosymbiont associations during and after a thermal stress event in the southern Great Barrier Reef. Coral Reefs 28:709–713
                          511 text ; Cunning et al. 
                          512 link Description: Reference 2016, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2169, Help: Cunning R, Ritson-Williams R, Gates RD (2016) Patterns of bleaching and recovery of Montipora capitata in Kāne ‘ohe Bay, Hawai ‘i, USA. Mar Ecol Prog Ser 551:131–139
                          513 text ) or to the same degree (Cunning et al. 
                          514 link Description: Reference 2018, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2173, Help: Cunning R, Silverstein RN, Baker AC (2018) Symbiont shuffling linked to differential photochemical dynamics of Symbiodinium in three Caribbean reef corals. Coral Reefs 37:145–152
                          515 text ), and often this trait is completely absent. In this study, we found no evidence for symbiont shuffling based on DIV profiles over time. However, ITS2 sequence composition present at low-abundance background levels can also influence the coral’s bleaching response (Berkelmans and Van Oppen 
                          516 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2176, Help: Berkelmans R, Van Oppen MJH (2006) The role of zooxanthellae in the thermal tolerance of corals: a ‘nugget of hope’ for coral reefs in an era of climate change. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 273:2305–2312
                          517 text ; LaJeunesse et al. 
                          518 link Description: Reference 2009, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2179, Help: LaJeunesse TC, Smith RT, Finney J, Oxenford H (2009) Outbreak and persistence of opportunistic symbiotic dinoflagellates during the 2005 Caribbean mass coral ‘bleaching’ event. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 276:4139–4148
                          519 text ) and recovery capacity (Bay et al. 
                          520 link Description: Reference 2016, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2182, Help: Bay LK, Doyle J, Logan M, Berkelmans R (2016) Recovery from bleaching is mediated by threshold densities of background thermo-tolerant symbiont types in a reef-building coral. Royal Society open science 3:160322
                          521 text ). Here, differences in low-abundance background symbiont types < 1% (Fig. S3) may have played a role in bleaching resilience, because symbiont community composition based on ITS2 sequences differed significantly between April and November (Fig. S4, Table 
                          522 link Description: 1, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          523 text ).
                      524 heading Decoupling of energy reserve consumption and bleaching resilience, Value: 3, ID: Sec15
                          525 text Decoupling of energy reserve consumption and bleaching resilience
                      526 container
                          527 text We found little evidence that energy-rich tissue reserves played a key role in promoting survival and rapid recovery from mass bleaching (Grottoli et al. 
                          528 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2196, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Palardy JE (2006) Heterotrophic plasticity and resilience in bleached corals. Nature 440:1186–1189
                          529 text ; Anthony et al. 
                          530 link Description: Reference 2009, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2199, Help: Anthony KRN, Hoogenboom MO, Maynard JA, Grottoli AG, Middlebrook R (2009) Energetics approach to predicting mortality risk from environmental stress: a case study of coral bleaching. Funct Ecol 23:539–550
                          531 text ). This was surprising as bleaching resistance and recovery of corals is typically associated with high levels of energy reserves (Anthony et al. 
                          532 link Description: Reference 2009, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2202, Help: Anthony KRN, Hoogenboom MO, Maynard JA, Grottoli AG, Middlebrook R (2009) Energetics approach to predicting mortality risk from environmental stress: a case study of coral bleaching. Funct Ecol 23:539–550
                          533 text ; Grottoli et al. 
                          534 link Description: Reference 2014, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2205, Help: Grottoli AG, Warner ME, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Schoepf V, McGinley M, Baumann J, Matsui Y (2014) The cumulative impact of annual coral bleaching can turn some coral species winners into losers. Glob Change Biol 20:3823–3833
                          535 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          536 link Description: Reference 2015b, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2208, Help: Schoepf V, Grottoli AG, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Baumann JH, Matsui Y, Warner ME (2015b) Annual coral bleaching and the long-term recovery capacity of coral. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 282:20151887
                          537 text ) which are often catabolized during bleaching to support metabolic energy needs (Rodrigues and Grottoli 
                          538 link Description: Reference 2007, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2212, Help: Rodrigues LJ, Grottoli AG (2007) Energy reserves and metabolism as indicators of coral recovery from bleaching. Limnol Oceanogr 52:1874–1882
                          539 text ). However, coral species differ in their efficiency to use energy reserves as alternative energy sources and often discriminate between different energy reserve pools (Grottoli et al. 
                          540 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2215, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Palardy JE (2006) Heterotrophic plasticity and resilience in bleached corals. Nature 440:1186–1189
                          541 text ; Rodrigues and Grottoli 
                          542 link Description: Reference 2007, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2218, Help: Rodrigues LJ, Grottoli AG (2007) Energy reserves and metabolism as indicators of coral recovery from bleaching. Limnol Oceanogr 52:1874–1882
                          543 text ; Levas et al. 
                          544 link Description: Reference 2013, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2221, Help: Levas SJ, Grottoli AG, Hughes A, Osburn CL, Matsui Y (2013) Physiological and biogeochemical traits of bleaching and recovery in the mounding species of coral Porites lobata: implications for resilience in mounding corals. PloS one 8(5):e63267
                          545 text ; Schoepf et al. 
                          546 link Description: Reference 2015b, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2224, Help: Schoepf V, Grottoli AG, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Baumann JH, Matsui Y, Warner ME (2015b) Annual coral bleaching and the long-term recovery capacity of coral. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 282:20151887
                          547 text ; Wall et al. 
                          548 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2227, Help: Wall CB, Ritson-Williams R, Popp BN, Gates RD (2019) Spatial variation in the biochemical and isotopic composition of corals during bleaching and recovery. Limnol Oceanogr 64:2011–2028
                          549 text ). Here, we found that this trait can also differ between populations of the same species occurring across fine-scale, strong environmental gradients (see also Kenkel et al. 
                          550 link Description: Reference 2013, Value: link.springer.com/a…, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2231, Help: Kenkel C, Meyer E, Matz M (2013) Gene expression under chronic heat stress in populations of the mustard hill coral (Porites astreoides) from different thermal environments. Mol Ecol 22:4322–4334
                          551 text ).
                      552 container
                          553 text In the subtidal, bleached corals mainly catabolized energy-poor carbohydrate stores during peak bleaching, but did not catabolize energy-rich lipid reserves, despite being severely bleached and likely in a state of resource limitation. Only one of these colonies survived the heat stress event (Fig. 
                          554 link Description: 3, Value: link.springer.com/a…
                          555 text , S2, Table S3), which is consistent with generally high mortality of the subtidal coral community during the 2016 bleaching event (Fig. S2, Schoepf et al. 
                          556 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2240, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          557 text ). In contrast, bleached intertidal corals largely maintained all three of their energy stores in April 2016 (Fig. 
                          558 link Description: 3, Value: …
                          559 text ), followed by rapid recovery within six months after peak bleaching. Although we observed these distinct environment-specific trends in energy reserve consumption, all bleached and recovered corals nevertheless had lower protein levels than healthy corals irrespective of environment and time (Fig. 
                          560 link Description: 3, Value: …
                          561 text a, b). This suggests that bleached corals generally catabolized this energy reserve during both bleaching and recovery, even though direct comparisons of bleached and healthy corals within each environment did not reveal significant catabolization of proteins in bleached corals. Furthermore, the significant interactive effect of environment and time for protein concentrations (Table S4) appears to be driven by declining protein levels in subtidal corals throughout recovery, while this was not the case for intertidal corals. Together, this suggests that even though both intertidal and subtidal corals catabolized protein levels, subtidal corals were likely not fully meeting their energetic demand, thus leading to the observed high mortality. Even though the visibly healthy corals in this study were exposed to heat stress, it is possible that differences in energy reserves could have been more pronounced between healthy and bleached corals within each environment if the former had not experienced any heat stress.
                      562 container
                          563 text Generally, the maintenance of lipid stores in bleached corals from both environments was surprising because it is often assumed that lipids are the primary source of nutrition during bleaching (Grottoli et al. 
                          564 link Description: Reference 2004, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2252, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Juarez C (2004) Lipids and stable carbon isotopes in two species of Hawaiian corals, Porites compressa and Montipora verrucosa, following a bleaching event. Mar Biol 145:621–631
                          565 text ) given their high energetic value compared to protein and carbohydrates (+ 40 and + 56%, respectively) (Gnaiger and Bitterlich 
                          566 link Description: Reference 1984, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2255, Help: Gnaiger E, Bitterlich G (1984) Proximate biochemical composition and caloric content calculated from elemental CHN analysis: a stoichiometric concept. Oecologia 62:289–298
                          567 text ). Furthermore, they constitute up to 40% of the total tissue biomass (Stimson 
                          568 link Description: Reference 1987, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2258, Help: Stimson JS (1987) Location, quantity and rate of change in quantity of lipids in tissue of Hawaiian hermatypic corals. Bull Mar Sci 41:889–904
                          569 text ; Grottoli et al. 
                          570 link Description: Reference 2004, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2261, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Juarez C (2004) Lipids and stable carbon isotopes in two species of Hawaiian corals, Porites compressa and Montipora verrucosa, following a bleaching event. Mar Biol 145:621–631
                          571 text ), serve as long-term energy reserves (Grottoli et al. 
                          572 link Description: Reference 2004, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2264, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Juarez C (2004) Lipids and stable carbon isotopes in two species of Hawaiian corals, Porites compressa and Montipora verrucosa, following a bleaching event. Mar Biol 145:621–631
                          573 text ) and are crucial for a successful reproduction cycle (Szmant and Gassman 
                          574 link Description: Reference 1990, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2268, Help: Szmant A, Gassman NJ (1990) The effects of prolonged “bleaching” on the tissue biomass and reproduction of the reef coral Montastrea annularis. Coral Reefs 8:217–224
                          575 text ; Hughes et al. 
                          576 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2271, Help: Hughes TP, Kerry JT, Baird AH, Connolly SR, Chase TJ, Dietzel A, Hill T, Hoey AS, Hoogenboom MO, Jacobson M (2019) Global warming impairs stock–recruitment dynamics of corals. Nature 568:387–390
                          577 text ) which heavily relies on lipid reserves (Ward et al. 
                          578 link Description: Reference 2002, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2274, Help: Ward S, Harrison P, Hoegh-Guldberg O (2002) Coral bleaching reduces reproduction of scleractinian corals and increases susceptibility to future stress. In: Proceedings of the ninth international coral reef symposium, Bali, 23–27 October 2000, vol 2. pp 1123–1128
                          579 text ). However, other studies have also shown that corals can maintain their individual energy pools irrespective of bleaching status during both experimental and natural heat stress (Levas et al. 
                          580 link Description: Reference 2013, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2277, Help: Levas SJ, Grottoli AG, Hughes A, Osburn CL, Matsui Y (2013) Physiological and biogeochemical traits of bleaching and recovery in the mounding species of coral Porites lobata: implications for resilience in mounding corals. PloS one 8(5):e63267
                          581 text ; Wall et al. 
                          582 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2280, Help: Wall CB, Ritson-Williams R, Popp BN, Gates RD (2019) Spatial variation in the biochemical and isotopic composition of corals during bleaching and recovery. Limnol Oceanogr 64:2011–2028
                          583 text ) and only partially consumed lipid stores during recovery (Wall et al. 
                          584 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2283, Help: Wall CB, Ritson-Williams R, Popp BN, Gates RD (2019) Spatial variation in the biochemical and isotopic composition of corals during bleaching and recovery. Limnol Oceanogr 64:2011–2028
                          585 text ). Importantly, not only biomass quality but also quantity can affect the bleaching mortality rate of corals (Thornhill et al. 
                          586 link Description: Reference 2011, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2287, Help: Thornhill DJ, Rotjan RD, Todd BD, Chilcoat GC, Iglesias-Prieto R, Kemp DW, LaJeunesse TC, Reynolds JM, Schmidt GW, Shannon T (2011) A connection between colony biomass and death in Caribbean reef-building corals. PLoS ONE 6:e29535
                          587 text ). Corals can experience a loss in biomass quantity during bleaching, while the quality can remain unchanged (Wall et al. 
                          588 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2290, Help: Wall CB, Ritson-Williams R, Popp BN, Gates RD (2019) Spatial variation in the biochemical and isotopic composition of corals during bleaching and recovery. Limnol Oceanogr 64:2011–2028
                          589 text ). In this study, tissue biomass quantity did not differ between healthy and bleached corals in each environment. It is surprising that most subtidal corals in our study not only bleached but mostly died as a consequence of the heat stress. Since this study only investigated total lipid amount, it is possible that relative changes in lipid metabolism, particularly in relation to storage vs. structural compounds, occurred (Imbs and Yakovleva 
                          590 link Description: Reference 2012, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2293, Help: Imbs AB, Yakovleva IM (2012) Dynamics of lipid and fatty acid composition of shallow-water corals under thermal stress: an experimental approach. Coral Reefs 31:41–53
                          591 text ). The preference for the consumption of carbohydrate stores during and after heat stress, as found in bleached subtidal corals (Fig. 
                          592 link Description: 3, Value: …
                          593 text c–d), has been observed in other studies (Schoepf et al. 
                          594 link Description: Reference 2015b, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2299, Help: Schoepf V, Grottoli AG, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Baumann JH, Matsui Y, Warner ME (2015b) Annual coral bleaching and the long-term recovery capacity of coral. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 282:20151887
                          595 text ; Wall et al. 
                          596 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2302, Help: Wall CB, Ritson-Williams R, Popp BN, Gates RD (2019) Spatial variation in the biochemical and isotopic composition of corals during bleaching and recovery. Limnol Oceanogr 64:2011–2028
                          597 text ). Given the low energetic value of carbohydrate and protein pools (Gnaiger and Bitterlich 
                          598 link Description: Reference 1984, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2306, Help: Gnaiger E, Bitterlich G (1984) Proximate biochemical composition and caloric content calculated from elemental CHN analysis: a stoichiometric concept. Oecologia 62:289–298
                          599 text ), bleached subtidal corals may have been limited in meeting their full metabolic energy needs over the duration of the bleaching event, resulting in high mortality by November 2016 (Fig. S2, Schoepf et al. 
                          600 link Description: Reference 2020, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2309, Help: Schoepf V, Jung MU, McCulloch MT, White N, Stat M, Thomas L (2020) Thermally variable, macrotidal reef habitats promote rapid recovery from mass coral bleaching. Front Mar Sci 7:245
                          601 text ).
                      602 container
                          603 text It generally remains poorly understood why some corals do not catabolize lipid or other energy reserves when bleached (Levas et al. 
                          604 link Description: Reference 2013, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2315, Help: Levas SJ, Grottoli AG, Hughes A, Osburn CL, Matsui Y (2013) Physiological and biogeochemical traits of bleaching and recovery in the mounding species of coral Porites lobata: implications for resilience in mounding corals. PloS one 8(5):e63267
                          605 text ; Schoepf et al., 
                          606 link Description: Reference 2013, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2318, Help: Schoepf V, Grottoli AG, Warner ME, Cai W-J, Melman TF, Hoadley KD, Pettay DT, Hu X, Li Q, Xu H (2013) Coral energy reserves and calcification in a high-CO2 world at two temperatures. PloS one. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0075049
                          607 text ; Wall et al. 
                          608 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2321, Help: Wall CB, Ritson-Williams R, Popp BN, Gates RD (2019) Spatial variation in the biochemical and isotopic composition of corals during bleaching and recovery. Limnol Oceanogr 64:2011–2028
                          609 text ). Heterotrophic feeding is one potential explanation that may have enabled corals from both environments to maintain their lipid stores (Grottoli et al. 
                          610 link Description: Reference 2006, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2324, Help: Grottoli AG, Rodrigues LJ, Palardy JE (2006) Heterotrophic plasticity and resilience in bleached corals. Nature 440:1186–1189
                          611 text ), and the generally highly turbid waters in the Kimberley region (Rosser and Veron 
                          612 link Description: Reference 2011, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2327, Help: Rosser NL, Veron JEN (2011) Australian corals thriving out of water in an extreme environment. Coral Reefs 30:21–21
                          613 text ; Richards et al. 
                          614 link Description: Reference 2015, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2331, Help: Richards ZT, Garcia RA, Wallace CC, Rosser NL, Muir PR (2015) A diverse assemblage of reef corals thriving in a dynamic intertidal reef setting (Bonaparte Archipelago, Kimberley, Australia). PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0117791
                          615 text ) suggest that particle feeding rates might be high in both environments. Furthermore, it is unlikely that feeding opportunities differed between intertidal and subtidal because long high-tide nights compensate for the brief aerial exposure of intertidal corals during evening low tides (V. Schoepf, pers. comm.). In addition, Wall et al. (
                          616 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2334, Help: Wall CB, Ritson-Williams R, Popp BN, Gates RD (2019) Spatial variation in the biochemical and isotopic composition of corals during bleaching and recovery. Limnol Oceanogr 64:2011–2028
                          617 text ) demonstrated that the maintenance of energy reserves during bleaching can be independent from feeding. In addition, it is possible that corals consumed energy reserves during early recovery (e.g., Schoepf et al. 
                          618 link Description: Reference 2015a, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2337, Help: Schoepf V, Stat M, Falter JL, McCulloch MT (2015a) Limits to the thermal tolerance of corals adapted to a highly fluctuating, naturally extreme temperature environment. Sci Rep 5:1–14
                          619 text , 
                          620 link Description: Reference b, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2340, Help: Schoepf V, Grottoli AG, Levas SJ, Aschaffenburg MD, Baumann JH, Matsui Y, Warner ME (2015b) Annual coral bleaching and the long-term recovery capacity of coral. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences 282:20151887
                          621 text ) which was not included in our sampling regime but that stores were replenished prior to November. Our findings highlight the complex interplay between coral nutritional pathways and tissue energy reserves in the context of bleaching resistance and recovery, and underpin the importance of investigating metabolic processes in bleached corals along strong environmental gradients.
                      622 heading Implications for future coral reef resilience, Value: 3, ID: Sec16
                          623 text Implications for future coral reef resilience
                      624 container
                          625 text The fact that heat-resistant corals from the highly variable intertidal were able to fully maintain their lipid reserves during bleaching provides hope for the persistence of extreme reef environments under rapid climate change. Bleaching often has long-lasting negative implications for the reproductive cycle of corals (Szmant and Gassman 
                          626 link Description: Reference 1990, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2352, Help: Szmant A, Gassman NJ (1990) The effects of prolonged “bleaching” on the tissue biomass and reproduction of the reef coral Montastrea annularis. Coral Reefs 8:217–224
                          627 text ; Hughes et al. 
                          628 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2355, Help: Hughes TP, Kerry JT, Baird AH, Connolly SR, Chase TJ, Dietzel A, Hill T, Hoey AS, Hoogenboom MO, Jacobson M (2019) Global warming impairs stock–recruitment dynamics of corals. Nature 568:387–390
                          629 text ), which heavily relies on lipid reserves (Ward et al. 
                          630 link Description: Reference 2002, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2358, Help: Ward S, Harrison P, Hoegh-Guldberg O (2002) Coral bleaching reduces reproduction of scleractinian corals and increases susceptibility to future stress. In: Proceedings of the ninth international coral reef symposium, Bali, 23–27 October 2000, vol 2. pp 1123–1128
                          631 text ). Intertidal corals may therefore be able to serve as brood stock for nearby reefs with high mortality and/or depleted lipid reserves and promote recruitment and recovery with heat-tolerant genotypes. Finally, natural migration of these more heat-tolerant coral larvae and the associated spread of heat-adapted alleles could ultimately enhance the persistence of coral reefs under future global warming (Morikawa and Palumbi 
                          632 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2361, Help: Morikawa MK, Palumbi SR (2019) Using naturally occurring climate resilient corals to construct bleaching-resistant nurseries. Proc Natl Acad Sci 116:10586–10591
                          633 text ). However, while corals from extreme environments are resistant to fluctuating stressors, Schoepf et al. (
                          634 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2364, Help: Schoepf V, Carrion SA, Pfeifer SM, Naugle M, Dugal L, Bruyn J, McCulloch MT (2019) Stress-resistant corals may not acclimatize to ocean warming but maintain heat tolerance under cooler temperatures. Nat Commun 10:1–10
                          635 text ) found that intertidal corals are highly vulnerable to future ocean warming, unless local physical parameters mediate bleaching susceptibility (Richards et al. 
                          636 link Description: Reference 2019, Value: …, ID: ref-link-section-d29278366e2368, Help: Richards ZT, Garcia R, Moore G, Fromont J, Kirkendale L, Bryce M, Bryce C, Hara A, Ritchie J, Gomez O (2019) A tropical Australian refuge for photosymbiotic benthic fauna. Coral Reefs 38:669–676
                          637 text ). This emphasizes the urgent need to rapidly restrict global CO 2  emissions in order to reduce further warming of the oceans.

                  69 heading Abstract, Value: 2
                      70 text Abstract
                  71 container section1
                      72 heading Background, Value: 3
                          73 text Background
                      74 text Premarital cohabitation is rampant and currently practiced worldwide, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. It is a known cause of marital instability and divorce. It is also associated with intimate partner violence and harms the psychology of children in later life. However, in Ethiopia, there has been limited attention given to premarital cohabitation.
                  75 container section2
                      76 heading Objective, Value: 3
                          77 text Objective
                      78 text The main goal of this study was to identify the determinants of time-to-premarital cohabitation among Ethiopian women.
                  79 container section3
                      80 heading Methods, Value: 3
                          81 text Methods
                      82 text The 2016 EDHS data was used to achieve the study’s goal. The survival information of 15683 women was analyzed based on their age at premarital cohabitation. The regional states of the women were used as a clustering effect in the models. Exponential, Weibull, and Log-logistic baseline models were used to identify factors associated with age at premarital cohabitation utilizing socioeconomic and demographic characteristics.
                  83 container section4
                      84 heading Results, Value: 3
                          85 text Results
                      86 text The median age of premarital cohabitation was found to be 18 years. Surprisingly, 72.7% of participants were cohabitated in the study area. According to the Log-logistic-Gamma shared frailty model, place of residence, occupation, educational status, and being pregnant were found to be factors determining the time to premarital cohabitation.
                  87 container section5
                      88 heading Conclusion, Value: 3
                          89 text Conclusion
                      90 text Premarital cohabitation among Ethiopian women was higher compared to women in the sub-Saharan Africa and East Africa. Place of residence, occupation, educational status, and being pregnant were found to be factors determining the time for premarital cohabitation. Therefore, we recommend the concerned bodies set out strategies to educate women about the influencing factors and dangers of premarital cohabitation.

                  132 container section1
                      133 heading Introduction, Value: 2
                          134 text Introduction
                      135 container
                          136 text Premarital cohabitation is defined as a woman and man living together and having a sexual relationship without being formally married [
                          137 link Description: 1, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          138 text ]. Some identified causes of premarital cohabitation include financial incapability, poor religious and moral values, and couples’ intention to test life [
                          139 link Description: 2, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          140 text ].
                      141 container
                          142 text In recent decades, premarital cohabitation has become more common around the world [
                          143 link Description: 3, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          144 text ]. It has been extensively examined from a demographic standpoint in various parts of the world, such as North America, Latin America, Western Europe, and Eastern Europe, where it has been observed to function as an alternative or stepping stone to marriage [
                          145 link Description: 4, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          146 text ]. In the United States of America (USA), about 70% of couples cohabited before their marriage [
                          147 link Description: 5, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          148 text ]. Cohabitation is also very common in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) [
                          149 link Description: 4, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          150 text ]. A study conducted in Nigeria found 65.2% of premarital cohabitation [
                          151 link Description: 6, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          152 text ]. In East Africa, about 44% of young women were cohabiting [
                          153 link Description: 7, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          154 text ]. Premarital cohabitation was frowned upon in Ethiopia and was regarded as a socially unacceptable practice [
                          155 link Description: 8, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          156 text ].
                      157 container
                          158 text When compared to married couples, cohabitated couples have a higher probability of divorce and exhibit inferior interpersonal skills and less predictable attitudes toward marriage [
                          159 link Description: 9, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          160 text ,
                          161 link Description: 10, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          162 text ]. Cohabitation may expose the couples to gender-based violence, particularly intimate partner violence [
                          163 link Description: 2, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          164 text ,
                          165 link Description: 11, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          166 text ]. As a result, cohabitation may alter an individual’s perceptions of marriage, making them less dedicated and devoted to the institution [
                          167 link Description: 12, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          168 text ]. Evidence shows that premarital cohabitation can decrease matrimonial satisfaction, increase unfaithfulness, and may cause dissolution or divorce among couples [
                          169 link Description: 13, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          170 text –
                          171 link Description: 16, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          172 text ]. Premarital cohabitation can also result in reproductive health problems such as unwanted pregnancy and sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) [
                          173 link Description: 2, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          174 text ]. In addition, marriage after premarital cohabitation can detriment the mental health of the couple [
                          175 link Description: 17, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          176 text ]. Besides its effect on the couple’s life, premarital cohabitation can cause various psychological, social, and economic traumas for their future children [
                          177 link Description: 15, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          178 text ,
                          179 link Description: 18, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          180 text ].
                      181 container
                          182 text The socio-demographic and economic status of individuals is the known influencer of premarital cohabitation. According to a study conducted in the USA, lower education, weak religious values, and poor backgrounds were found to be inducing factors in premarital cohabitation [
                          183 link Description: 5, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          184 text ]. Similarly, socio-demographic factors, including age, level of education, religion, wealth index, and residence place, showed a significant association with premarital cohabitation, according to a systematic review conducted in SSA [
                          185 link Description: 4, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          186 text ]. Another demographic study conducted in East Africa identified age, religion, educational status, occupational status, wealth index, and Ugandan women as determinants of premarital cohabitation [
                          187 link Description: 7, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          188 text ]. Economic insufficiencies such as lack of shelter (accommodation) and poverty are also determining premarital cohabitation [
                          189 link Description: 19, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                          190 text ].
                      191 text Despite its rising nature and noted negative life outcomes among couples and their children, premarital cohabitation gets little attention from the scientific community, particularly in Ethiopia. Hence, the current study was intended to fill the literature gap by investigating the determinants of time-to-premarital cohabitation among Ethiopian women using the parametric shared frailty models. The findings of this study can benefit individuals and policymakers in understanding the influencers of premarital cohabitation.
                  192 container section2
                      193 heading Materials and methods, Value: 2
                          194 text Materials and methods
                      195 container section1
                          196 heading Data source, Value: 3
                              197 text Data source
                          198 container
                              199 text The information for this study came from the Ethiopian Demographic and Health Survey data (EDHS-2016). For this study, the 2016 EDHS sample was selected using a stratified, two-stage cluster sampling design, and house-to-house cross-sectional survey data extracted from the 2016 EDHS were used [
                              200 link Description: 20, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                              201 text ]. Since this study was observational, we have used a "Strengthening the reporting of observational studies in epidemiology (StroBE) statement: guidelines for reporting observational studies." to report the methodical flows and findings (
                              202 link Description: S1 File, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                              203 text ).
                      204 heading Study population and variables, Value: 3
                          205 text Study population and variables
                      206 container section1
                          207 heading Study population., Value: 4
                              208 text Study population.
                          209 text In the families of selected clusters (regions), a total of 15,683 women between the ages of 10 and 43 were identified. As a result, the risk variables for women’s premarital cohabitation were examined in this study, which included 15,683 women.
                          210 container
                              211 text Study variables. Outcome variable :—The time to premarital cohabitation among Ethiopian women, assessed in years, is the response variable in this study. It is calculated as the time between birth and the age of first cohabitation. For this study, cohabited women were an event of interest, and women who did not participate in the event (not cohabited) were censored.
                          212 container
                              213 text Independent factors :—Place of residence, education status, occupation, wealth index, pregnancy, and religion were all believed to have an impact on women’s time for premarital cohabitation.
                      214 container section3
                          215 heading Statistical analysis, Value: 3
                              216 text Statistical analysis
                          217 text Descriptive analysis and shared frailty models were applied to achieve the main goal of the study and draw significant conclusions.

It was done with all significant factors from the univariable analysis.
                  285 container section3
                      286 heading Results, Value: 2
                          287 text Results
                      288 container section1
                          289 heading Descriptive analysis, Value: 3
                              290 text Descriptive analysis
                          291 container
                              292 text The study included a total of 15,683 women from nine regional states and two city administrations. This study was interested in the time interval between the woman’s birth date and the time of cohabitation. About 11,405 (72.7%) of study participants had experienced the occurrence (cohabited). Premarital cohabitation occurred at a median age of 18 years, with a minimum and maximum observed event time of 10 and 43 years, respectively. Premarital cohabitation was most common among women under the age of 15 years, with 1653 (10.5 percent) of them (
                              293 link Description: Table 1, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                              294 text ).

                          307 container
                              308 text In this study, the AIC value of the Log-logistic-Gamma shared frailty model (65144.36) was found to be the lowest of all shared frailty models, indicating that the Log-logistic-Gamma shared frailty model is the most efficient model for describing time-to-premarital cohabitation data (
                              309 link Description: Table 2, Value: journals.plos.org/p…

                          319 link Description: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0303206.t002, Value: doi.org/10.1371/jou…
                          320 container
                              321 text Women’s education, occupation, pregnancy, and place of residence were significant covariates of premarital cohabitation, according to an analysis based on a Log-logistic-Gamma shared frailty model; however, wealth index and religion were not. The women’s survival duration of premarital cohabitation was shortened by a factor of ( ɸ =  0.714, 0.455, and 0.385) for primary, secondary, and higher education, respectively, at a 5% level of significance. In other words, women who have completed at least primary school have a shorter premarital cohabitation survival period than the reference group. For pregnant women, premarital cohabitation survival time was shortened by a factor of ( ɸ =  0.826), at a 5% level of significance. An acceleration factor larger than one suggests that premarital cohabitation is being prolonged.
                          322 container
                              323 text Accordingly, women who had occupation ( ɸ =  1.095) and women of rural Ethiopia ( ɸ =  1.138) have prolonged time to premarital cohabitation when compared to their corresponding reference categories. In other words, they have a higher expected survival time than their corresponding reference categories. The frailty in this model is assumed to follow a Gamma distribution with a mean of 1 and a variance equal to theta ( θ ). The heterogeneity in the population of the region that was used as a cluster was estimated by the selected model is  θ  = 0.524 and the dependence within the clusters (region) is measured by Kendall’s tau at  τ  = 0.207 (20.7%). A variance of zero ( θ  = 0) would indicate that the frailty component does not contribute to the model. A likelihood ratio test for the hypothesis  θ  = 0 is shown at the bottom of 
                              324 link Description: Table 3, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                              325 text  and indicates that a chi-square value of 434.66 with one degree of freedom resulted in a highly significant  p- value <0.001. This implied that the frailty component had a significant contribution to the model. The estimate of the shape parameter in the Log-Logistic-Gamma shared frailty model is  γ  = 8.405. This value shows the shape of the hazard function is unimodal because the value is greater than unity, i.e., it increases up to some time and then decreases (
                              326 link Description: Table 3, Value: journals.plos.org/p…
                              327 text ).
